0.title: Ecclesiastes: Fear God and Keep His Commandments
0.overview:
The message. Ecclesiastes is God’s honest word about life in a fallen world. It looks hard at everything people live for (pleasure, work, money, wisdom, success) and finds that none of it lasts: all of it is “vanity” (1:2), a breath that is real but cannot be held, and death takes it all away. Yet the same God who makes us feel that emptiness gives the good things of life as gifts to enjoy from his hand, and calls us to fear him, because he will judge every deed. The book clears away every false hope, so that we build our lives on God alone: “Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole duty of man” (12:13).

Background: the Preacher. The book opens, “The words of the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem” (1:1). “Preacher” translates the Hebrew Qoheleth, a title rather than a name: one who gathers an assembly to speak to it, and who gathers wise sayings (12:9). The description fits Solomon, son of David, to whom “God gave … wisdom and understanding beyond measure” (1 Kings 4:29), and who reigned over all Israel from about 970 to 930 BC. If anyone could have made life under the sun work, it was he. Yet “when Solomon was old his wives turned away his heart after other gods” (1 Kings 11:4).

Did Solomon write it? Christians who hold the book to be God’s word differ here. Most readers through the church’s history took Solomon as the author, and the book claims his experience: “I the Preacher have been king over Israel in Jerusalem” (1:12). But many scholars, including conservative ones such as Franz Delitzsch and E. J. Young, hold that a later wise man wrote in Solomon’s person. They note that the book never names him; that he speaks of “all who were over Jerusalem before me” (1:16), when only David had reigned there before him as king of Israel; and that its Hebrew is late, with a word borrowed from Persian (pardes, “parks”, 2:5). Defenders of Solomon’s authorship reply that Jerusalem had kings long before David, such as Melchizedek and Adoni-zedek (Genesis 14:18; Joshua 10:1), and that a book’s wording could be updated in copying. This commentary’s view is that the question cannot be settled, and need not be: the book gives us Solomon’s search, in his own words or set down in his person by a later wise man, framed by the voice that speaks at the end (12:9–14). Its authority rests not on a human name but on God, for these words are “given by one Shepherd” (12:11).

When and where. If Solomon wrote it, it comes from Jerusalem late in his reign, about 940 BC. Those who think a later writer used Solomon’s voice usually place it after the exile, when Judah was a small province of the Persian empire. Either way, it speaks to anyone, anywhere: it says almost nothing of Israel’s history and never uses God’s covenant name, the LORD; it speaks of “God”, the Creator with whom every human being must reckon.

The kind of writing. Ecclesiastes is wisdom literature, like Job and Proverbs, mixing the Preacher’s own story (chapters 1–2), poems (3:1–8; 12:1–7) and short proverbs (chapters 7 and 10). Two phrases are its keys. Vanity translates the Hebrew hebel, “mist” or “breath”. “All is vanity” does not first mean that life is worthless, but that everything is breath: real, like your breath on a cold morning, and gone when you try to grasp it. Under the sun, which comes twenty-eight times, is the Preacher’s vantage point: life as anyone can see it, looking no higher than this world.

How to read the hard sayings. Some sayings startle: “man has no advantage over the beasts” (3:19); “the dead know nothing” (9:5). Some scholars read the Preacher as a sceptic whose doubts the closing voice corrects; others hear him chiefly as a preacher of joy. This commentary reads him as a believing wise man who shows life as it looks from under the sun alone, to strip away false hopes, and whose words the closing voice commends: “uprightly he wrote words of truth” (12:10). Each hard saying is true to what can be seen from here, read in the light of the whole book, which also says that “the spirit returns to God who gave it” (12:7). The Preacher does not deny life after death; he says no one can prove it from under the sun.

How the book makes its case. The question that drives the book comes first: “What does man gain by all the toil at which he toils under the sun?” (1:3). In the first half (1:12–6:12) the Preacher searches: wisdom, pleasure, great works and wealth (1:12–2:11), and finds that death levels the wise and the fool (2:12–23). Then the first light breaks in: eating, drinking and enjoying one’s toil is “from the hand of God” (2:24). God “has put eternity into man’s heart” (3:11), yet hides the whole of his work. The Preacher faces oppression, envy and the love of money (chapters 4–6). The second half (7:1–12:7) gives wisdom for living when we cannot see the whole: “better” sayings, justice delayed, death faced squarely and the fullest call to joy (chapters 7–10); bold generosity in an uncertain world (11:1–6); and a call to the young to rejoice and to “Remember also your Creator in the days of your youth” (12:1). The verdict returns (12:8), and the closing voice gives the conclusion (12:9–14). All along, the call to joy keeps returning (2:24–26; 3:12–13; 5:18–20; 8:15; 9:7–10; 11:7–10), and the fear of God grows from a quiet thread (3:14; 5:7; 8:12–13) into the last word.

Where it leads: to Christ. Ecclesiastes holds no direct prophecy of Christ; it leads to him chiefly by the need it exposes. Paul uses the Greek Old Testament’s word for hebel when he says that “the creation was subjected to futility” (Romans 8:20), but adds what cannot be seen from under the sun: “in hope that the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption” (Romans 8:20–21). The Preacher asked what gain there is in toil; because Christ rose, Paul could say, “in the Lord your labor is not in vain” (1 Corinthians 15:58). He asked who knows where the spirit goes (3:21); Christ “abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel” (2 Timothy 1:10). He warned that God will judge every deed (12:14), and admitted that “there is not a righteous man on earth who does good and never sins” (7:20); the Judge God has appointed (Acts 17:31) is the one who bore judgment for sinners. And the wisest son of David asked the questions, while Jesus, the greater Son of David, said, “something greater than Solomon is here” (Matthew 12:42). The Shepherd who gave the Preacher’s words came in person: “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11).

For us. Ecclesiastes tells a restless age the truth it hides: we are dust, the clock is running, and nothing we chase under the sun can bear the weight of a soul. It frees us from asking good things to be God. Work, money, pleasure and love are breath when we live for them, and gifts when we receive them from his hand. So a Christian can “eat your bread with joy” (9:7) and work with all his might (9:10), not anxiously, because in Christ toil is not lost and death has lost its sting. And the book brings us to the God we must all meet. Fear him, and run to the Shepherd who was judged in his sheep’s place, for “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1).

1.title: Vanity of Vanities: What Does Man Gain?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Verdict and the Endless Round
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Preacher gives his verdict first and his question second: all is breath, so what does anyone gain from a lifetime of toil (vv. 1–3)? Then he lets creation answer. Generations come and go while the earth stays; the sun, the wind and the streams move endlessly and arrive nowhere (vv. 4–7). The same restlessness lives in us, for the eye and the ear are never satisfied (v. 8). Nothing is truly new, and no one is remembered by those who come after (vv. 9–11). Seen from under the sun alone, the world is a treadmill.
verseByVerse.theology: Life seen only from under the sun is constant movement that never gets anywhere, and the book makes us feel that before it shows us any way out.

verseByVerse.quote: The words of the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These are the words of the wisest and most successful man of his age, a son of David and king in Jerusalem.

The words of the Preacher. A title rather than a name, Qoheleth: someone who gathers people to listen, and gathers sayings, “weighing and studying and arranging many proverbs with great care” (12:9). Here is a man speaking to an assembly about the most serious questions a human being can ask.

The son of David, king in Jerusalem. The book never names Solomon, and it may be meant to be read as written in his voice rather than signed by him (see the introduction). But the description fits only one son of David who reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel (v. 12), the king to whom “God gave … wisdom and understanding beyond measure” (1 Kings 4:29). That is the point: the man about to say that everything under the sun is vanity is no failure grumbling in a corner. If anyone could have made life under the sun work, it was he.

Something greater than Solomon. “Something greater than Solomon is here”, Jesus said (Matthew 12:42). The wisest son of David asks the question, and the greater Son of David is the answer.

Uncertain wording. The exact sense of Qoheleth is not certain. It is related to the Hebrew word for an assembly (see the note), and the ESV footnote offers “Convener” or “Collector” as other renderings; its unusual feminine form, used of a man, may mark an office. The likely meaning is one who gathers an assembly and speaks to it, which “Preacher” conveys well.
verseByVerse.note: Qoheleth is related to the Hebrew word for an assembly, the gathering he addresses.

verseByVerse.quote: Vanity of vanities, says the Preacher, vanity of vanities! All is vanity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything is breath: real, but impossible to hold, and none of it can bear the weight of a soul.

Vanity of vanities. Before a single argument, the verdict. The phrase is built like “king of kings” or “holy of holies”: vanity at its utmost, said twice.

All is vanity. The word is hebel, a “mist” or “mere breath” (see the note), and it is the key to the whole book. “All is vanity” does not first say that everything is worthless. It says that everything is breath: real, as your breath on a cold morning is real, but grasp it and your hand closes on nothing. That is a more precise and more painful diagnosis than “life is pointless”: work, pleasure, wisdom, wealth, reputation and youth cannot bear the weight of a soul that leans on them. James uses the same picture for life itself: “For you are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes” (James 4:14).

Says the Preacher. The phrase is spoken about him, not by him. That voice is heard again in 7:27 and at the end (12:8–14), and it frames the whole book.
verseByVerse.note: “Vanity” translates hebel: literally a mist, vapor or mere breath — something fleeting (ESV note). It appears five times in this verse and in 29 other verses of the book.

verseByVerse.quote: What does man gain by all the toil at which he toils under the sun?
verseByVerse.commentary:
After a lifetime of work, what is left over that lasts? From under the sun alone, the answer is nothing.

What does man gain? The question that drives the book. “Gain” is what is left over when everything is added up.

All the toil at which he toils under the sun. “Toil” is the whole effort of a life, with the sweat God spoke of to Adam: “cursed is the ground because of you; in pain you shall eat of it all the days of your life” (Genesis 3:17). “Under the sun” is where the Preacher stands to look: life as anyone can see it, looking no higher than this world. From there alone his answer, for now, is nothing, and if this life is all there is, he is right. Jesus asked the same question more sharply: “For what will it profit a man if he gains the whole world and forfeits his soul?” (Matthew 16:26).

Not in vain. After Christ rose from the dead, Paul could write the sentence that answers verse 3: “Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain” (1 Corinthians 15:58). Under the sun, toil evaporates. In the Lord, it does not. Ecclesiastes does not yet say that; it makes us feel our need of it.

Can’t we simply make our own meaning? Many thoughtful people today accept the diagnosis and shrug at the question: meaning is not found but made, and it is braver to make it than to wait for a God to hand it out. Albert Camus gave that view its most memorable form in The Myth of Sisyphus. Sisyphus is condemned to roll his stone up the hill for ever and watch it roll down again, the treadmill of verses 4 to 7 in a single picture, and Camus ends by saying that we must imagine Sisyphus happy. Notice the word imagine. The Preacher will not pretend. A meaning I give my life is only as strong as I am, and it goes into the grave with me: breath holding up breath. This book does not argue the sceptic out of his honesty; it makes him more honest still, until he feels the full weight of verse 3. And the gospel does not ask anyone to imagine anything. It points to an empty tomb, and says that because one man came back, nothing done in the Lord is lost.
verseByVerse.note: “Under the sun” — life viewed from this world alone — occurs 28 times in the book.

verseByVerse.quote: A generation goes, and a generation comes, but the earth remains forever. The sun rises, and the sun goes down, and hastens to the place where it rises. The wind blows to the south and goes around to the north; around and around goes the wind, and on its circuits the wind returns. All streams run to the sea, but the sea is not full; to the place where the streams flow, there they flow again.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Creation is a treadmill: generations, sun, wind and streams are always moving and never arriving, and human toil has the same shape.

A generation goes, and a generation comes. Read the dates in any cemetery: generation after generation walked these streets, and the streets outlasted them. Man was made to rule the earth, and the earth outlives him.

The sun rises, and the sun goes down. Psalm 19 sees the sun as a strong man who “runs its course with joy” (Psalm 19:5). The Preacher feels its weariness: “hastens” may be rendered “returns panting” (ESV note), back round to do it all again.

Around and around goes the wind. The wind goes round and the streams run on. Every part of creation is busy, and none of it arrives. Human toil has the same shape: you get up, work, sleep and do it again, and the inbox fills back up.

Is this how God sees the world? Not finally. The same sun “knows its time for setting” because God appointed it (Psalm 104:19). Paul says creation really was “subjected to futility” after the fall, but “because of him who subjected it, in hope” (Romans 8:20). The treadmill is real; it is not the last word.

verseByVerse.quote: All things are full of weariness; a man cannot utter it; the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The weariness moves inside us: our eyes and ears take in more and more and are never satisfied.

All things are full of weariness. The world is more tiring than words can say: “a man cannot utter it”. And our appetite, which ought to be content with what it takes in, never is. “The eye is not satisfied with seeing.” Scroll through another hundred images and the eye wants the next one; hear the new song and the ear is already waiting for another.

Never satisfied. Proverbs says the same with a darker comparison: “Sheol and Abaddon are never satisfied, and never satisfied are the eyes of man” (Proverbs 27:20). The grave is never full, and neither is the human heart.

A clue, not a defect. We were made with an appetite that nothing under the sun can fill, and that is a clue. Jesus stood by a well and said, “Everyone who drinks of this water will be thirsty again, but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again” (John 4:13–14). Of anything you hope will finally satisfy, ask: has anything like it ever satisfied you for long?

verseByVerse.quote: What has been is what will be, and what has been done is what will be done, and there is nothing new under the sun. Is there a thing of which it is said, "See, this is new"? It has been already in the ages before us. There is no remembrance of former things, nor will there be any remembrance of later things yet to be among those who come after.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Under the sun nothing is truly new and no one is remembered; real newness comes from God, and God does not forget.

Nothing new. Technology changes; the human story does not. The same pride, lust, greed and grief are acted out in every generation with new props, and the claim to be new is itself very old.

“See, this is new.” Only one voice in Scripture can truly say it. At the end of the Bible, the one seated on the throne says, “Behold, I am making all things new” (Revelation 21:5). Newness does not come up from under the sun but down from God, and it has already begun: “if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come” (2 Corinthians 5:17).

There is no remembrance. The hardest line: you will be forgotten. Try naming your great-great-grandparents. Under the sun, even the memory of a life is breath. The believer’s comfort is not that history will remember him, but that God will.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that “former things” and “later things” may be rendered “former people” and “later people”; the Hebrew does not say which. Either way, neither what was done nor those who did it will be remembered.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–18 — The King Who Searched and Found Sorrow
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king searched everything by wisdom and found that wisdom can diagnose the world but cannot cure it. He gave himself wholly to the search, and found it an unhappy business that God has laid on human beings (vv. 12–13). Everything he saw was breath and a feeding on wind: the crooked cannot be straightened, and what is missing cannot be supplied (vv. 14–15). Even his unrivalled wisdom, set against madness and folly, only multiplied his sorrow (vv. 16–18).
verseByVerse.theology: Wisdom can see how broken the world is, but it cannot mend it. Only the one who made the world can make the crooked straight.

verseByVerse.quote: I the Preacher have been king over Israel in Jerusalem. And I applied my heart to seek and to search out by wisdom all that is done under heaven. It is an unhappy business that God has given to the children of man to be busy with.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king gave his whole self to understanding life by wisdom, and found the search an unhappy business that God himself has given.

I the Preacher have been king. Having shown us the world, the Preacher tells his own story, as a man with every advantage for the search: a throne, wealth, time and the best minds of the kingdom at his call.

I applied my heart. In Hebrew the heart is the centre of a person’s inner life, mind, will and emotions together (ESV note). He gave all of himself to understanding life, “by wisdom”, the best tool human beings have.

An unhappy business. Here God is named for the first time in the book. It is God who has given this business, and the Preacher calls it unhappy. The drive to understand our lives is itself a burden, because we ask questions we cannot answer. Yet he does not say there is no God; he says God has laid this weight on us, and he feels it. Faith in Ecclesiastes is not the absence of hard questions. It is holding on to God while asking them.

verseByVerse.quote: I have seen everything that is done under the sun, and behold, all is vanity and a striving after wind. What is crooked cannot be made straight, and what is lacking cannot be counted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom can see what is wrong with the world but cannot put it right: what is crooked stays crooked, and what is missing cannot be supplied.

Striving after wind. The verdict of verse 2 returns with a new picture, “a feeding on wind” (see the note), as in Hosea: “Ephraim feeds on the wind and pursues the east wind all day long” (Hosea 12:1). Try to live on wind, and you starve.

What is crooked. Wisdom can diagnose but not cure. It sees that a marriage is bent, a nation corrupt, a heart twisted, and cannot straighten them or add back what is missing. Later the Preacher will say who made things crooked: “Consider the work of God: who can make straight what he has made crooked?” (7:13). No man can, but God can. When John the Baptist prepared the way for Christ, the promise was that “the crooked shall become straight, and the rough places shall become level ways” (Luke 3:5). What wisdom cannot mend, the Lord who came can.

In everyday life. Think of the thing you have tried longest to straighten. Verse 15 is not despair. It is permission to stop pretending you can fix it alone, and to bring it to him.
verseByVerse.note: “Striving after wind” may be rendered “a feeding on wind” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: I said in my heart, "I have acquired great wisdom, surpassing all who were over Jerusalem before me, and my heart has had great experience of wisdom and knowledge." And I applied my heart to know wisdom and to know madness and folly. I perceived that this also is but a striving after wind. For in much wisdom is much vexation, and he who increases knowledge increases sorrow.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even the greatest human wisdom only multiplies sorrow, because it sees more of what is wrong without the power to mend it.

I have acquired great wisdom. Not idle boasting: Solomon “was wiser than all other men” (1 Kings 4:31), and he lays out his credentials so that his conclusion cannot be dismissed. He studied wisdom and folly alike, like someone reading every philosophy on the shelf for the key, and even that was chasing wind.

In much wisdom is much vexation. The more you know, the more it hurts. The child is happy in the car because he does not know about the mortgage; the doctor knows what the shadow on the scan means. To know what is wrong, with no way of putting it right, only sharpens the pain.

Where human wisdom ends. So Paul says that “the world did not know God through wisdom”, and “it pleased God through the folly of what we preach to save those who believe” (1 Corinthians 1:21). Human wisdom climbs to the top of the ladder and finds only sorrow there. God comes down, and when he came, he took the sorrow on himself. The one who knew every heart and every grief was “a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief” (Isaiah 53:3). He carried the sorrow of knowing, so that those who come to him might find in him what the Preacher could not find under the sun: “Christ Jesus, who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption” (1 Corinthians 1:30).

1.overview:
Where we are. This is the opening of the book. Before a single argument, the Preacher gives his verdict and asks the question the whole of Ecclesiastes will pursue, and then begins to tell the story of his own search.

The message. Everything under the sun is breath: real, but impossible to hold. Nature turns on its endless rounds, human appetite is never satisfied, nothing is truly new and no one is remembered; and even the best human wisdom can see what is wrong with the world without being able to put it right. God is telling us honestly that this world, taken on its own, cannot give a human life lasting gain.

Why it was said. The Preacher speaks to people who expect work, wisdom and success to give life its meaning, and he speaks as the one man who had all of them (see the introduction). He clears away false hopes so that his hearers will look to God alone.

How the chapter makes its case. The title presents the speaker, a son of David and king in Jerusalem (v. 1). The verdict comes first, “All is vanity” (v. 2), and then the driving question, “What does man gain?” (v. 3). Creation is shown as a treadmill: generations, sun, wind and streams all moving and none arriving (vv. 4–7). The weariness moves inside us, to eyes and ears that are never satisfied (v. 8), and nothing is new and no one is remembered (vv. 9–11). Then the king tells his story: he searched everything by wisdom, found the search an unhappy business given by God (vv. 12–13), found that the crooked cannot be straightened (vv. 14–15), and found that more wisdom brings more sorrow (vv. 16–18).

Where it leads. To Christ chiefly by the need the chapter exposes. The Preacher asks what gain there is in toil; because Christ rose, “in the Lord your labor is not in vain” (1 Corinthians 15:58). He finds nothing new under the sun; the risen Christ says, “Behold, I am making all things new” (Revelation 21:5). He finds that wisdom cannot straighten what is crooked; Christ Jesus “became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption” (1 Corinthians 1:30). And the wisest son of David asks the question, while the greater Son of David is the answer (Matthew 12:42).

For us. Stop asking breath to carry the weight of your soul: no job, achievement, experience or legacy can. Let your restlessness send you to Christ, who gives water after which you “will never be thirsty again” (John 4:14), and then do your work in him, knowing that nothing done in the Lord is lost.
1.theology:
Life viewed only under the sun yields no lasting gain (v. 3). Creation has been subjected to futility since the fall, but in hope of being set free (Rom 8:20-21), and the Preacher never says that there is no God; he says that God has given this burden (v. 13).

Human wisdom can diagnose what is crooked but cannot straighten it (v. 15; 7:13). God does what wisdom cannot: the crooked is made straight in the coming of Christ (Luke 3:5), who makes all things new (Rev 21:5; 2 Cor 5:17), and in whom labour is not in vain (1 Cor 15:58).

The restless eye (v. 8) shows that people are made for more than the world can give (John 4:13-14). The wisest son of David asks the question; something greater than Solomon is its answer (Matt 12:42; 1 Cor 1:30).
1.examples:
Your breath on a cold morning is the Preacher's picture: visible and real, and gone when you try to grasp it.

The treadmill of verses 4-11 is familiar today. The inbox fills back up as soon as it is cleared, and the eye scrolls on for the next image without ever being satisfied. Few of us can name our great-great-grandparents, and few will be able to name us.

The sorrow of knowledge is familiar too. The child is happy in the back of the car because he does not know about the mortgage; the parent in the front seat does.

keyVerse.quote: What does man gain by all the toil at which he toils under the sun?
keyVerse.note: This is the question that drives the whole book, asked straight after the verdict of verse 2. The rest of the chapter answers it from under the sun: nothing that lasts. Only the resurrection of Christ gives the answer that toil in the Lord is not in vain.

1.reflection:
The Preacher says that everything is “vanity”, a breath that is real but cannot be held (v. 2). Which things in your life are you most tempted to lean your whole weight on? What happens when you try?

“The eye is not satisfied with seeing” (v. 8). Where do you see this restless appetite in our culture, and in yourself? Why might it be a clue rather than simply a defect?

Many people today say that we must make our own meaning in life. How does verse 3 answer that, and how does the resurrection of Christ answer verse 3 (1 Corinthians 15:58)?

“What is crooked cannot be made straight” (v. 15). What have you been trying to straighten by your own wisdom or effort? What would it look like to bring it to Christ instead?

2.title: The King's Experiment: Pleasure, Greatness and the Hand of God

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Experiment with Pleasure and Greatness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The greatest king of his age tested everything the world offers, and found that seizing it brings nothing that lasts. He tried pleasure, laughter and wine, keeping his head as he went (vv. 1–3). He made great works: houses, vineyards, gardens and pools, slaves and herds, silver and gold, singers and concubines (vv. 4–8). He became greater than all before him, denied his eyes nothing, and enjoyed his toil (vv. 9–10). Then he looked at it all and found nothing gained under the sun (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: The man who had everything the world can offer is the best witness that the world cannot satisfy.

verseByVerse.quote: I said in my heart, "Come now, I will test you with pleasure; enjoy yourself." But behold, this also was vanity. I said of laughter, "It is mad," and of pleasure, "What use is it?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pleasure pursued as the meaning of life is empty: laughter is good, but it has no answer when asked what life is for.

I will test you with pleasure. Chapter 1 ended with more knowledge bringing more sorrow, so the Preacher tries the obvious alternative: if thinking hurts, start enjoying. It is a deliberate test, and he gives the result before describing what he did: “this also was vanity”.

I said of laughter, “It is mad.” Laughter is good; the Preacher is no killjoy, as the end of this chapter will prove. But laughter pursued as the meaning of life is mad. Everyone knows the party where the laughter gets louder as the evening goes on and emptier with every glass. Pleasure offers itself as the answer to life, but asked “What use is it?”, it has nothing to say.

Lovers of pleasure. Our culture has rerun the experiment on a vast scale, with the same result. Paul’s description of the last days includes people who are “lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God” (2 Timothy 3:4). Pleasure is a wonderful gift and a cruel god.

verseByVerse.quote: I searched with my heart how to cheer my body with wine—my heart still guiding me with wisdom—and how to lay hold on folly, till I might see what was good for the children of man to do under heaven during the few days of their life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king tasted wine and folly deliberately, keeping his head, to find what is truly good for people in their few short days.

My heart still guiding me with wisdom. This is not a man falling into drunkenness but a scientist experimenting on himself. He wants to know one thing: what is actually “good for the children of man to do under heaven during the few days of their life”? Life is short, and Moses prayed, “So teach us to number our days that we may get a heart of wisdom” (Psalm 90:12).

A warning. Many have told themselves they could taste folly while keeping their head. Most cannot. The prodigal son also went looking for life in a far country and “squandered his property in reckless living” (Luke 15:13).

verseByVerse.quote: I made great works. I built houses and planted vineyards for myself. I made myself gardens and parks, and planted in them all kinds of fruit trees. I made myself pools from which to water the forest of growing trees. I bought male and female slaves, and had slaves who were born in my house. I had also great possessions of herds and flocks, more than any who had been before me in Jerusalem. I also gathered for myself silver and gold and the treasure of kings and provinces. I got singers, both men and women, and many concubines, the delight of the sons of man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He built and gathered everything the world calls delight, as if to make Eden again with his own hands.

I made great works. Now he tries achievement. Listen to the repeated words: “I made”, “I built”, “for myself”, “I made myself”. He builds a private paradise, as if he could build Eden again with his own hands.

The delight of the sons of man. Then come slaves and livestock, silver and singers: people, money, art and sex, “the delight of the sons of man”. He had every delight. Scripture records that “King Solomon excelled all the kings of the earth in riches and in wisdom” (1 Kings 10:23). This list is the modern dream fully achieved. Most people never get it, and imagine that if they did, they would be satisfied. The Preacher got it.

Does the Bible approve his slaves and concubines? No. It records them as a king’s excess, not as a model. The law told Israel’s king not to multiply wives or silver and gold (Deuteronomy 17:17), and Solomon’s wives “turned away his heart after other gods” (1 Kings 11:4). Slavery in Israel was a regulated institution of a fallen world, not God’s design; the gospel makes slave and free one in Christ (Galatians 3:28) and condemns man-stealing (1 Timothy 1:10). And the garden he built for himself could not bring back Eden. Only Christ opens paradise again (Luke 23:43), where the tree of life stands by the river of God (Revelation 22:1–2).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew behind “many concubines” is a rare phrase found nowhere else, and its meaning is uncertain (ESV note). Older translations guessed at musical instruments or cups; most modern ones take it of women, which suits the phrase that follows, “the delight of the sons of man”, and Solomon’s many wives and concubines (1 Kings 11:3).

verseByVerse.quote: So I became great and surpassed all who were before me in Jerusalem. Also my wisdom remained with me. And whatever my eyes desired I did not keep from them. I kept my heart from no pleasure, for my heart found pleasure in all my toil, and this was my reward for all my toil. Then I considered all that my hands had done and the toil I had expended in doing it, and behold, all was vanity and a striving after wind, and there was nothing to be gained under the sun.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He reached the top with his judgment intact, enjoyed the work, and found that the enjoyment was all it paid: nothing was left over.

So I became great. He reached the top and kept his head while doing it. The experiment was not spoiled by a man who lost his judgment on the way up.

My heart found pleasure in all my toil. He is honest: it was enjoyable. But see the limit: “this was my reward”. The enjoyment he had while working was the only wages the work paid. Once it was spent, nothing was left over.

Then I considered. Everything he dreamed of stands finished in front of him, and he feels nothing. The athlete stands on the podium and wonders why it is not enough; the executive reaches the corner office and lies awake.

The rich fool. Jesus told of a rich man who did exactly what the Preacher did, and said to his soul, “relax, eat, drink, be merry.” “But God said to him, ‘Fool! This night your soul is required of you, and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?’” (Luke 12:19–20). Moses saw the same truth from the other side, choosing the people of God rather than “the fleeting pleasures of sin”, “for he was looking to the reward” (Hebrews 11:25–26). Ask it plainly of your own ambitions: if you had all of it, what would you have?

The disappointment of arrival. The psychologist Tal Ben-Shahar has a name for what the Preacher felt: the arrival fallacy, the belief that once we reach the goal we will be happy at last. We reach it, the happiness is thinner and shorter than it promised, and so we set the next goal. But underneath ambition there is usually a quieter hope: if I build this, I will matter. That is why arrival hurts. The houses and gardens were real; it was the hope beneath them that was breath. Religious people run the same race on a different track, piling up good works as proof that they count, and find the same emptiness. The gospel reverses the order. In Christ a person is given his worth at the start, before the work, so the work no longer has to tell him who he is. Then he can build and plant and succeed with real joy, because none of it has to save him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–17 — Wise and Fool Die Alike
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wisdom really is better than folly, yet it cannot save a man from the grave or from being forgotten. The king weighs the two, and wisdom wins as light wins over darkness: the wise see where they walk (vv. 12–14). But the same death comes to the wise and the fool, and both are soon forgotten, so all his wisdom seems pointless to him (vv. 15–16). Seen from under the sun alone, life becomes hateful to him (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: Wisdom is better than folly for living, but under the sun it cannot answer death.

verseByVerse.quote: So I turned to consider wisdom and madness and folly. For what can the man do who comes after the king? Only what has already been done. Then I saw that there is more gain in wisdom than in folly, as there is more gain in light than in darkness. The wise person has his eyes in his head, but the fool walks in darkness. And yet I perceived that the same event happens to all of them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom is truly better than folly for walking through life, but it cannot stop the road ending in the same grave.

Wisdom and madness and folly. Pleasure failed, so he weighs wisdom against madness and folly. No one after him can run the experiment on a bigger scale, so no one else need try.

More gain in wisdom than in folly. The Preacher is not against wisdom. A wise person sees where he is walking; the fool walks into walls. Every word of Proverbs stands: for living, wisdom brings real “gain”, the same word as in 1:3.

And yet. “The same event”, which he will name in a moment, is death. The wise and the fool walk different roads to the same grave.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I said in my heart, "What happens to the fool will happen to me also. Why then have I been so very wise?" And I said in my heart that this also is vanity. For of the wise as of the fool there is no enduring remembrance, seeing that in the days to come all will have been long forgotten. How the wise dies just like the fool! So I hated life, because what is done under the sun was grievous to me, for all is vanity and a striving after wind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Facing a death that levels the wise and the fool, and a forgetting that swallows both, the Preacher hates life seen from under the sun.

Why so very wise? The question becomes personal. He spent his life becoming wise, the fool across the street did nothing, and both will be buried. It is the student who worked hard beside the one who never did, watching both fail the same exam.

No enduring remembrance. Worse than death is being forgotten, and the cry is almost a lament. Psalm 49 says the same: “For he sees that even the wise die; the fool and the stupid alike must perish and leave their wealth to others” (Psalm 49:10).

Under the sun. He hated life “under the sun”, seen from that level alone. Hold on to those three words. Everything under the sun ends in death. But God has not left us there: “it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment” (Hebrews 9:27), and Christ came to “deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery” (Hebrews 2:15).

So I hated life. The Preacher does not pretend. Some readers know what it is to lie awake and feel exactly this, and it matters that God put these words in his book. You are not the first believer to feel it, and the feeling is not the end of the story. If it has become a wish not to live, tell someone you trust today and seek help at once; God gives doctors, friends and pastors for such nights.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Work done under the sun alone ends in despair, because the worker must hand everything over at death. The king hates his toil, since he must leave it all to a successor who may be a fool, yet will be master of it (vv. 18–19). He gives his heart up to despair at the injustice of one person labouring and another enjoying the fruit (vv. 20–21). Work done for self brings sorrow by day and sleeplessness by night (vv. 22–23).
verseByVerse.theology: Everything gathered for self is finally handed to someone else.

verseByVerse.quote: I hated all my toil in which I toil under the sun, seeing that I must leave it to the man who will come after me, and who knows whether he will be wise or a fool? Yet he will be master of all for which I toiled and used my wisdom under the sun. This also is vanity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything he built must pass to a successor he cannot control, who may squander it.

The man who will come after me. A man spends forty years building a business, and his heir sells it in three; a woman saves all her life, and relatives she barely knew fight over the estate.

Rehoboam. For a son of David these words are painful. Solomon’s own son Rehoboam came to the throne and “answered the people harshly, and forsaking the counsel that the old men had given him” (1 Kings 12:13), and the kingdom his father had built was torn in two. “Who knows whether he will be wise or a fool?” Solomon did not know. Nobody does.

The only safe inheritance. “Man heaps up wealth and does not know who will gather!” (Psalm 39:6). The only safe inheritance is one that cannot be squandered: “lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys and where thieves do not break in and steal” (Matthew 6:20).

verseByVerse.quote: So I turned about and gave my heart up to despair over all the toil of my labors under the sun, because sometimes a person who has toiled with wisdom and knowledge and skill must leave everything to be enjoyed by someone who did not toil for it. This also is vanity and a great evil. What has a man from all the toil and striving of heart with which he toils beneath the sun? For all his days are full of sorrow, and his work is a vexation. Even in the night his heart does not rest. This also is vanity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Work done for self alone ends in despair: sorrow by day, no rest by night, and the fruit handed to someone else.

A great evil. The Preacher reaches the bottom of his despair. It is wrong that skill, wisdom and years of labour should be handed to someone who did nothing; under the sun there is no justice in inheritance.

What has a man from all the toil? The question of 1:3 returns, this time with the cost added. Work done for self alone consumes the worker. His days are sorrow, his work is vexation, and “Even in the night his heart does not rest.” Anyone who has lain awake in the small hours running through the numbers knows this verse.

He gives to his beloved sleep. The psalmist names the cure: “It is in vain that you rise up early and go late to rest, eating the bread of anxious toil; for he gives to his beloved sleep” (Psalm 127:2). The sleepless night is not a sign that you care enough. It is often a sign that you are carrying what only God can carry.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–26 — Nothing Better: From the Hand of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What cannot be seized from the world can be received as a gift from God. For the first time the Preacher says there is nothing better than to eat, drink and enjoy one’s toil, because these come from the hand of God, and without him no one can truly enjoy anything (vv. 24–25). God gives wisdom, knowledge and joy to the one who pleases him, while the sinner gathers only to hand it on (v. 26). Even so, the gifts themselves are breath: good, but not God.
verseByVerse.theology: Joy cannot be seized from the world; it is received from the hand of God.

verseByVerse.quote: There is nothing better for a person than that he should eat and drink and find enjoyment in his toil. This also, I saw, is from the hand of God, for apart from him who can eat or who can have enjoyment?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Food, drink and work cannot be seized as life’s meaning, but received from the hand of God they are good gifts, truly enjoyed.

Nothing better. And then, suddenly, light. These words open the first of several such passages in the book (3:12–13, 22; 5:18–20; 8:15; 9:7–10), the thread of hope running through it.

From the hand of God. What has changed? One phrase. The experiment of verses 1–11 tried to seize enjoyment from the world, and it evaporated. Here enjoyment is received from God as a gift, and it is good. The same bread and wine, the same work, taste different when they come from a Father’s hand. The ESV notes that “find enjoyment” may be rendered “make his soul see good”: God opens the soul’s eyes to the good in front of it.

Not the rich fool’s merriment. This is not the rich fool’s “eat, drink, be merry”, which leaves God out. It is Paul’s “God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy” (1 Timothy 6:17), and “whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31).

For apart from him who can eat or who can have enjoyment? Without God, no one can truly enjoy anything; the rich man with every delight could not. Enjoyment is God’s to give: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above” (James 1:17). Tonight’s supper can be received that way.

Two ways to ruin a pleasure. There are two ways to spoil God’s gifts, and both are alive today. The old moralist treats pleasure as suspect and feels safer the less he delights in anything. Our culture makes pleasure the point of life, and expects the next meal, holiday or romance to deliver what the last one did not. They look like opposites, but they share a root. The moralist refuses pleasure to prove that he is good; the hedonist demands it to prove that his life is worth living. Both are using the gift to save themselves, and both lose the taste of it. G. K. Chesterton ended Orthodoxy by saying that joy, which was the small publicity of the pagan, is the gigantic secret of the Christian. The Preacher has stumbled on the secret. Received from the hand of God, a meal is neither a temptation nor a saviour. It is a Father’s gift, and it can be enjoyed to the full precisely because no one is asking it to be God.

Textual note. Most Hebrew manuscripts read “apart from me”; the ESV follows others in reading “apart from him”, which makes the point directly: enjoyment is God’s to give.

verseByVerse.quote: For to the one who pleases him God has given wisdom and knowledge and joy, but to the sinner he has given the business of gathering and collecting, only to give to one who pleases God. This also is vanity and a striving after wind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gives wisdom, knowledge and joy to the one who pleases him, while the sinner gathers only to hand it on; yet even these gifts are breath, good but not God.

To the one who pleases him. Two people, two gifts. To the one who pleases God, “wisdom and knowledge and joy”: the very things the king could not get by his own effort. To the sinner, the busy work of gathering, only to hand it all over to someone else. Proverbs has the same pattern: “the sinner’s wealth is laid up for the righteous” (Proverbs 13:22).

Who pleases God? Not the one who earns it, but the one who trusts him: “without faith it is impossible to please him” (Hebrews 11:6). The joy offered here belongs to a person who has stopped trying to wring meaning out of the world and received it from God.

This also is vanity. The closing words probably refer to the sinner’s gathering, but they also keep the reader honest: even God’s good gifts under the sun are breath. The meal ends, the joy passes. They are good, and they are not God. So the psalmist: “Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you” (Psalm 73:25).

2.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 1 ended with the king finding that more wisdom brings more sorrow. Now he runs an experiment no one else could afford, testing pleasure, achievement and wealth on a royal scale, and then weighing wisdom itself against death.

The message. What we try to seize from the world turns to breath in our hands, but what we receive from the hand of God can be enjoyed. Pleasure, great works and wealth cannot give lasting gain; wisdom is better than folly, yet the wise man dies and is forgotten like the fool, and leaves his labour to someone else. Then the first light of the book breaks in: food, drink and work are good gifts, enjoyed by those who please God.

Why it was said. Every age believes that the right mix of pleasure, success and money will satisfy. The Preacher speaks as the one who had them all (see the introduction), so that no one need waste a life finding out.

How the chapter makes its case. The king tests pleasure and laughter, and finds them empty (vv. 1–3). He builds, gathers and denies his eyes nothing (vv. 4–10), and when he looks at it all, nothing is gained (v. 11). He weighs wisdom against folly: wisdom is better, as light is better than darkness, but the same death comes to both, and the wise are forgotten like fools, so he hates life (vv. 12–17). He hates his toil, because he must leave it to someone who may be a fool, and he gives his heart up to despair (vv. 18–23). Then: nothing is better than to eat, drink and enjoy one’s toil, for this is “from the hand of God”, who gives wisdom, knowledge and joy to the one who pleases him (vv. 24–26).

Where it leads. To Christ by the need the chapter exposes and by contrast. The son of David built himself a garden and found it could not bring back Eden; the greater Son of David opens paradise again (Luke 23:43). The king could not make his work outlast him or secure an heir who would not squander it; in Christ believers receive “an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading” (1 Peter 1:4). And the joy the Preacher glimpses as God’s gift is given in full in him, “who richly provides us with everything to enjoy” (1 Timothy 6:17).

For us. Ask honestly what you expect your pleasures, achievements and savings to do for you. If they are meant to save you, they will fail you. Received with thanks from a Father’s hand, tonight’s supper and tomorrow’s work can be truly enjoyed, because none of them has to be God.
2.theology:
Pleasure and achievement pursued as the meaning of life cannot satisfy (vv. 1-11; Luke 12:15-21). Wisdom is genuinely better than folly, but it cannot overcome death (vv. 13-16; Ps 49:10); only Christ delivers from the fear of death (Heb 2:14-15).

Enjoyment is a gift from the hand of God, not a prize seized from the world (vv. 24-25; Jas 1:17; 1 Tim 6:17). The same things that are vanity when a person lives for them become good when received from God with thanksgiving (1 Tim 4:4). God gives joy to those who please him, and the sinner's gathering passes to others (v. 26; Prov 13:22).
2.examples:
The Preacher's experiment is still being run. The athlete stands on the podium and wonders why it is not enough; the heir sells in three years the business his father built over forty; the owner lies awake in the small hours running through the numbers.

The answer of verses 24-26 is just as ordinary. The same supper that could be another grab at pleasure can be received tonight as a gift from a Father's hand, with thanks.

keyVerse.quote: There is nothing better for a person than that he should eat and drink and find enjoyment in his toil. This also, I saw, is from the hand of God, for apart from him who can eat or who can have enjoyment?
keyVerse.note: After the king’s great experiment ends in emptiness, this is the book’s first ray of light. The difference is one phrase, “from the hand of God”: what could not be seized from the world can be received as a gift. It is the first of the passages that call God’s people to joy throughout the book.

2.reflection:
The king tested pleasure, achievement and wealth on a scale few could imagine (vv. 1–11). Which of these do you most expect to satisfy you? What does verse 11 say to that hope?

Verses 12–17 say that wisdom is truly better than folly, yet the wise die like fools. How can both be true? How does the gospel change the way we face death and being forgotten?

The Preacher hated that he must leave his work to someone who might squander it (vv. 18–21). What are you building that you cannot control after you are gone? What does it mean to lay up treasure in heaven (Matthew 6:20)?

What changes when food, drink and work are received “from the hand of God” (v. 24) rather than seized from the world? What would it look like for you to enjoy God’s gifts this week without asking them to be God?

3.title: A Time for Everything, and Eternity in the Heart

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — A Time for Every Matter Under Heaven
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Every part of human life has its appointed time, and the times are in God’s hand. “For everything there is a season, and a time for every matter under heaven” (v. 1). Fourteen pairs of opposites follow, covering the whole of life as “day and night” covers all of time: birth and death, planting and uprooting, killing and healing, weeping and laughing, embracing and refraining, keeping and casting away, silence and speech, love and hate, war and peace (vv. 2–8). The poem is not fatalism but wisdom: we cannot choose our seasons, but we can learn to discern which one we are in and act rightly in it.
verseByVerse.theology: Every moment of a human life has its appointed time, and the one who appoints the times is God.

verseByVerse.quote: For everything there is a season, and a time for every matter under heaven:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every event in life has its appointed time, and God is the one who appoints it.

For everything there is a season. Usually heard as gentle poetry about life’s rhythms, in the Preacher’s mouth it is stronger. Chapter 1 showed the world going round; chapter 3 shows that the round is not random, and who appointed it: “He has made everything beautiful in its time” (v. 11).

Cage or comfort. That can feel like a cage or a comfort, depending on who you believe sets the times. The psalmist, surrounded by enemies, found it a comfort: “My times are in your hand” (Psalm 31:15).

Does “a time for everything” mean fatalism? No. It is wisdom about discerning the right moment: there is a time to plant and a time to uproot, and the wise know which. God appoints the times (v. 11), and we are still responsible for how we act in them.

verseByVerse.quote: a time to be born, and a time to die; a time to plant, and a time to pluck up what is planted; a time to kill, and a time to heal; a time to break down, and a time to build up;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Life is made of seasons we do not choose, and wisdom acts rightly in each.

A time to be born, and a time to die. The list begins at the edges of life, with two appointments no one chooses. Then comes the farmer’s year: plant in the wrong season and the crop is lost, however hard you work.

A time to kill. This is no licence for private violence. Scripture gives the sword to rightful authority, for justice: “Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed” (Genesis 9:6), and the ruler “does not bear the sword in vain” (Romans 13:4). There is a time when justice or defence requires it, and a time when healing is called for.

A time to break down, and a time to build up. A rotten house must sometimes come down before a sound one is built; so with habits, churches and hearts.

verseByVerse.quote: a time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance; a time to cast away stones, and a time to gather stones together; a time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing;
verseByVerse.commentary:
There are times for tears and for laughter, for holding close and for letting go, and love learns which time it is.

Weep and laugh. The Christian life is not a permanent smile: Jesus wept at the grave of his friend. Wisdom knows which time it is: “Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15). Telling a grieving friend to cheer up is not faith. It is getting the time wrong.

Casting away and gathering stones. Set beside embracing and refraining from embracing, the pair suggests coming close and holding back: a time to hold someone near and a time to let them go.

Uncertain wording. The meaning of casting away and gathering stones is not certain. It may picture clearing a field and collecting stones for a wall; other explanations have been offered.

verseByVerse.quote: a time to seek, and a time to lose; a time to keep, and a time to cast away; a time to tear, and a time to sew; a time to keep silence, and a time to speak; a time to love, and a time to hate; a time for war, and a time for peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Losing and mending, silence and speech, love and hate, war and peace each have their time, and history is moving towards God’s peace.

Seek and lose. There is a time to look for what is lost, and a time to accept that it is gone. Anyone who has emptied a parent’s house after a death knows both halves in a single afternoon.

Tear and sew. Tearing a garment was the sign of grief in Israel (see mourning customs); sewing is the work of mending, when the worst of the grief has passed. The next pair belongs with them, for grief has its time to be quiet and its time to speak. Job’s friends did best in the first seven days, when they sat with him and said nothing (Job 2:13). Yet there are also moments when silence is cowardice, and love must speak.

Love and hate. “A time to hate” startles us, but Scripture does not ask us to feel nothing about evil: “Abhor what is evil; hold fast to what is good” (Romans 12:9). The psalmist could say, “Do I not hate those who hate you, O LORD?” (Psalm 139:21). A person who cannot hate cruelty does not truly love its victims.

A time for peace. The list ends with peace, towards which God is bringing history. The time the whole Bible looks towards is “the fullness of time”, when “God sent forth his Son” (Galatians 4:4). Jesus lived by his Father’s times: “My hour has not yet come” (John 2:4), and at the end, “Father, the hour has come” (John 17:1). “At the right time Christ died for the ungodly” (Romans 5:6).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God has made us for eternity and given us a few years, so we are to receive his gifts with joy and fear him. The Preacher asks his old question, “What gain has the worker from his toil?” (v. 9), and sees that God has given the business of life (v. 10). God has made everything beautiful in its time and put eternity into man’s heart, yet we cannot find out the whole of his work (v. 11). So there is nothing better than to rejoice, do good and enjoy God’s gift of food and work (vv. 12–13). God’s work endures, so that people fear him, and he seeks out what has passed (vv. 14–15).
verseByVerse.theology: We are made for eternity and cannot see it whole; God's gifts are to be received now, and God himself feared.

verseByVerse.quote: What gain has the worker from his toil? I have seen the business that God has given to the children of man to be busy with.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Our work cannot change God’s seasons, but the business of life is not an accident: God has given it.

What gain has the worker from his toil? After the poem, the question of 1:3 again. If God has set every time, what can our work add? We cannot change the seasons; we plant when it is time to plant and die when it is time to die. So where is the gain?

The business that God has given. In 1:13 he called the business of life “unhappy”; here he simply says God has given it. The work of life is not an accident but an assignment, and the one who assigned it knows why.

verseByVerse.quote: He has made everything beautiful in its time. Also, he has put eternity into man's heart, yet so that he cannot find out what God has done from the beginning to the end.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has a design in every season and has made us for eternity, yet he hides the whole of his work, so we must trust what we cannot see.

Beautiful in its time. Does that include weeping, losing and dying? Not as if death were lovely: it is still “the last enemy to be destroyed” (1 Corinthians 15:26). The claim is that even these times are held within God’s design and are not wasted. People speak of a tapestry seen from behind, all knots and loose threads; but we may not see the front in this life, and those who grieve need not pretend that they do. Joseph lived more than twenty years on the wrong side of it, and at the end could say to his brothers, “you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (Genesis 50:20). Most of us are not shown so much, yet Paul’s promise holds in the dark: “we know that for those who love God all things work together for good” (Romans 8:28).

Eternity in the heart. This is why we cannot be content with the treadmill of chapter 1. Animals do not ask what their life means; people do. We long for love not to end, for justice to be done, for the dead not to be lost. God put that longing there, and it is why nothing under the sun satisfies.

The limit. But the same verse sets a limit. We have eternity in the heart and a few decades in the hand: we sense that there is a whole and cannot see it. Only God is “declaring the end from the beginning” (Isaiah 46:10). So we see, as Paul says, “in a mirror dimly, but then face to face” (1 Corinthians 13:12).

Eternity entered our few decades. The longing for eternity is finally a longing for God. The eternal Son entered our few decades, so that people with eternity in their hearts and dust in their bodies could have eternal life in him (John 17:3). He said, “I am the resurrection and the life” (John 11:25).

Why does a secular age still feel homesick? The modern world tells us that this life is all there is, and we cannot quite be content with it. The novelist Julian Barnes, who does not believe, opened his book on death by admitting that he does not believe in God but misses him. People sure there is nothing beyond the grave still speak at funerals as though the dead could hear, still feel that a betrayal is wrong and not merely unwelcome, still stand under a night sky and feel small in a way close to worship. These are usually explained as leftovers, habits from a religious past or tricks of evolution. The Preacher says God put them there. The ache does not prove God by itself, but it is a signpost: why should a creature made only for time keep longing for what time cannot give? Augustine’s restless heart and our own secular homesickness are the same thing, and both point to the same door.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “eternity” (olam) usually means a long or unending time, as most modern translations take it. The KJV reads “he hath set the world in their heart”, giving it a later sense, and other meanings have been suggested. “Eternity” fits both the usual sense and the verse.

verseByVerse.quote: I perceived that there is nothing better for them than to be joyful and to do good as long as they live; also that everyone should eat and drink and take pleasure in all his toil—this is God's gift to man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since we cannot see the whole, we are to be joyful, do good and receive daily food and work as God’s gifts.

To be joyful and to do good. The second “nothing better” passage (the first is 2:24). Joy and doing good belong together. Joy without doing good is selfish; doing good without joy is grim. “As long as they live”: not someday, when the whole picture makes sense, but now.

God’s gift to man. Meals, drink and daily work are “God’s gift to man”. A person who cannot see how his life fits together can still thank God for the bread tonight. That is faith in its daily form: “For everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving” (1 Timothy 4:4).

verseByVerse.quote: I perceived that whatever God does endures forever; nothing can be added to it, nor anything taken from it. God has done it, so that people fear before him. That which is, already has been; that which is to be, already has been; and God seeks what has been driven away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s work endures and cannot be improved or undone, so that people fear him, and nothing in the past escapes him.

Whatever God does endures forever. Human work evaporates; God’s work stands, and no one can improve on it or undo it. “The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever” (Isaiah 40:8).

So that people fear before him. The first mention of the fear of God in the book, and where it will end (12:13). When a person sees that his own work is breath and God’s is permanent, the right response is reverent awe. The fear of God is not terror before a tyrant. It is taking God seriously as God.

What has been driven away. The first half echoes 1:9. The past seems chased away by time, but God goes after it and calls it to account, as the next verses on judgment confirm: nothing done in time escapes him.

God seeks the lost. Many Christians also hear a wider truth that Scripture states elsewhere, though it is not the Preacher’s point here. God seeks the lost: “I will seek the lost, and I will bring back the strayed” (Ezekiel 34:16), and his Son came on that errand: “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost” (Luke 19:10).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew is literally “what has been pursued” (ESV note), a compressed phrase. It most likely means the past, which God seeks out and calls to account; some take it of the persecuted, whom God seeks to vindicate.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–22 — Injustice, Judgment and the Dust
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Injustice and death are real under the sun, but God will judge, and only he knows what lies beyond the grave. The Preacher sees wickedness even in the courts, and holds on to the truth that God will judge both righteous and wicked in his time (vv. 16–17). God tests people to show them that they are creatures: man and beast share the same breath, die alike and return to the same dust (vv. 18–20). No one under the sun can see where the spirit goes (v. 21), so a man should rejoice in his work as his portion, since no one can show him what will come after (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: Under the sun, man and beast die alike; but God, who is above the sun, will judge, and the spirit returns to him.

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, I saw under the sun that in the place of justice, even there was wickedness, and in the place of righteousness, even there was wickedness. I said in my heart, God will judge the righteous and the wicked, for there is a time for every matter and for every work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wickedness sits even in the courts of justice, but God will judge the righteous and the wicked, and his day is coming.

In the place of justice. From the beauty of God’s times to injustice in the worst place of all, the courtroom. When the judge is corrupt, where can the wronged go?

God will judge. Here he looks beyond what can be seen under the sun. The verdict too has its time, and the corrupt judge has his own day in court coming.

The day and the judge. The New Testament names the day and the judge: God “has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed; and of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead” (Acts 17:31). For the oppressed, that is the best news there is. For all of us, it is a reason to flee to the judge while he is offering mercy, for the one who will judge is the one who died for sinners.

Is final judgment a cruel idea? Many would rather believe in a universe that forgives everything or notices nothing. But stand in a courtroom where the judge has been bought, and the question changes. The Polish poet Czesław Miłosz, who lived through Nazi occupation and communist rule, turned Marx on his head: the real opium of the people, he argued, is not the hope of heaven but the belief that there is nothing after death, the great comfort of thinking that our betrayals, greed and cruelty will never be judged. Without final judgment, every torturer who died in his bed simply got away with it, which is no kindness to his victims. Judgment is good news for the oppressed. It is hard news for all of us too, since every heart has its own verdict to fear, and there the gospel surprises. The Judge has come down from the bench to bear the sentence himself, so that the day which will put the world right can be, for those who trust him, a day without dread.

verseByVerse.quote: I said in my heart with regard to the children of man that God is testing them that they may see that they themselves are but beasts. For what happens to the children of man and what happens to the beasts is the same; as one dies, so dies the other. They all have the same breath, and man has no advantage over the beasts, for all is vanity. All go to one place. All are from the dust, and to dust all return.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God humbles our pride by showing that, as far as the eye can see, we die like the beasts and return to dust.

Like the beasts. God tests people to let them see that in themselves they are creatures, as mortal as the animals. Pride says, we are the masters of the world. Death answers, you are creatures. “Man in his pomp yet without understanding is like the beasts that perish” (Psalm 49:20).

As one dies, so dies the other. From under the sun this is simply true: a man and a dog both stop breathing. “When you take away their breath, they die and return to their dust” (Psalm 104:29).

All go to one place. It is the grave, as God said to Adam: “for you are dust, and to dust you shall return” (Genesis 3:19). The Preacher wants his hearers to feel it, because only a person who knows he is dust will look to God for life. He is describing what can be seen, the body going to the grave like an animal’s, not denying what lies beyond (see the note on v. 21).

verseByVerse.quote: Who knows whether the spirit of man goes upward and the spirit of the beast goes down into the earth?
verseByVerse.commentary:
From under the sun no one can prove where the spirit goes at death; what sight cannot settle, God has revealed in Christ.

Who knows? The Preacher does not deny that the spirit goes upward; he says observation cannot settle it, and lets the question sting. But he will say at the end that “the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it” (12:7). What sight cannot establish, God has revealed.

Someone has come back. Christ Jesus “abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel” (2 Timothy 1:10). Paul knew where the believer’s spirit goes: “we would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord” (2 Corinthians 5:8). The dying thief heard it from Christ himself: “today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). The Preacher’s “Who knows?” is a real question, and it finds its answer in Jesus.

Where Christians differ. Does verse 20, “All go to one place”, mean that the dead simply cease, or sleep unaware until the resurrection? Some sincere Christians have read this verse and 9:5 that way, wanting to honour the plain words. Most Christians have answered that the Preacher describes what can be seen: the body goes to the grave like an animal’s.

This commentary’s view. This commentary holds, with the Westminster Confession (32.1) and the 1689 London Baptist Confession (31.1), two seventeenth-century statements of Reformed belief whose sections on death say this, that the souls of believers go at death to be with Christ, awake and at rest, awaiting the resurrection of the body (Philippians 1:23).

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that the verse may be rendered “Who knows the spirit of man, which goes upward”, close to the KJV, which reads it as a statement that the spirit does go upward. The difference lies in how one small Hebrew letter is read, as “whether” or as “which”.

verseByVerse.quote: So I saw that there is nothing better than that a man should rejoice in his work, for that is his lot. Who can bring him to see what will be after him?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since no one can see what comes after him, a man should gladly do today’s work as the portion God has given him.

Rejoice in his work. His work is his “lot”, the share God has assigned him.

Not resignation but freedom. The person who must see how everything turns out will never be at peace; the one who does today’s work gladly and leaves the future with God can rest. Paul put it this way: “Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward” (Colossians 3:23–24).
