3.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 2 ended with the first light of the book: joy received as a gift “from the hand of God” (2:24). Now the Preacher looks at time itself, and the God who holds it.

The message. Every moment of life has its time, and God has appointed them all. He has put eternity into our hearts, so that nothing under the sun can satisfy us, yet he hides the whole of his work, so that we cannot see how it fits together. So we are to receive his daily gifts with joy, fear him, and trust him to judge what is wrong, for from under the sun we are dust, and only God knows what lies beyond.

Why it was said. The Preacher speaks to people who want to control their lives and see the whole picture (see the introduction). He teaches them to live within God’s times rather than against them.

How the chapter makes its case. The poem sets out fourteen pairs of opposites: every part of life has its season (vv. 1–8). The old question returns (v. 9), and the answer is God: he has made everything beautiful in its time and put eternity into man’s heart, yet we cannot find out the whole of his work (vv. 10–11). So there is nothing better than to rejoice, do good and receive God’s gifts (vv. 12–13), and to fear the God whose work endures and who seeks out what is past (vv. 14–15). Facing injustice in the very courts, the Preacher holds on to the truth that God will judge (vv. 16–17). From under the sun man and beast die alike, and no one can see where the spirit goes (vv. 18–21), so a man should rejoice in his work as his portion (v. 22).

Where it leads. To Christ by the character of God revealed in him and by the need the chapter exposes. The God of the times sent his Son “when the fullness of time had come” (Galatians 4:4). The eternity God put in our hearts finds its answer in the eternal Son, who entered our few decades to give eternal life (John 17:3). The judgment the Preacher longs for is fixed on a day, by “a man whom he has appointed” (Acts 17:31). And “Who knows?” (v. 21) is answered by the one who “abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel” (2 Timothy 1:10).

For us. Your times are in God’s hand, so you need not see the whole picture to live faithfully today. Weep and laugh in their seasons, do good, thank God for your bread, and leave the rest with him. And fear him, for he will judge; but run to Christ, the Judge who died for sinners, and the day of judgment holds no dread.
3.theology: God appoints every time of human life and holds even its sorrows within his design (vv. 1-11; Rom 8:28). He has set eternity in the human heart, so that nothing that passes away can satisfy, while keeping the whole of his purpose beyond our sight (v. 11; 1 Cor 13:12). His work endures and calls for reverent fear, and nothing in the past escapes him (vv. 14-15). He will judge the righteous and the wicked (v. 17), on a day he has fixed, through the risen Christ (Acts 17:31). Under the sun man dies like the beasts (vv. 18-20); the question of v. 21 is answered in 12:7 and fully in the gospel (2 Tim 1:10).
3.examples:
Then: the Preacher's hearers lived by the farmer's year, and he used it to teach that every part of life has its time, set by God.

Now: we cannot choose most of our seasons, but we can learn to recognise them. A visit to a friend in grief is a time to weep, not to hurry them on. And tomorrow morning's ordinary work can be done gladly, as the share God has given, without knowing how everything will turn out.

keyVerse.quote: He has made everything beautiful in its time. Also, he has put eternity into man’s heart, yet so that he cannot find out what God has done from the beginning to the end.
keyVerse.note: The verse holds together the chapter’s comfort and its limit. God has a design in every season, and he has made us for more than time, which is why nothing under the sun satisfies us. Yet he hides the whole from us, so that we must trust him rather than see it all.

3.reflection:
Read the poem of verses 1–8 slowly. Which “time” are you in at the moment? Is it a comfort or a struggle to believe that God has appointed it (Psalm 31:15)?

“He has put eternity into man’s heart” (v. 11). Where do you see this longing in yourself and in people around you, even in those who do not believe? How does Christ answer it?

The Preacher’s answer to not seeing the whole picture is to be joyful, do good, receive God’s gifts and fear him (vv. 12–14). Which of these comes hardest to you, and why?

Verses 16–17 say that God will judge, and the New Testament says he will do it through Christ (Acts 17:31). Why is that good news for the oppressed? How can it also be good news for us?

4.title: Tears, Envy and the Threefold Cord

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Tears with No One to Comfort
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The oppressed weep with no one to comfort them, and the sight is so heavy that the Preacher envies the dead. He sees all the oppressions done under the sun: the tears of the oppressed, power on the side of the oppressors, and twice, “no one to comfort them” (v. 1). From under the sun alone the weight is crushing, and he calls the dead more fortunate than the living, and the unborn, who have never seen such evil, more fortunate still (vv. 2–3). Scripture does not look away from this grief, and neither should we.
verseByVerse.theology: Under the sun, the oppressed have no comforter; the God of all comfort is the answer the chapter longs for.

verseByVerse.quote: Again I saw all the oppressions that are done under the sun. And behold, the tears of the oppressed, and they had no one to comfort them! On the side of their oppressors there was power, and there was no one to comfort them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Preacher looks squarely at the tears of the oppressed, who have no one to comfort them.

The tears of the oppressed. God will judge (3:17), but judgment is future and the tears are now, so he looks again and sees the faces: the worker cheated of wages, the widow whose land was taken, the prisoner beaten.

No one to comfort. He says it twice, and the repetition is a cry. Lamentations has the same grief: “my eyes flow with tears; for a comforter is far from me” (Lamentations 1:16).

Comfort for the oppressed. The Bible does not look away, and Christians must not either: “Remember those who are in prison, as though in prison with them, and those who are mistreated” (Hebrews 13:3). And the Bible answers the double cry with a double name: “the Father of mercies and God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction” (2 Corinthians 1:3–4). The one who was himself oppressed and stood silent before his accusers promised his followers “another Helper, to be with you forever” (John 14:16), the Holy Spirit. No believer is left with no one to comfort him, and no believer should leave the oppressed with no one either.

verseByVerse.quote: And I thought the dead who are already dead more fortunate than the living who are still alive. But better than both is he who has not yet been and has not seen the evil deeds that are done under the sun.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seen from under the sun alone, evil weighs so heavily that death, or never being born, seems better than life.

More fortunate than the living. This is as dark as Scripture gets. Job said it too: “Why did I not die at birth, come out from the womb and expire?” (Job 3:11). So did Jeremiah: “Why did I come out from the womb to see toil and sorrow” (Jeremiah 20:18).

Why these words are here. God put these words in his book as a kindness: people crushed by what they have seen need to know that the Bible has said it aloud. The Preacher is not recommending death but showing how heavy evil is when seen only from under the sun. If you have felt this, say it to God as honestly as these men did, and tell someone you trust; if you have begun to think of ending your life, seek help today, from a doctor, a pastor or an emergency line. Then keep reading. The book does not stop here, and neither does God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–8 — Envy, Idleness and the Lonely Miser
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Work driven by envy or done for no one is breath, and a quiet handful is better than both. Much toil and skill come from rivalry with one’s neighbour (v. 4). The idle fool, who folds his hands, ruins himself (v. 5), but a handful of quietness is better than two hands full of toil and striving after wind (v. 6). Then comes the man with no son or brother, who never stops working, is never satisfied with riches, and never asks for whom he is depriving himself (vv. 7–8).
verseByVerse.theology: Work driven by envy or greed empties the worker; a quiet handful is richer than two restless fists.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw that all toil and all skill in work come from a man's envy of his neighbor. This also is vanity and a striving after wind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Much of our hard work springs from envy of our neighbour, and that too is chasing wind.

A man’s envy of his neighbor. From oppression he turns to a sickness inside us. Why do people work so hard? Much of it is envy: the bigger house next door, the colleague’s promotion. We call it ambition. He calls it envy, and he calls it breath.

Who is watching? Not all work is envious. But ask honestly how much of your effort would continue if no one else could see the result. “A tranquil heart gives life to the flesh, but envy makes the bones rot” (Proverbs 14:30).

The envy that calls itself ambition. Bertrand Russell, no friend of Christianity, observed in The Conquest of Happiness that beggars do not envy millionaires; they envy other beggars who are doing better. Envy is local. We measure ourselves not against kings but against the neighbour, the colleague one desk over, and now the polished lives of hundreds of people on a screen, every one a step ahead. A culture that runs on comparison will be busy and productive, and will never rest. The moralist’s answer is to try harder not to want things. The Preacher goes deeper. Envy is a quiet verdict that God has been unfair to me, and effort cannot cure it; only gift can. At the cross the one who had everything took the lowest place for people who deserved nothing. Someone who has received that can look at a neighbour’s success and be glad, because he is no longer competing for a worth that has already been given. So he can work for others rather than against them: “Let each of you look not only to his own interests, but also to the interests of others” (Philippians 2:4).

verseByVerse.quote: The fool folds his hands and eats his own flesh. Better is a handful of quietness than two hands full of toil and a striving after wind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Idleness ruins the fool and grasping wears out the envious; a quiet handful is better than both.

The fool folds his hands. Idleness is not the answer either: the fool “eats his own flesh”, ruining himself by doing nothing. “A little folding of the hands to rest, and poverty will come upon you like a robber” (Proverbs 6:10–11).

A handful of quietness. The wise middle way. Picture three pairs of hands: the fool’s folded, the envious worker’s both full and clutching, and the wise person’s one hand full and at peace.

Paying with peace. “Better is a little with the fear of the LORD than great treasure and trouble with it” (Proverbs 15:16). Many people are already paying for their income with their peace. Jesus offers what the overfilled hands cannot hold: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28).

verseByVerse.quote: Again, I saw vanity under the sun: one person who has no other, either son or brother, yet there is no end to all his toil, and his eyes are never satisfied with riches, so that he never asks, "For whom am I toiling and depriving myself of pleasure?" This also is vanity and an unhappy business.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man alone who works without end and never asks for whom has turned life into breath.

One person who has no other. A man with no son or brother, no one to share with or leave anything to, works without end. His eyes, like those of 1:8, are “never satisfied”. The Preacher is not faulting anyone for being single or childless. The vanity is the endless grasping that has no one to share it with and no reason to stop.

For whom? The tragedy is the question he never asks, as he denies himself every pleasure to pile up money for no one he loves. The rich fool in Jesus’ parable heard the same question from God: “the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” (Luke 12:20).

In everyday life. Ask it of your own week. For whom are you working? If the honest answer is “no one, really”, something has gone wrong that more money will not fix.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–12 — Two Are Better Than One
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God made us for companionship, and two are better than one. Against the lonely man the Preacher sets the blessing of a companion. Two have a good reward for their toil (v. 9). When one falls, the other lifts him up, but woe to the one who falls alone (v. 10). Two lying together keep warm on a cold night (v. 11), and two can withstand an attacker who would overpower one; a threefold cord is not quickly broken (v. 12). Friendship, marriage and the fellowship of God’s people are gifts against the loneliness of life under the sun.
verseByVerse.theology: God did not make people to live alone, and the answer to the lonely miser is companionship.

verseByVerse.quote: Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their toil. For if they fall, one will lift up his fellow. But woe to him who is alone when he falls and has not another to lift him up!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two are better than one, because a companion shares the work and lifts you when you fall.

Two are better than one. The answer to the lonely miser is companionship. Being alone is the first thing in all creation that God called not good: “It is not good that the man should be alone” (Genesis 2:18).

If they fall. Everyone falls, into sin, sickness or grief. The question is whether anyone will be close enough to reach you.

Why God gives us churches. This is one reason God puts believers in churches: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2). Who would lift you up if you fell tomorrow? If the honest answer is no one, that is not a verdict on you, but it may be a reason to let a church family come closer. And whom are you close enough to lift?

verseByVerse.quote: Again, if two lie together, they keep warm, but how can one keep warm alone? And though a man might prevail against one who is alone, two will withstand him—a threefold cord is not quickly broken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Companions keep each other warm and stand together, and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.

If two lie together, they keep warm. A traveller’s picture: two people sharing warmth on a cold night on the road. It applies to marriage, but not only to marriage. Friendship, fellowship and family all keep a person warm in a cold world.

Two will withstand him. A robber can overpower one traveller; two stand him off, and three strands twisted together hold what none could hold alone.

A threefold cord. Often read at weddings, with Christ as the third strand. The Preacher meant companions in general, but it is a true application: a marriage or friendship bound together with Christ holds in the storm. “Let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works, not neglecting to meet together” (Hebrews 10:24–25).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–16 — The Wise Youth and the Fickle Crowd
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Popularity is breath: even the wise youth who rises to the throne is soon forgotten. A poor and wise young man is better than an old and foolish king who will no longer take advice (v. 13). He rises from prison to the throne (v. 14), and all the people follow him in great numbers (vv. 15–16). Yet the next generation will not rejoice in him; they will want their own new face. Every king who rises is replaced, and the crowd’s favour passes like a breath (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology: Popularity is breath. The crowd that crowns a king today will forget him tomorrow.

verseByVerse.quote: Better was a poor and wise youth than an old and foolish king who no longer knew how to take advice. For he went from prison to the throne, though in his own kingdom he had been born poor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A poor but teachable youth is better than an old king who will no longer listen.

An old and foolish king. A short story. An old king has become a man who cannot be told anything; age and power often make a person unwilling to learn.

From prison to the throne. The youth rises from prison to the throne. The Bible has such stories: Joseph was brought quickly “out of the pit” to stand before Pharaoh (Genesis 41:14), and David was a shepherd boy before he was king.

verseByVerse.quote: I saw all the living who move about under the sun, along with that youth who was to stand in the king's place. There was no end of all the people, all of whom he led. Yet those who come later will not rejoice in him. Surely this also is vanity and a striving after wind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowds flock to the new king, and the next generation forgets him: popularity is breath.

That youth. Everyone flocks to the new man, who is in Hebrew “the second”, the successor (ESV note). Then comes the sting: the next generation will not rejoice in him; they will want their own new face.

Popularity is breath. Jerusalem’s crowds shouted Hosanna to Jesus as he rode in, and within the week a crowd was shouting for his death. He never entrusted himself to the crowd’s applause (John 2:24), and his kingdom does not depend on its favour. The Preacher’s youth is not a picture of Christ, but the contrast is plain: every king who rises is replaced by the next, and the King who rose from the grave to the throne has no successor. “Of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1:33).

Uncertain wording. The details are hard to pin down. It is not clear whether “in his own kingdom he had been born poor” (v. 14) refers to the youth or the old king, nor whether “that youth”, literally “the second”, is the same young man or a further successor. Attempts to identify a particular king have not won agreement. The point is clear on any reading: every rise to power is followed by another, and the crowd forgets.

4.text: <sup>1</sup>Again I saw all the oppressions that are done under the sun. And behold, the tears of the oppressed, and they had no one to comfort them! On the side of their oppressors there was power, and there was no one to comfort them.<sup>2</sup>And I thought the dead who are already dead more fortunate than the living who are still alive.<sup>3</sup>But better than both is he who has not yet been and has not seen the evil deeds that are done under the sun.<sup>4</sup>Then I saw that all toil and all skill in work come from a man's envy of his neighbor. This also is vanity and a striving after wind.<sup>5</sup>The fool folds his hands and eats his own flesh.<sup>6</sup>Better is a handful of quietness than two hands full of toil and a striving after wind.<sup>7</sup>Again, I saw vanity under the sun:<sup>8</sup>one person who has no other, either son or brother, yet there is no end to all his toil, and his eyes are never satisfied with riches, so that he never asks, "For whom am I toiling and depriving myself of pleasure?" This also is vanity and an unhappy business.<sup>9</sup>Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their toil.<sup>10</sup>For if they fall, one will lift up his fellow. But woe to him who is alone when he falls and has not another to lift him up!<sup>11</sup>Again, if two lie together, they keep warm, but how can one keep warm alone?<sup>12</sup>And though a man might prevail against one who is alone, two will withstand him—a threefold cord is not quickly broken.<sup>13</sup>Better was a poor and wise youth than an old and foolish king who no longer knew how to take advice.<sup>14</sup>For he went from prison to the throne, though in his own kingdom he had been born poor.<sup>15</sup>I saw all the living who move about under the sun, along with that youth who was to stand in the king's place.<sup>16</sup>There was no end of all the people, all of whom he led. Yet those who come later will not rejoice in him. Surely this also is vanity and a striving after wind.
4.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 3 ended with injustice in the courts, the dust that awaits man and beast, and the call to rejoice in one’s work. Now the Preacher looks again at life among other people: what we do to one another, and to ourselves.

The message. Under the sun, people are terribly alone: the oppressed have no one to comfort them, the envious compete with their neighbours, the lonely miser has no one to work for, and even the popular king is soon forgotten. Against all this the Preacher sets one of the warmest truths in the book: two are better than one. God made us for companionship, and life lived for self alone, whether in rivalry or isolation, is breath.

Why it was said. The Preacher writes for people who live among oppression, rivalry, overwork and the fickle crowd, and who are tempted to look after themselves alone (see the introduction). He shows them the emptiness of the self-made life and the worth of a faithful companion.

How the chapter makes its case. He sees the tears of the oppressed with no one to comfort them, and calls the dead and the unborn more fortunate than the living (vv. 1–3). He sees that much work springs from envy, that the idle fool ruins himself, and that a handful of quietness is better than both (vv. 4–6). He sees the man alone who toils without end and never asks for whom (vv. 7–8). Then he praises companionship: two lift each other, keep each other warm and stand together (vv. 9–12). Last, a short story: a poor, wise youth rises from prison to replace a foolish old king, and the crowds follow him, until the next generation forgets him too (vv. 13–16).

Where it leads. To Christ by the need the chapter exposes and by the character of God revealed in him. The oppressed who have “no one to comfort them” (v. 1) meet the “God of all comfort” (2 Corinthians 1:3), and the Son who was himself oppressed promised “another Helper, to be with you forever” (John 14:16). The envious are freed by a worth given in Christ, and the lonely are drawn into a family. And where every popular king is replaced and forgotten, the King who rose from the grave has no successor: “of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1:33).

For us. Ask for whom you are working, and whether envy or love drives it. Be the companion who lifts others when they fall, and let a church family come close enough to lift you. Do not leave the oppressed with no one to comfort them. And do not live for the crowd’s applause, which passes; live for the King whose reign does not.
4.theology:
Scripture looks honestly at oppression and at the despair it produces (vv. 1-3; Job 3:11; Jer 20:18). The answer to the cry for a comforter is the God of all comfort (2 Cor 1:3-4) and the Helper Christ promised (John 14:16), and his people are to comfort the oppressed (Heb 13:3).

Envy corrupts work, and idleness destroys the idle; contentment with quietness is better (vv. 4-6; Prov 15:16). God made people for companionship (vv. 9-12; Gen 2:18) and gives the church to bear one another's burdens (Gal 6:2). Human popularity is fleeting (vv. 13-16); only Christ's reign has no end.
4.examples:
Then: a traveller on the roads of Israel risked cold nights and robbers, and no one travelled alone if he could help it. The Preacher's hearers knew exactly what a companion was worth on a dark road.

Now: much of our overwork is fuelled by the neighbour's bigger house or the colleague's promotion, and some of us work on with no one to share the result. The same crowd that cheers a public figure this year will have moved on by the next, as Jerusalem's crowd moved from Hosanna to "Crucify" in a week.

keyVerse.quote: Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their toil. For if they fall, one will lift up his fellow. But woe to him who is alone when he falls and has not another to lift him up!
keyVerse.note: In a chapter full of loneliness, from the oppressed with no comforter to the man who has no other, these verses shine out. They echo God’s first “not good”, that man should be alone (Genesis 2:18). God made us for one another, and in Christ he gives his people to one another to bear each other’s burdens.

4.reflection:
“They had no one to comfort them” (v. 1). Who around you, near or far, might be in that place? How does knowing the “God of all comfort” (2 Corinthians 1:3) send us to them?

Verse 4 says much of our work comes from envy. Be honest: how much of your effort would continue if no one else could see the result? How does the gospel free us from comparison?

“For whom am I toiling?” (v. 8). Ask the Preacher’s question of your own week. What answer would you give, and what does it show?

Two are better than one (vv. 9–12). Who would lift you up if you fell tomorrow, and whom are you close enough to lift? What could you do this week to strengthen those bonds in your church?

5.title: Guard Your Steps: Worship, Vows and the Love of Money

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Guard Your Steps in the House of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before God, listen more than you speak, and mean what you say. The Preacher’s first commands concern worship, because how we come to God shows whether we fear him. The fool brings sacrifices and words to earn a hearing; the wise draws near to listen (v. 1). God is in heaven and we are on earth, so our words to him should be few and weighed (vv. 2–3). A vow is a debt to God, to be paid promptly and never explained away as a mistake (vv. 4–6). Many dreams and many words are only breath; what is solid is the fear of God (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: True worship begins with listening to God, and reverence shows itself in few, honest words.

verseByVerse.quote: Guard your steps when you go to the house of God. To draw near to listen is better than to offer the sacrifice of fools, for they do not know that they are doing evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Come to God to listen, not to perform: worship without a hearing heart is the sacrifice of fools.

Guard your steps. After four chapters of observing, the Preacher gives commands, and he sends us first to the house of God, the temple. If life is breath, approach the God above it all with care.

Draw near to listen. The fool comes to worship to do something: say his piece, tick the box. The wise person comes to hear. Samuel told Saul the same: “to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams” (1 Samuel 15:22). The fool thinks religious activity pleases God whatever the state of his heart, but Jesus, quoting Isaiah, said of such worshippers, “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Matthew 15:8).

The sacrifice already made. We can come at all only because “we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus” (Hebrews 10:19). The fool brings his sacrifice to earn a hearing. The Christian comes because the sacrifice has already been made, and so is free simply to listen.

How do I draw near to listen? It begins before the service. Prepare. Go to bed on Saturday with Sunday in mind, and read the passage beforehand if you know it. Ask before you hear. On the way in, pray, “Open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law” (Psalm 119:18). Listen for one thing. Listen less as a critic of the preacher than as someone waiting for a word, and write down one thing God is saying to you. Do it before Wednesday. “Be doers of the word, and not hearers only” (James 1:22): one specific step, taken this week. Jesus said, “Take care then how you hear” (Luke 8:18).

Uncertain wording. The last clause is literally “they do not know to do evil”. The ESV takes it to mean that fools sin in their worship without realising it; others, that they know nothing but doing evil. Either way, thoughtless worship is not harmless.
verseByVerse.note: Ecclesiastes 5:1 is 4:17 in the Hebrew numbering (ESV note at 5:2).

verseByVerse.quote: Be not rash with your mouth, nor let your heart be hasty to utter a word before God, for God is in heaven and you are on earth. Therefore let your words be few. For a dream comes with much business, and a fool's voice with many words.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is in heaven and you are on earth, so let your words to him be few and meant.

God is in heaven. Rashness is words tumbling out before the heart has weighed them, and here is the reason against it: the distance between Creator and creature is infinite. “Our God is in the heavens; he does all that he pleases” (Psalm 115:3). So the fitting response is few words, carefully meant.

A dream comes with much business. As a crowded, busy day produces restless dreams, so a fool produces a stream of talk.

Our Father in heaven. Jesus taught the same: “when you pray, do not heap up empty phrases as the Gentiles do, for they think that they will be heard for their many words” (Matthew 6:7). Then he gave his disciples a prayer that begins, “Our Father in heaven” (Matthew 6:9). He is in heaven, so we come with awe; he is our Father, so we come without fear. In Christ we may “with confidence draw near to the throne of grace” (Hebrews 4:16), and still “offer to God acceptable worship, with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire” (Hebrews 12:28–29). Confidence without reverence becomes chatter. Reverence without confidence becomes dread. Jesus prayed all night (Luke 6:12): the fault is not length but words that run ahead of the heart.

verseByVerse.quote: When you vow a vow to God, do not delay paying it, for he has no pleasure in fools. Pay what you vow. It is better that you should not vow than that you should vow and not pay. Let not your mouth lead you into sin, and do not say before the messenger that it was a mistake. Why should God be angry at your voice and destroy the work of your hands?
verseByVerse.commentary:
A promise made to God is a debt: do not make it rashly, pay it promptly, and never excuse breaking it as a mistake.

When you vow a vow. A vow was a voluntary promise to God, often made in a moment of need. The law said the same as the Preacher: “If you make a vow to the LORD your God, you shall not delay fulfilling it”, and “if you refrain from vowing, you will not be guilty of sin” (Deuteronomy 23:21–22). Think of the promises made in hospital waiting rooms and forgotten when the danger passed.

Let not your mouth lead you into sin. The ESV notes that “your mouth” is in Hebrew “your flesh”. The picture is of someone going back on his promise before God’s representative and calling it an honest mistake. God is not fooled, and the work of his hands can come to nothing.

Rash vows. “It is a snare to say rashly, ‘It is holy,’ and to reflect only after making vows” (Proverbs 20:25). Jephthah made a rash vow and lived to say, “I have opened my mouth to the LORD, and I cannot take back my vow” (Judges 11:35). Ananias and Sapphira pretended to give everything and kept part back, and Peter said, “You have not lied to man but to God” (Acts 5:4).

The one who kept every vow. Every promise God has made finds its Yes in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20), the one man who kept every vow, and his faithfulness covers our failures: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us” (1 John 1:9).

Christian vows. Christians make vows too: at baptism, marriage, membership, ordination. Jesus’ rule covers all our words: “Let what you say be simply ‘Yes’ or ‘No’” (Matthew 5:37). Is there a promise you made to God that you have quietly decided to call a mistake? Do not hide it; confess it and, where you still can, keep it.

Uncertain wording. “The messenger” may be rendered “angel” (ESV note). Most take it as the priest to whom a vow was paid, for Malachi calls the priest “the messenger of the LORD of hosts” (Malachi 2:7).
verseByVerse.note: “The messenger” may be rendered “angel” (ESV note); probably the priest or temple official.

verseByVerse.quote: For when dreams increase and words grow many, there is vanity; but God is the one you must fear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many dreams and many words are only breath; the one solid thing is to fear God.

When dreams increase and words grow many. The verse gathers up vv. 1–6. Religious talk and elaborate promises can be vapour.

God is the one you must fear. This is the second time the book names the fear of God (3:14), and here it stands at the centre of true worship. It is not a feeling to work up but a settled seriousness about who God is, the awe of a child who loves his Father and would not grieve him. A person who fears God will say less to him and mean more of it.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew is compressed, and the ESV notes another rendering: “For when dreams and vanities increase, words also grow many.” The sense is the same either way.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Neither power nor money can make life solid. The Preacher is not shocked by corruption: oppression of the poor runs up through layers of officials, each watching the one below and watched by the one above, though a land is better off with a king who cares for its fields (vv. 8–9). Money is no better a refuge. Whoever loves it is never satisfied (v. 10); more goods bring more people to eat them (v. 11); and the labourer sleeps soundly while the rich man lies awake (v. 12). What we hoped would give us rest becomes the thing that takes it away.
verseByVerse.theology: Money promises satisfaction and security; it delivers neither.

verseByVerse.quote: If you see in a province the oppression of the poor and the violation of justice and righteousness, do not be amazed at the matter, for the high official is watched by a higher, and there are yet higher ones over them. But this is gain for a land in every way: a king committed to cultivated fields.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Corruption in government should not surprise us, for officials shelter one another all the way up; but none of them is beyond the reach of God.

Do not be amazed. From the house of God the Preacher turns to the halls of government, and he is a realist: layer on layer of officials watch one another, each guarding his position and taking his cut, and a poor man’s appeal is lost somewhere up the chain.

A higher one still. But above the highest official there is one higher still. “God has taken his place in the divine council; in the midst of the gods he holds judgment” (Psalm 82:1). Every authority will answer to him, and the King he has appointed will judge the poor with righteousness (Isaiah 11:4).

What it does not mean. “Do not be amazed” is not “do not care”. The Preacher refuses naivety, not compassion (4:1), and Scripture commands, “Open your mouth for the mute, for the rights of all who are destitute” (Proverbs 31:8).

Uncertain wording. In v. 8, “watched” may mean that officials protect one another or spy on one another. The Hebrew of v. 9 is uncertain (ESV note). As the ESV renders it, a land gains from a king who cares for the fields that feed his people; older translations say that even the king is served by the field.

verseByVerse.quote: He who loves money will not be satisfied with money, nor he who loves wealth with his income; this also is vanity. When goods increase, they increase who eat them, and what advantage has their owner but to see them with his eyes?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Money cannot satisfy the one who loves it, and the more you have, the more people there are to consume it.

He who loves money will not be satisfied with money. Few sentences have been proved true more often. Money promises that the next level will be enough, and when you reach it, “enough” has moved further on.

When goods increase, they increase who eat them. More income brings more mouths: staff, taxes, upkeep, relatives, and a bigger house to heat. The owner’s only advantage is looking at it. “One’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions” (Luke 12:15).

Money and the love of it. Money is not the problem; the love of it is. “For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils” (1 Timothy 6:10). The cure is not poverty but contentment rooted in God’s presence: “Keep your life free from love of money, and be content with what you have, for he has said, ‘I will never leave you nor forsake you’” (Hebrews 13:5). That promise is kept in Christ, who is with his people always (Matthew 28:20): the only wealth that is enough.

verseByVerse.quote: Sweet is the sleep of a laborer, whether he eats little or much, but the full stomach of the rich will not let him sleep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The worker who has little sleeps in peace, while the rich man’s abundance keeps him awake.

Sweet is the sleep of a laborer. The tired worker sleeps; the rich man lies awake, overfed or overloaded with things to guard. Sleep is one thing money cannot buy.

Sleep as a gift. The psalmist found its secret in God: “You have put more joy in my heart than they have when their grain and wine abound. In peace I will both lie down and sleep; for you alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety” (Psalm 4:7–8). Where does your mind go when you cannot sleep? It often shows where your treasure is.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–17 — Riches Lost, and Naked We Go
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Riches hoarded for security can betray their owner in this life, and must be left behind at death. The Preacher calls it a grievous evil: wealth kept to its owner’s hurt is lost in one bad venture, and his son inherits nothing (vv. 13–14). Even had it not been lost, he would go out as naked as he came (v. 15). So the question of 1:3 returns with a sharper picture: what gain has a man who toils for the wind? (v. 16). The love of money cost him his present too, for he ate all his days in darkness, vexation, sickness and anger (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: Everyone leaves the world with empty hands; the only question is what he lived for.

verseByVerse.quote: There is a grievous evil that I have seen under the sun: riches were kept by their owner to his hurt, and those riches were lost in a bad venture. And he is father of a son, but he has nothing in his hand. As he came from his mother's womb he shall go again, naked as he came, and shall take nothing for his toil that he may carry away in his hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wealth hoarded for security can be lost in a moment, and even if it is kept, death strips it all away.

A grievous evil. The Preacher calls it that, and it is a story everyone has seen: riches kept to their owner’s hurt, gone in one bad venture, and a son with nothing to receive.

Naked as he came. Even if the venture had succeeded, the end would be the same. Job said it as he lost everything: “Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return” (Job 1:21). Paul said it to Timothy: “we brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out of the world” (1 Timothy 6:7). There are no pockets in a burial shroud.

Treasure sent ahead. Jesus showed a way to send treasure ahead: “Sell your possessions, and give to the needy. Provide yourselves with moneybags that do not grow old, with a treasure in the heavens that does not fail” (Luke 12:33). Christ became poor so that we might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9).

verseByVerse.quote: This also is a grievous evil: just as he came, so shall he go, and what gain is there to him who toils for the wind? Moreover, all his days he eats in darkness in much vexation and sickness and anger.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A life spent piling up money for oneself is toil for the wind, and it ruins the present as well as the future.

What gain is there to him who toils for the wind? The question of 1:3 returns with a new picture: a lifetime of work, and the wages paid in wind.

All his days he eats in darkness. The love of money failed to give him a future, and it spoiled his present too: he ate in gloom, with vexation, sickness and anger. Paul says that some who craved money have “pierced themselves with many pangs” (1 Timothy 6:10).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joy in ordinary life is not something we seize but something God gives. After the dark portrait of the hoarder, the Preacher says “Behold”: look at this instead. To eat, drink and find enjoyment in one’s toil through the few days God gives is good and fitting (v. 18). Wealth is a gift, and so, separately, is the power to enjoy it and to accept one’s lot (v. 19). The one who receives life this way is not haunted by the shortness of his days, because God fills his heart with joy (v. 20). Chapter 6 will show a man who had the first gift without the second.
verseByVerse.theology: The ability to enjoy what we have is itself God's gift, and it frees us from the anxious counting of days.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, what I have seen to be good and fitting is to eat and drink and find enjoyment in all the toil with which one toils under the sun the few days of his life that God has given him, for this is his lot. Everyone also to whom God has given wealth and possessions and power to enjoy them, and to accept his lot and rejoice in his toil—this is the gift of God. For he will not much remember the days of his life because God keeps him occupied with joy in his heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The good life under the sun is to receive food, work and wealth from God and enjoy them contentedly, and that joy is itself his gift.

Behold, what I have seen to be good. Look at this instead, says the Preacher, as the refrain of 2:24 and 3:12–13, 22 returns. The hoarder ate in darkness; the receiver “sees good” (ESV note on “find enjoyment”).

This is the gift of God. There are three gifts here: wealth; the power to enjoy it, a separate gift (chapter 6 shows a man with the first and not the second); and the ability to accept one’s lot, content with the portion God has given. “But godliness with contentment is great gain” (1 Timothy 6:6). The rich are to set their hope “on God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy”, and to be “generous and ready to share” (1 Timothy 6:17–18).

Occupied with joy. Like a child absorbed in play who forgets the clock, the person who receives life as God’s gift is too taken up with it to be consumed by fear of losing it. This joy is a gift, not a method to master.

From the Giver’s hand. “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above” (James 1:17), and the Father who did not spare his own Son will with him “graciously give us all things” (Romans 8:32).

Uncertain wording. In v. 20 the verb rendered “keeps him occupied” may instead mean “answers”: God answers him with joy in his heart. Either way the joy comes from God.
