To draw near to listen is better than to offer the sacrifice of fools, for they do not know that they are doing evil.<sup>2</sup>Be not rash with your mouth, nor let your heart be hasty to utter a word before God, for God is in heaven and you are on earth. Therefore let your words be few.<sup>3</sup>For a dream comes with much business, and a fool's voice with many words.<sup>4</sup>When you vow a vow to God, do not delay paying it, for he has no pleasure in fools. Pay what you vow.<sup>5</sup>It is better that you should not vow than that you should vow and not pay.<sup>6</sup>Let not your mouth lead you into sin, and do not say before the messenger that it was a mistake. Why should God be angry at your voice and destroy the work of your hands?<sup>7</sup>For when dreams increase and words grow many, there is vanity; but God is the one you must fear.<sup>8</sup>If you see in a province the oppression of the poor and the violation of justice and righteousness, do not be amazed at the matter, for the high official is watched by a higher, and there are yet higher ones over them.<sup>9</sup>But this is gain for a land in every way: a king committed to cultivated fields.<sup>10</sup>He who loves money will not be satisfied with money, nor he who loves wealth with his income; this also is vanity.<sup>11</sup>When goods increase, they increase who eat them, and what advantage has their owner but to see them with his eyes?<sup>12</sup>Sweet is the sleep of a laborer, whether he eats little or much, but the full stomach of the rich will not let him sleep.<sup>13</sup>There is a grievous evil that I have seen under the sun: riches were kept by their owner to his hurt,<sup>14</sup>and those riches were lost in a bad venture. And he is father of a son, but he has nothing in his hand.<sup>15</sup>As he came from his mother's womb he shall go again, naked as he came, and shall take nothing for his toil that he may carry away in his hand.<sup>16</sup>This also is a grievous evil: just as he came, so shall he go, and what gain is there to him who toils for the wind?<sup>17</sup>Moreover, all his days he eats in darkness in much vexation and sickness and anger.<sup>18</sup>Behold, what I have seen to be good and fitting is to eat and drink and find enjoyment in all the toil with which one toils under the sun the few days of his life that God has given him, for this is his lot.<sup>19</sup>Everyone also to whom God has given wealth and possessions and power to enjoy them, and to accept his lot and rejoice in his toil—this is the gift of God.<sup>20</sup>For he will not much remember the days of his life because God keeps him occupied with joy in his heart.
5.overview:
Where we are. Chapters 1 to 4 have shown that everything under the sun is breath: wisdom, pleasure, work and even popularity slip through our fingers. Now, for the first time, the Preacher turns from watching to commanding, and the first place he sends us is the house of God.

The message. God is in heaven and you are on earth, so come to him to listen, mean what you say to him, and fear him. And do not look to money for what only God can give: the love of it never satisfies, and you will leave the world as naked as you came. Wealth, and the power to enjoy it, are both gifts from God’s hand.

Why it was said. The Preacher’s hearers knew the two refuges every age runs to when life feels like breath: busy religion and money (see the introduction). Both promise solid ground. He shows that only God himself is solid, and that his gifts are good when they are received from him.

How the chapter makes its case. First, worship (vv. 1–7): draw near to listen rather than offer the sacrifice of fools, let your words be few, pay what you vow, and fear God. Then the world outside the temple (vv. 8–9): oppression climbs through layers of officials, yet no one is finally unaccountable. Then money (vv. 10–17): its lover is never satisfied, more goods bring more mouths, the rich man cannot sleep, and a hoard can vanish in one bad venture, leaving its owner to go out naked. Last, the light returns (vv. 18–20): to eat, drink and enjoy one’s toil, and to accept one’s lot, is the gift of God.

Where it leads. To Christ by the need the chapter exposes and by the character of God revealed in him. The distance between heaven and earth (v. 2) is real, and Christ crossed it from God’s side, so that “we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus” (Hebrews 10:19). He is the one man who kept every vow, in whom all God’s promises are Yes (2 Corinthians 1:20). And he who, “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9), left the world stripped of everything on a cross, so that we might have a treasure death cannot take away.

For us. Come to church to hear God before you speak to him, and keep the promises you have made to him. Hold money with an open hand: it is a good servant from God and a cruel master. And if you can enjoy your daily bread with a quiet heart, thank God: that too is his gift.
5.theology:
Worship begins with listening and reverent fear, not many words (vv. 1-7; 1 Sam 15:22; Matt 6:7). God is in heaven, and in Christ believers may draw near with confidence and with reverence (Heb 4:16; 12:28-29). Promises to God are binding (vv. 4-6; Deut 23:21-23; Matt 5:37).

All earthly authority is accountable to a higher, and finally to God (vv. 8-9; Ps 82:1). The love of money cannot be satisfied and brings misery (vv. 10-17; 1 Tim 6:6-10); everyone leaves the world with nothing (v. 15; Job 1:21). Wealth, the power to enjoy it and contentment with one's lot are separate gifts of God (vv. 18-20; 1 Tim 6:17).
5.examples:
Then: worshippers came to the temple with sacrifices and vows, and the Preacher warned them that God wanted listening ears more than many offerings or rash promises.

Now: we may come to church to say our piece rather than to hear, or make promises to God in a hospital waiting room and forget them when the danger has passed. Lottery winners often find that “enough” keeps moving, while a tired labourer sleeps soundly on very little.

keyVerse.quote: For when dreams increase and words grow many, there is vanity; but God is the one you must fear.
keyVerse.note: The verse gathers up the chapter’s teaching on worship and names what is solid when words, dreams and, as the rest of the chapter shows, money are only breath: the fear of God. It is the quiet thread that becomes the book’s last word (12:13), and it explains the rest of the chapter, for only the one who fears God can hold his gifts with an open hand.

5.reflection:
Verse 1 says that to draw near to listen is better than to offer the sacrifice of fools. What do you usually come to church to do? What one change would help you come ready to listen?

Is there a promise you made to God, in a crisis, at baptism, in marriage or in church membership, that you have quietly treated as a mistake (vv. 4–6)? What would keeping it, or confessing it, look like?

“He who loves money will not be satisfied with money” (v. 10). Where have you seen “enough” keep moving, in your own life or in others’? What cure does Hebrews 13:5 give?

Verse 19 calls the power to enjoy what we have, and to accept our lot, a gift of God. How does knowing Christ, who became poor for our sake, change the way you enjoy and hold what God has given you?

6.title: Wealth Without Enjoyment

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Wealth Without the Power to Enjoy It
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: To have everything is not the same as to enjoy it, and the power to enjoy is God’s gift. Chapter 5 ended with joy as a gift; here is its absence. A man has wealth, possessions and honour, lacking nothing he desires, yet God does not give him the power to enjoy them, and a stranger does (vv. 1–2). Another has a hundred children and many years, but his soul is never satisfied and he is not even buried with honour; the Preacher says a stillborn child is better off, for it finds rest (vv. 3–5). Two thousand years without joy would add nothing, for all go to the one place (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: Having everything is not the same as enjoying anything; enjoyment is a separate gift of God.

verseByVerse.quote: There is an evil that I have seen under the sun, and it lies heavy on mankind: a man to whom God gives wealth, possessions, and honor, so that he lacks nothing of all that he desires, yet God does not give him power to enjoy them, but a stranger enjoys them. This is vanity; it is a grievous evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God may give someone everything and withhold the power to enjoy it, for enjoyment is a separate gift.

It lies heavy on mankind. This is no rare misfortune. Set it beside 5:19: wealth and enjoyment are two different gifts, and God can give the first and withhold the second. So a stranger enjoys what he worked for, while he never tastes it.

Why would God withhold it? The Preacher does not say. But Scripture shows that gifts loved apart from the Giver cannot satisfy, and the restlessness they leave can be a mercy that drives a person to God himself.

The second gift. Many people pray for the house, the job or the money and never ask for the ability to be happy in them. Ask God first for a heart that can receive with joy what he has already given. Paul learned that secret in Christ: “I have learned in whatever situation I am to be content” (Philippians 4:11).

verseByVerse.quote: If a man fathers a hundred children and lives many years, so that the days of his years are many, but his soul is not satisfied with life's good things, and he also has no burial, I say that a stillborn child is better off than he. For it comes in vanity and goes in darkness, and in darkness its name is covered. Moreover, it has not seen the sun or known anything, yet it finds rest rather than he.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man may have a huge family and a long life and still be worse off than a stillborn child, if his soul is never satisfied.

A hundred children. Many children and long life were Israel’s highest blessings, and this man has both in exaggerated measure. But his soul is not satisfied with life’s good things, and he is not even buried with honour. Scripture treats an unburied body as disgrace; Jeremiah said of a faithless king, “With the burial of a donkey he shall be buried” (Jeremiah 22:19).

A stillborn child. It came in vanity and went in darkness; it never saw the sun or had its name spoken, yet it finds rest. The rich man never did.

For grieving parents. Parents who have lost a child before birth may find these verses hard. The Preacher is not saying the child’s life did not matter. He is saying, from under the sun, that even the shortest life is not the worst fate; the worst is a long life with a restless soul. And the God who knows the name that was never spoken aloud has not lost that child.

verseByVerse.quote: Even though he should live a thousand years twice over, yet enjoy no good—do not all go to the one place?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The longest life without joy adds nothing, for it ends where every life ends.

A thousand years twice over. Two thousand years is more than double the longest life in Scripture, Methuselah’s 969 years (Genesis 5:27). But if the man enjoys no good in all that time (Hebrew “sees” no good, ESV note), what has the length added? Nothing, for all go to the one place (3:20).

Adding life to years. A long life without joy is only a long walk to the same grave; a short life lived with God is full. We spend fortunes adding years to life; have we thought as hard about adding life to our years? Christ gives the life the grave cannot end (John 11:25).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — Who Knows What Is Good for Man?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Nothing under the sun can fill the human appetite or answer our deepest questions. We toil to feed our mouths and are hungry again; wisdom and good manners do not fill the hole, and the best we can manage is to be content with what is before our eyes (vv. 7–9). God has already named all things and knows what man is, so man cannot win an argument with his Maker, and more words only add more breath (vv. 10–11). The first half of the book ends with two questions: who knows what is good for man in his shadow-like life, and who can tell him what will come after him? (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: The book's first half ends with a question only God can answer.

verseByVerse.quote: All the toil of man is for his mouth, yet his appetite is not satisfied. For what advantage has the wise man over the fool? And what does the poor man have who knows how to conduct himself before the living? Better is the sight of the eyes than the wandering of the appetite: this also is vanity and a striving after wind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Toil feeds an appetite that is never filled, and wisdom cannot fill it; the best we can do under the sun is be content with what is in front of us.

All the toil of man is for his mouth. We work to eat, and we are hungry again. “Satisfied” is in Hebrew “filled” (ESV note): the appetite is a vessel with a hole in the bottom, and the soul’s deeper hunger is never filled by what we work for. “Why do you spend your money for that which is not bread, and your labor for that which does not satisfy?” (Isaiah 55:2).

The sight of the eyes. Here is practical wisdom, if not a final answer: be content with what is in front of you, the meal on the table rather than the one in the advertisement, instead of letting desire wander. Yet even that contentment, on its own, is breath. It helps; it does not save.

The food that endures. Jesus spoke to exactly this hunger: “Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give to you” (John 6:27).

Uncertain wording. Verse 8 is compressed. It seems to ask what the wise man, or the poor man who knows how to get on among the living, gains over the fool; the implied answer is nothing that fills the appetite.

verseByVerse.quote: Whatever has come to be has already been named, and it is known what man is, and that he is not able to dispute with one stronger than he. The more words, the more vanity, and what is the advantage to man?
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has named everything and knows what man is, so arguing with him is useless; more words only mean more breath.

Already named. In Scripture, to name something is often to know it and have authority over it. God “determines the number of the stars; he gives to all of them their names” (Psalm 147:4). And it is known what man is: adam, taken from the ground (adamah), a creature of dust (Genesis 2:7). So he cannot take God to court and win. “Woe to him who strives with him who formed him” (Isaiah 45:9); “But who are you, O man, to answer back to God?” (Romans 9:20).

The more words, the more vanity. Arguing with God multiplies words, and words are breath (5:2–3). When we cannot understand him, the answer is not more talk but trust. Job came to the same place: after all his speeches, he laid his hand on his mouth (Job 40:4).

Not an opponent but an advocate. Job longed for an arbiter between God and man (Job 9:33). In Christ we need not dispute with one stronger than we are: “we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (1 John 2:1).

Uncertain wording. “One stronger than he” is most likely God, though some take it as death; the Preacher does not name him. “Words” in v. 11 may also be rendered “things”.

verseByVerse.quote: For who knows what is good for man while he lives the few days of his vain life, which he passes like a shadow? For who can tell man what will be after him under the sun?
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one under the sun can say what is good for our shadow-like life or what comes after it; the answer must come from above, and it has.

Who knows what is good for man? The first half of the book ends with two questions, and they are the right ones. What is good for us in our short life? The ESV notes that “vain” is hebel again: a breath of a life. And what will happen after we are gone?

Like a shadow. David prayed, “Our days on the earth are like a shadow, and there is no abiding” (1 Chronicles 29:15). “Man is like a breath; his days are like a passing shadow” (Psalm 144:4).

An answer from above. Chapters 7 to 12 offer wisdom for how to live, but the final answer comes from God. “He has told you, O man, what is good” (Micah 6:8), and the answer has come in a person, who said, “I came that they may have life and have it abundantly” (John 10:10). He went into death and came back, so he has answered the second question too: the shadow is not the end for those who belong to him, because he is the light of the world (John 8:12).

6.text: <sup>1</sup>There is an evil that I have seen under the sun, and it lies heavy on mankind:<sup>2</sup>a man to whom God gives wealth, possessions, and honor, so that he lacks nothing of all that he desires, yet God does not give him power to enjoy them, but a stranger enjoys them. This is vanity; it is a grievous evil.<sup>3</sup>If a man fathers a hundred children and lives many years, so that the days of his years are many, but his soul is not satisfied with life's good things, and he also has no burial, I say that a stillborn child is better off than he.<sup>4</sup>For it comes in vanity and goes in darkness, and in darkness its name is covered.<sup>5</sup>Moreover, it has not seen the sun or known anything, yet it finds rest rather than he.<sup>6</sup>Even though he should live a thousand years twice over, yet enjoy no good—do not all go to the one place?<sup>7</sup>All the toil of man is for his mouth, yet his appetite is not satisfied.<sup>8</sup>For what advantage has the wise man over the fool? And what does the poor man have who knows how to conduct himself before the living?<sup>9</sup>Better is the sight of the eyes than the wandering of the appetite: this also is vanity and a striving after wind.<sup>10</sup>Whatever has come to be has already been named, and it is known what man is, and that he is not able to dispute with one stronger than he.<sup>11</sup>The more words, the more vanity, and what is the advantage to man?<sup>12</sup>For who knows what is good for man while he lives the few days of his vain life, which he passes like a shadow? For who can tell man what will be after him under the sun?
6.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 5 ended with joy as the gift of God: wealth, and the power to enjoy it. Chapter 6 shows the same truth from the dark side, and closes the first half of the book, the Preacher’s search (1:12–6:12), with two questions no one under the sun can answer.

The message. To have everything is not to enjoy anything, and enjoyment, like everything else, is God’s to give. Wealth, honour, a hundred children and two thousand years cannot fill a human soul, and arguing with God will not change what we are. So the chapter leaves us asking the right question: who can tell us what is good for man, and what comes after him?

Why it was said. In Israel, riches, many children and long life were the blessings everyone hoped for (see the introduction). The Preacher shows people who assume such things would satisfy them that a soul can have them all and still be starving.

How the chapter makes its case. First, the man who has everything except the power to enjoy it, so that a stranger enjoys it instead (vv. 1–2). Then the man with a hundred children and many years whose soul is never satisfied and who has no burial: a stillborn child is better off, for it at least finds rest (vv. 3–6). Then the appetite that toil never fills, for the wise and the poor alike (vv. 7–9). Man is already named and known, and cannot win an argument with one stronger than he; more words are only more breath (vv. 10–11). The chapter ends on two questions (v. 12).

Where it leads. To Christ by the need the chapter exposes. The hunger that wealth and long life cannot fill is the hunger Jesus meant when he said, “I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger” (John 6:35). The man who cannot dispute with one stronger than he finds in Christ not an opponent but an advocate. And the questions of v. 12 are answered not from under the sun but from above: God has told us what is good (Micah 6:8), and Christ, risen from the dead, has shown what lies beyond the shadow.

For us. Pray for the second gift: not only for good things, but for a heart that can enjoy them as from God. Stop expecting the next possession or achievement to fill a hunger only God can fill. And bring your unanswerable questions to the one who came from above to answer them.
6.theology:
Wealth and the power to enjoy it are separate gifts of God; he may give one and withhold the other (v. 2; 5:19). Neither long life nor many children can satisfy the soul (vv. 3-6). Human appetite is never filled by what it works for (v. 7; Isa 55:2), but Christ gives food that endures to eternal life (John 6:27).

God has named and defined all things, and man cannot contend with his Maker (v. 10; Isa 45:9; Rom 9:20). Life is a shadow (v. 12; Ps 144:4), and what is good for man is revealed by God, not discovered under the sun (Mic 6:8; John 10:10).
6.examples:
Then: in Israel a large family and a long life were the blessings everyone hoped for, which is why the Preacher's picture of a man with a hundred children and no one to mourn him was so shocking.

Now: many people pray for the house or the promotion and never for a heart to enjoy it. Advertising lives on the appetite the Preacher describes, always showing us a better meal than the one on our table.

keyVerse.quote: For who knows what is good for man while he lives the few days of his vain life, which he passes like a shadow? For who can tell man what will be after him under the sun?
keyVerse.note: The first half of the book ends on this double question, and it is the right one. Nothing under the sun can say what is truly good for a shadow-like life or what lies beyond it, so the answer must come from God, as it does in the rest of Scripture and finally in Christ, who has come back from the place to which all go.

6.reflection:
Verse 2 describes a man with everything except the power to enjoy it. Why do we pray far more often for good things than for a heart to enjoy them? What would it look like to ask God for that second gift?

The man in v. 3 has the blessings everyone in Israel longed for, yet his soul is not satisfied. What do people around you expect to satisfy them? Where have you found that it does not?

“All the toil of man is for his mouth, yet his appetite is not satisfied” (v. 7). How do Jesus’ words in John 6:27 and 6:35 speak to the restlessness of our appetites?

The first half of the book ends with two questions (v. 12). How does the gospel answer them, and how might they open a conversation with a friend who does not yet believe?

7.title: Better Things: Mourning, Patience and the Upright Made Crooked

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wisdom for a life we cannot control begins by choosing the harder good. The Preacher answers the question of 6:12 with a string of “better” sayings: a good name over perfume, the day of death over the day of birth, mourning over feasting (vv. 1–4); the rebuke of the wise over the laughter of fools, though even the wise can be corrupted (vv. 5–7); the end over the beginning, patience over pride, the present over nostalgia (vv. 8–10); and wisdom, which shelters like money but also preserves life (vv. 11–12). Then he calls us to consider the work of God, who makes both the good day and the bad (vv. 13–14).
verseByVerse.theology: The things that humble and sober us are often better for the soul than the things that please us.

verseByVerse.quote: A good name is better than precious ointment, and the day of death than the day of birth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A life well lived is worth more than any luxury, and the end of such a life tells more truth than its beginning.

A good name. The first half ended by asking “who knows what is good for man” (6:12), and chapter 7 begins to answer with “better” sayings. Perfume fades; a good name lasts. The first hearers would have caught the play on words, for in Hebrew a name is shem and ointment is shemen. “A good name is to be chosen rather than great riches” (Proverbs 22:1).

The day of death than the day of birth. Then the shock. At a birth nothing is settled; at a death the life is complete, and all know what name the person has earned.

The day of going home. This is not a call to love death, which remains an enemy and a cause of real grief. But for the believer the day of death is also the day of going home. Paul could say, “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain”, and “My desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better” (Philippians 1:21, 23). The Preacher saw that death finishes a life; the gospel shows that for those in Christ it begins a better one.
verseByVerse.note: A sound-play: a good name (shem) is better than precious ointment (shemen).

verseByVerse.quote: It is better to go to the house of mourning than to go to the house of feasting, for this is the end of all mankind, and the living will lay it to heart. Sorrow is better than laughter, for by sadness of face the heart is made glad. The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, but the heart of fools is in the house of mirth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Facing death honestly does the heart more good than escaping into constant entertainment, so the wise are willing to go where grief is.

The house of mourning. Offered a party and a funeral on the same weekend, almost everyone chooses the party. The Preacher says the funeral is better for you. At the party you forget that you will die; at the funeral you remember, and the living lay it to heart. That is not morbid: someone who has stood at a graveside and let it sink in makes different decisions on Monday.

Sorrow is better than laughter. Sorrow that faces reality does a deep work laughter cannot. “For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret” (2 Corinthians 7:10), and Jesus said, “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matthew 5:4). The gladness on the far side of mourning is deeper than the gladness that avoids it.

The heart of the wise. Where does your heart go when it is free to go anywhere? The fool’s runs to entertainment, so as not to think. The wise heart is willing to sit with grief, its own and others’. Our culture has built a house of mirth that never closes, with a screen in every pocket. Ask what it is helping you not to feel.

Why do we hold parties instead of funerals? More families now ask for a celebration of life: bright clothes, favourite songs, perhaps no coffin. There is something good in it, gratitude for a life. But we have turned the house of mourning into the house of feasting, and the one thing we no longer do there is look at death, the lesson the day was for. Montaigne gave one of his essays the title “That to Philosophise Is to Learn to Die”, and thought that whoever has learned to die has unlearned being a slave. Scripture goes further. We fear death not only because it ends things but because its sting is sin (1 Corinthians 15:56): something in us knows we must give an account. So denial never finally works, and honest mourning is the first step towards hope. Only someone who has looked at the grave will listen to the one who walked out of it.

Uncertain wording. In v. 3, “the heart is made glad” may also be rendered “the heart is made better”: sorrow improves the heart as well as leading it to joy.

verseByVerse.quote: It is better for a man to hear the rebuke of the wise than to hear the song of fools. For as the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of the fools; this also is vanity. Surely oppression drives the wise into madness, and a bribe corrupts the heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Honest correction from the wise helps far more than the empty laughter of fools, and even the wise can be corrupted by oppression and bribes.

The rebuke of the wise. The wise friend who tells you the truth does more good than a room full of people telling you what you want to hear. “Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of an enemy” (Proverbs 27:6). David prayed for such wounds: “let him rebuke me”, he said, for “it is oil for my head” (Psalm 141:5). Who in your life is allowed to tell you that you are wrong?

The crackling of thorns under a pot. Thorns burned under a pot make a quick, loud blaze and are gone before the pot boils. So is the fool’s laughter. The Hebrew has its own sound-play: the thorns (sirim) crackle under the pot (sir), a noise as quick and empty as the laughter it describes.

A bribe corrupts the heart. Even the wise are not safe. Long oppression can drive a wise man to folly, and a bribe can bend his heart, “for a bribe blinds the clear-sighted” (Exodus 23:8). Wisdom must be guarded, not assumed.

Uncertain wording. “Oppression” in v. 7 can also mean extortion. Then the verse may warn that practising it, like taking a bribe, makes a fool of the wise man, not only that suffering it unhinges him.

verseByVerse.quote: Better is the end of a thing than its beginning, and the patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit. Be not quick in your spirit to become angry, for anger lodges in the heart of fools. Say not, "Why were the former days better than these?" For it is not from wisdom that you ask this.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Patience that sees a thing through is better than pride that wants it now, and the wise neither nurse anger nor pine for the past.

Better is the end. Anyone can start a marriage, a project, a Christian life; the end tells the truth. What gets a person there is patience, not pride: the proud want the result now and quit when it does not come. Christ is the pattern, who “for the joy that was set before him endured the cross” (Hebrews 12:2).

Anger lodges. Anger nursed and held close (“in the bosom”, see the note) settles in and makes a home. It may flash in a wise person; it lodges in a fool. “Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger” (Ephesians 4:26), “for the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God” (James 1:20).

The former days. Nostalgia feels wise, and it is not. Israel in the wilderness remembered “the fish we ate in Egypt that cost nothing” (Numbers 11:5) and forgot the whips. To ask why the former days were better is to refuse the present God has given. Paul’s way is better: “forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead” (Philippians 3:13).
verseByVerse.note: “Lodges in the heart” is literally “in the bosom” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Wisdom is good with an inheritance, an advantage to those who see the sun. For the protection of wisdom is like the protection of money, and the advantage of knowledge is that wisdom preserves the life of him who has it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom, like money, gives shelter, but it does more: it keeps its owner alive.

Wisdom is good with an inheritance. An inheritance without wisdom is soon wasted; with wisdom it becomes a blessing.

The protection of wisdom. Money gives a kind of shelter, and so does wisdom, but wisdom preserves the life of its owner. Money can be lost in a bad venture (5:14); wisdom keeps a person from walking into disasters money cannot repair. And the wisdom of God has a name: Christ, “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3).

Uncertain wording. Verse 11 may also mean that wisdom is as good as an inheritance. In v. 12, “protection” is literally “shade”, the shelter a traveller seeks from the sun.

verseByVerse.quote: Consider the work of God: who can make straight what he has made crooked? In the day of prosperity be joyful, and in the day of adversity consider: God has made the one as well as the other, so that man may not find out anything that will be after him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is at work in both the good days and the bad, so rejoice in the one, reflect in the other, and trust him with a future you cannot see.

Who can make straight what he has made crooked? In 1:15 the Preacher said, “What is crooked cannot be made straight.” Here he says who bent it: God. Some things in your life God has made crooked: the illness, the child who was never born, the marriage that never came. You cannot straighten them and are not asked to; you are asked to see them as his work, not random chaos. That does not mean he enjoys your pain, or that it punishes some hidden sin.

A hard comfort. That is hard, and also a comfort, for what God has bent, he can straighten, and one day will: “The uneven ground shall become level, and the rough places a plain” (Isaiah 40:4), words the Gospels apply to the coming of Christ (Luke 3:4–6).

Prosperity and adversity. On a good day, rejoice; do not spoil it with worry. On a bad day, consider: remember who made this day. Both come from the same hand. Job said, “Shall we receive good from God, and shall we not receive evil?” (Job 2:10), and Lamentations asks, “Is it not from the mouth of the Most High that good and bad come?” (Lamentations 3:38).

Why God mixes them. He mixes them so that we cannot predict our lives, and are left to trust him, knowing that “for those who love God all things work together for good” (Romans 8:28).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–22 — The Fear of God Between Two Ditches
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because the righteous sometimes perish and the wicked live long, there are two tempting ditches, and the fear of God keeps us out of both. The Preacher has seen a righteous man die young and a wicked man prosper (v. 15). One response is to try to guarantee a good life by a show of extra righteousness; the other is to give up on goodness and plunge into wickedness. Both destroy; the one who fears God comes out from both (vv. 16–18). Wisdom is strong, but no one on earth does good and never sins (vv. 19–20), and remembering our own sin makes us slow to be crushed by what others say about us (vv. 21–22).
verseByVerse.theology: The fear of God keeps a person from both self-righteousness and careless sin, and knowing his own sin keeps him gentle.

verseByVerse.quote: In my vain life I have seen everything. There is a righteous man who perishes in his righteousness, and there is a wicked man who prolongs his life in his evildoing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In this life the righteous sometimes die young and the wicked live long, so this life cannot be the whole of God’s justice.

A righteous man who perishes. Proverbs teaches that, as a rule, the righteous do well. In his own breath of a life (“vain” is hebel again), the Preacher has seen the exceptions. A righteous man dies young in his righteousness, while still living rightly; a wicked man lives to ninety.

Scripture does not hide it. “The righteous man perishes, and no one lays it to heart” (Isaiah 57:1). Asked about people killed when a tower fell, Jesus said, “do you think that they were worse offenders than all the others who lived in Jerusalem?” (Luke 13:4). Suffering in this life is not a precise measure of sin.

The righteous man who perished. The clearest case of all is the cross: the one truly righteous man perished in his righteousness while the guilty went free, and on the third day God showed that his story did not end there (Acts 2:23–24). Because he lives, the righteous who perish young are not lost.

verseByVerse.quote: Be not overly righteous, and do not make yourself too wise. Why should you destroy yourself? Be not overly wicked, neither be a fool. Why should you die before your time? It is good that you should take hold of this, and from that withhold not your hand, for the one who fears God shall come out from both of them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not try to secure your life by a show of extra goodness, nor give up on goodness and throw yourself into sin; the fear of God keeps you out of both ditches.

Be not overly righteous. This is often misread as “don’t be too religious”. It cannot mean that; Scripture never warns against too much real holiness. The warning is against a self-made righteousness, a performance of goodness that tries to force God’s hand and guarantee a good life. Seeing that the righteous sometimes perish (v. 15), a person might try harder, with stricter rules and more show, as if he could buy protection from trouble. The Pharisee in the temple prayed, “God, I thank you that I am not like other men” (Luke 18:11). That road breeds pride, exhaustion and harshness, and never reaches God.

Be not overly wicked. The opposite ditch. Having seen the wicked live long, a person might decide that goodness does not pay and throw himself into evil. That road also kills, for folly digs its own early grave.

The one who fears God. Hold on to both warnings (v. 18). The way between the ditches is not moderation, a little goodness and a little sin. The fear of God frees a person from both performance and rebellion. He does not try to earn God’s favour, which is given, and he does not despise it. He trusts God, obeys him in the strength of the Spirit God gives his people (Ezekiel 36:27; Galatians 5:16), and leaves the outcome with him.

Uncertain wording. “Shall come out from both of them” (v. 18) most likely means that the God-fearer escapes both ruinous extremes; some take it as doing justice to both warnings. Either way the fear of God, not a calculated balance, is the way through.

verseByVerse.quote: Wisdom gives strength to the wise man more than ten rulers who are in a city. Surely there is not a righteous man on earth who does good and never sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom is a strong defence, yet no one, however wise, is free of sin, so the only hope for anyone is mercy.

Not a righteous man on earth. Wisdom is a stronger defence than a council of ten rulers, and yet even the wise man sins. This is one of the clearest Old Testament statements that everyone sins. Solomon prayed at the temple dedication, “for there is no one who does not sin” (1 Kings 8:46). Paul gathered the Old Testament’s witness: “None is righteous, no, not one” (Romans 3:10). “If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (1 John 1:8).

The only hope. This is also why v. 16 matters: no one can be righteous enough to guarantee himself a good life. There has been one righteous man who did good and never sinned, and “by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19). His obedience is counted to all who trust him, and so failure is not the end: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).

verseByVerse.quote: Do not take to heart all the things that people say, lest you hear your servant cursing you. Your heart knows that many times you yourself have cursed others.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not hang on every word people say about you, for you know you have said such things about others.

Do not take to heart all the things that people say. A practical application of v. 20. People will say things about you. Go listening for every word and you will hear something cruel, even from someone who works for you. Before you grow indignant, remember your own mouth: your heart knows. Knowing your own sin makes you slower to be crushed by other people’s words, and slower to condemn them. “Judge not, that you be not judged” (Matthew 7:1). Grace received makes a thick skin and a soft heart.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–29 — Searching for Wisdom, Finding Sin
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The deepest search for wisdom ends not with the whole answer but with the truth about ourselves. The Preacher resolved to be wise, and found wisdom far off and very deep (vv. 23–24). Searching for the scheme of things, he found first a deadly trap, the woman whose heart is snares, from whom only those who please God escape (vv. 25–26), and then how rare uprightness is: one man in a thousand, and among the women none (vv. 27–28). His one sure discovery is the fall: God made man upright, but they have sought out many schemes (v. 29).
verseByVerse.theology: The deepest thing the search uncovers is the fall: God made us upright, and we made ourselves crooked.

verseByVerse.quote: All this I have tested by wisdom. I said, "I will be wise," but it was far from me. That which has been is far off, and deep, very deep; who can find it out?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wisest of men confesses that the full truth about life lies deeper than he can reach.

“I will be wise,” but it was far from me. Here is a confession from the wisest man in Jerusalem: the more he learned, the further off the full answer seemed.

Deep, very deep. Reality itself is deeper than he can plumb. Job asked, “But where shall wisdom be found?” and answered, “it is not found in the land of the living” (Job 28:12–13). Paul, at the end of his greatest argument, could only worship: “Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments” (Romans 11:33). The right response to a depth you cannot plumb is not despair but humility.

verseByVerse.quote: I turned my heart to know and to search out and to seek wisdom and the scheme of things, and to know the wickedness of folly and the foolishness that is madness. And I find something more bitter than death: the woman whose heart is snares and nets, and whose hands are fetters. He who pleases God escapes her, but the sinner is taken by her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Searching for the meaning of things, the Preacher first finds a deadly trap, the seductive woman, and only those who walk with God escape her.

More bitter than death. Once more he gives himself to the search for “the scheme of things”, the way everything adds up, and the first thing he finds is a trap. This is the seductress Proverbs warns against: “For the lips of a forbidden woman drip honey … but in the end she is bitter as wormwood” (Proverbs 5:3–4); “Her house is the way to Sheol” (Proverbs 7:27). Sexual sin promises sweetness and leaves a person caught in snares, nets and fetters. Many have found it more bitter than death, because it destroyed the marriage, the family and the name that death would have left intact.

He who pleases God escapes her. The escape is not cleverness but God: the one who walks with God is kept. And for those who have already been caught, the way back is open. Of people with just such a past Paul wrote, “you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 6:11).

What it does not mean. Not that women are the danger and men the victims: Proverbs warns its first readers, sons, and the same trap is laid by men. Some also see Folly personified here (Proverbs 9:13–18); either way the snare is sin, not womanhood.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, this is what I found, says the Preacher, while adding one thing to another to find the scheme of things— which my soul has sought repeatedly, but I have not found. One man among a thousand I found, but a woman among all these I have not found. See, this alone I found, that God made man upright, but they have sought out many schemes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Preacher’s long search found very few upright people and one sure fact: God made humanity upright, and we have turned aside into schemes of our own.

This is what I found. The narrator who frames the book speaks again (“says the Preacher”, as in 1:2 and 12:8). Looking for the truly upright person, he found almost no one.

Not a verdict on women. This hard verse is not the Bible’s verdict on women. The same wisdom literature says “He who finds a wife finds a good thing and obtains favor from the LORD” (Proverbs 18:22), and celebrates the excellent wife as “far more precious than jewels” (Proverbs 31:10). The Preacher is reporting his own search in his own world, and his real point is how rare uprightness is at all: one in a thousand is almost none. If the voice is Solomon’s, it is hard not to think of the thousand women he gathered into his household, who turned away his heart (1 Kings 11:3); a man who collects people will not find a true companion among them. The next verse makes clear that the problem he found is not one sex but the whole race.

Upright, but many schemes. Here is the one sure thing his search uncovered: the fall, our turning from God, in a sentence. Humanity, male and female, was created in God’s image and called very good (Genesis 1:27, 31). The Preacher searched for “the scheme of things”; what human beings have produced is “many schemes” for getting around God.

We bent it. The world is not crooked because God made it badly; it is crooked because we bent it. “Sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin” (Romans 5:12). That is humbling, and hopeful: what was made upright can be made upright again, and in Christ it is: “you are all one in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:28), men and women alike, forgiven and renewed.
