7.overview:
Where we are. The first half of the book ended with the question “who knows what is good for man” in a life that passes like a shadow (6:12). Chapter 7 opens the second half (7:1–12:7), wisdom for living when we cannot see the whole, and it begins with a string of “better” sayings.

The message. What is good for us is often the harder thing: facing death, hearing rebuke, waiting patiently, and accepting from God both the good day and the bad. Life here will not always reward the righteous, but the way through is neither a show of goodness nor a plunge into sin; it is the fear of God. And when the search for wisdom goes deepest, it finds that no one is righteous: God made us upright, and we have bent ourselves.

Why it was said. The Preacher’s hearers wanted life to work by formula: be good and prosper (see the introduction). He teaches them to live wisely when it does not, and to look honestly at themselves.

How the chapter makes its case. First, the “better” sayings (vv. 1–12): a good name, mourning, rebuke, patience, and wisdom that preserves life. Then the call to consider the work of God, who makes both the crooked and the straight, the day of prosperity and the day of adversity (vv. 13–14). Seeing the righteous perish and the wicked live long, he warns against two ditches, self-made righteousness and wickedness, which the God-fearer escapes (vv. 15–18). No one on earth does good and never sins, which makes us slow to be crushed by others’ words (vv. 19–22). Last, the search for wisdom proves too deep and ends with one sure finding: God made man upright, but they have sought out many schemes (vv. 23–29).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern and by the need the chapter exposes. The righteous man who perishes in his righteousness (v. 15) is seen most clearly at the cross, where the one truly righteous man died while the guilty went free, and God raised him. The verse that no one does good and never sins (v. 20) has one exception, and “by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19). Because of him, the day of death can be for his people better than the day of birth (Philippians 1:21).

For us. Go to the funeral, welcome the friend who tells you the truth, and stop pining for the old days. On the good day, rejoice; on the bad day, remember who made it. And give up trying to make yourself righteous enough to be safe: confess the schemes you have sought out, and rest in the righteousness of Christ.
7.theology:
Facing death and sorrow honestly produces wisdom (vv. 1-4; Ps 90:12; Matt 5:4); for believers, death is gain (Phil 1:21). God sovereignly ordains both prosperity and adversity (vv. 13-14; Lam 3:38) and works all things for good for those who love him (Rom 8:28).

The fear of God delivers from both self-righteousness and licence (vv. 16-18; Luke 18:11). All people sin (v. 20; 1 Kgs 8:46; Rom 3:10), and the only hope is God's forgiveness (1 John 1:9).

God created humanity upright, and humanity fell by its own schemes (v. 29; Gen 1:27, 31; Rom 5:12). The problem of sin belongs to men and women alike, and so does the remedy in Christ (Gal 3:28).
7.examples:
Then: Israel in the wilderness looked back to the fish of Egypt and forgot the whips, and the Pharisee in Jesus' parable thanked God that he was not like other men. Both show the follies this chapter warns against: nostalgia, and a righteousness of one's own making.

Now: faced with a party and a funeral on the same weekend, most of us would choose the party. Few of us have a friend who is allowed to tell us we are wrong, and many of us listen too closely to what others say about us.

keyVerse.quote: In the day of prosperity be joyful, and in the day of adversity consider: God has made the one as well as the other, so that man may not find out anything that will be after him.
keyVerse.note: The verse gives the chapter’s wisdom for days we cannot control. Prosperity and adversity both come from God’s hand, so the good day is to be enjoyed without anxiety and the bad day considered without despair. Because we cannot see what comes after, we are left to trust the one who makes both.

7.reflection:
Verses 2–4 say the house of mourning is better than the house of feasting. Why might facing death honestly make us wiser? How does Christ’s resurrection change what we see at a graveside?

“It is better for a man to hear the rebuke of the wise than to hear the song of fools” (v. 5). Who in your life is allowed to tell you that you are wrong? How do you usually respond when they do?

Verse 14 tells us to be joyful on the good day and to consider on the bad. Which do you find harder? What difference does it make that God has made both?

Verses 16–18 describe two ditches: a performance of goodness and a plunge into sin. Which are you more prone to, and how do v. 20 and Romans 5:19 free you from both?

8.title: The King's Word and the Delay of Justice

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — The Wise Man Before the King
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wisdom lives faithfully under earthly power while remembering the limits of all power. The wise man’s face shines (v. 1). He keeps the king’s command because of an oath sworn before God, does not walk out in haste or join an evil cause, and knows that the king’s word is supreme (vv. 2–4). Wisdom discerns the proper time and way, though the future is hidden and trouble presses on everyone (vv. 5–7). Yet no one, king or subject, can hold back his spirit or command the day of death, and wickedness cannot rescue those who serve it (vv. 8–9), for power over others so often does them harm.
verseByVerse.theology: Earthly rulers deserve wise submission, but every ruler stands powerless before death and before God.

verseByVerse.quote: Who is like the wise? And who knows the interpretation of a thing? A man's wisdom makes his face shine, and the hardness of his face is changed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
True wisdom is rare, and it shows: it softens a hard face and makes it shine.

A man’s wisdom makes his face shine. Few can truly interpret a situation, and the wise man’s wisdom shows on his face: the hard, set expression of anxiety or pride is softened. Many of us have met people whose faces have been made gentle by years of walking wisely with God.

Beholding the glory. Moses came down from meeting God with his face shining (Exodus 34:29). Paul says that something like it is happening to every believer: “we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image” (2 Corinthians 3:18). The wisdom that changes the face is finally the wisdom of knowing Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: I say: Keep the king's command, because of God's oath to him. Be not hasty to go from his presence. Do not take your stand in an evil cause, for he does whatever he pleases. For the word of the king is supreme, and who may say to him, "What are you doing?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Obey the king as part of your duty to God, without rash rebellion, for his word carries power; yet God alone is beyond all question.

Keep the king’s command. Obedience to the king is tied to God: obeying rulers is part of obeying God. In the ancient Near East a king’s officials swore loyalty to him in the name of their god, and Israel’s leaders did the same before the LORD: when Solomon came to the throne, the leaders and mighty men pledged their allegiance to him (1 Chronicles 29:24). A courtier who broke faith with the king broke an oath sworn before God, so he must not storm out of the king’s presence or join a rebellion (v. 3).

Good citizens. The New Testament says the same: “Let every person be subject to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God” (Romans 13:1), and “Fear God. Honor the emperor” (1 Peter 2:17). A Christian is to be a good citizen, not because rulers are always good, but because God ordains authority.

The limit. But Scripture marks a limit. When a ruler commands what God forbids, the answer is Peter’s: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego honoured Nebuchadnezzar and refused his idol: “But if not, be it known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods” (Daniel 3:18).

“What are you doing?” No one may question an earthly king, for a while; no one may question God, ever. Nebuchadnezzar himself learned to say of God, “none can stay his hand or say to him, ‘What have you done?’” (Daniel 4:35). Yet the King no one may question has shown us his heart in a Son who “came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45).

Uncertain wording. “I say” is not in the Hebrew, and “because of God’s oath to him” may be rendered “because of your oath to God” (ESV note): either God’s oath to the king, or the subject’s oath of loyalty sworn in God’s name. Either way, obedience to the king is bound up with God.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever keeps a command will know no evil thing, and the wise heart will know the proper time and the just way. For there is a time and a way for everything, although man's trouble lies heavy on him. For he does not know what is to be, for who can tell him how it will be?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom knows there is a right time and way to act, but none of us knows the future, and that uncertainty should drive us to depend on God.

The proper time and the just way. Wisdom knows not only what to do but when and how (“the just way” may be rendered “judgment”, ESV note): the right words at the wrong moment can be as foolish as the wrong words.

A time and a way for everything. This echoes chapter 3 with a weight added: man’s trouble (or “evil”, ESV note) lies heavy on him, for knowing there is a right time is not knowing when it is.

If the Lord wills. James draws the Christian conclusion: “you do not know what tomorrow will bring”, so “you ought to say, ‘If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that’” (James 4:14–15). Uncertainty is meant to drive us to dependence on the Father who knows the end from the beginning.

verseByVerse.quote: No man has power to retain the spirit, or power over the day of death. There is no discharge from war, nor will wickedness deliver those who are given to it. All this I observed while applying my heart to all that is done under the sun, when man had power over man to his hurt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one, not even a king, can hold back his last breath or put off the day of death, and wickedness will get no one out of it.

No man has power. The king has great power, but not this: no one can hold on to his breath or move the day of his death. “You have appointed his limits that he cannot pass” (Job 14:5). Death is a war from which no soldier is sent home, and wickedness, which won so many battles, cannot win this one.

No ransom. “Truly no man can ransom another, or give to God the price of his life” (Psalm 49:7). Only one man ever had power over the day of his death. Jesus said of his life, “I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again” (John 10:18). He entered the war that has no discharge and won it, “that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death” (Hebrews 2:14).

Uncertain wording. The word rendered “spirit” (ruach) also means breath and wind. The line may mean holding on to one’s life-breath, or, as a proverb, restraining the wind; either way, death is in view.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–15 — When the Sentence Is Delayed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Justice is slow, but faith knows how the story ends, and so it chooses joy. The Preacher sees wicked men who frequented the holy place buried with honour (v. 10), and notes how delayed sentence makes people bold in evil (v. 11). Yet against all appearances he knows that it will be well with those who fear God and not with the wicked (vv. 12–13). He does not pretend the meantime is fair: the righteous often get what the wicked deserve, and the wicked what the righteous deserve (v. 14). So he commends joy, God’s gift that goes with us in our toil (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: God's patience is not his indifference; judgment delayed is not judgment denied.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw the wicked buried. They used to go in and out of the holy place and were praised in the city where they had done such things. This also is vanity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wicked people may be buried with honour and praised by the very city that watched their evil, but the city’s verdict is only breath.

Then I saw the wicked buried. The Preacher pictures a funeral with honours for a man who had been a regular at worship, praised by the city that watched him do his evil. Every generation has heard the eulogy that bore no resemblance to the life.

God’s verdict. Jesus spoke of religious men who were “like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful, but within are full of dead people’s bones” (Matthew 23:27). The city’s praise settles nothing; God’s verdict does.

Textual note. Most Hebrew manuscripts read “forgotten” for “praised” (ESV note); either way, their end is breath.

Uncertain wording. This is one of the hardest verses in the book. Some take the second half to mean that the godly, who had gone in and out of the holy place, were forgotten, while the wicked were buried with honour.

verseByVerse.quote: Because the sentence against an evil deed is not executed speedily, the heart of the children of man is fully set to do evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When God’s judgment is slow, people conclude it will never come and grow bolder in evil; but the delay is his patience, calling them to repent.

Not executed speedily. When punishment is slow, people conclude it is not coming. The child who is never corrected and the fraudster who goes unnoticed for years both learn to go further. So with God: because judgment has not fallen, they assume it never will.

The delay is mercy. Scripture reads the delay the other way: “The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance” (2 Peter 3:9). To use it as permission is to be “storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath” (Romans 2:5). Is there a sin you continue in because nothing has happened yet? The patience is meant for you: turn now, and the mercy is there.

verseByVerse.quote: Though a sinner does evil a hundred times and prolongs his life, yet I know that it will be well with those who fear God, because they fear before him. But it will not be well with the wicked, neither will he prolong his days like a shadow, because he does not fear before God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
However long the wicked seem to prosper, faith knows that it will be well with those who fear God, and not with the wicked.

Yet I know. Now the Preacher speaks as a believer. He does not deny that a sinner may do evil a hundred times and still live long. Yet against all appearances, it will be well with those who fear God. This is not observation but faith in what God has said. “Tell the righteous that it shall be well with them” (Isaiah 3:10).

Like a shadow. Does v. 13 contradict v. 12? No: v. 12 is what is seen now, v. 13 how it ends. However long he lives, the wicked man’s days are an evening shadow, lengthening just before it vanishes. The dividing line is fear before God, not wealth or reputation. “Fret not yourself because of evildoers … For they will soon fade like the grass” (Psalm 37:1–2).

Well with them. Those who fear God and trust his Son will one day hear the King say, “Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom” (Matthew 25:34).

verseByVerse.quote: There is a vanity that takes place on earth, that there are righteous people to whom it happens according to the deeds of the wicked, and there are wicked people to whom it happens according to the deeds of the righteous. I said that this also is vanity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For now the righteous often receive what the wicked deserve and the wicked what the righteous deserve; faith does not deny it, but knows that the meantime is not the end.

The meantime. The Preacher does not let faith become a slogan that ignores the facts: the good man’s business fails and the crook’s thrives. Both are true at once: vv. 12–13 speak of the end, v. 14 of the meantime.

Not the end. Malachi heard people say, “It is vain to serve God”, and “Evildoers not only prosper but they put God to the test and they escape”; God answered, “Then once more you shall see the distinction between the righteous and the wicked” (Malachi 3:14–15, 18). Abraham said to the rich man in Jesus’ story, “you in your lifetime received your good things, and Lazarus in like manner bad things; but now he is comforted here” (Luke 16:25). The meantime is not the end.

verseByVerse.quote: And I commend joy, for man has nothing better under the sun but to eat and drink and be joyful, for this will go with him in his toil through the days of his life that God has given him under the sun.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because we can neither fix nor understand the world’s injustice, the Preacher deliberately commends joy in God’s daily gifts as the companion of our work.

I commend joy. After injustice, joy again, the fourth “nothing better” in the book (2:24; 3:12, 22). It is not a shrug but a deliberate choice in the face of everything he has described: receive God’s daily gifts with gladness, and let that joy go with you in your toil.

Joy as trust. Joy in a broken world is not denial; it is trust. The same God who will set everything right has given this meal, this work, this day. When Nehemiah’s people wept over their sins, he told them to eat, drink and send portions to those who had nothing, “for the joy of the LORD is your strength” (Nehemiah 8:10). “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I will say, rejoice” (Philippians 4:4).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–17 — The Work of God No One Can Find Out
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The search for wisdom ends in an honest limit: no one can find out the whole work of God. The Preacher has watched people toil day and night without sleep, and has applied his own heart to understand it all (v. 16). But three times in one verse he says that man cannot find it out: not by effort, not by wisdom, not by claiming to know (v. 17). This is not despair but humility. God’s work is bigger than any human mind, and what he has revealed is enough to live by.
verseByVerse.theology: We cannot understand all God does, not for lack of effort, but because we are creatures and he is the Creator.

verseByVerse.quote: When I applied my heart to know wisdom, and to see the business that is done on earth, how neither day nor night do one's eyes see sleep, then I saw all the work of God, that man cannot find out the work that is done under the sun. However much man may toil in seeking, he will not find it out. Even though a wise man claims to know, he cannot find it out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
However hard the wise may search, no one can find out the whole of what God is doing; we are to trust him and obey what he has revealed.

Man cannot find out. The Preacher returns to his search and to a race too busy to sleep. Then three times in one verse he says that man cannot find out the work of God. No effort will uncover its full meaning, and the wise man who claims to know is mistaken.

The size of God. This is not anti-intellectual but honest about the size of God. “Behold, these are but the outskirts of his ways, and how small a whisper do we hear of him!” (Job 26:14). The humble response is to rest in this: “The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children forever, that we may do all the words of this law” (Deuteronomy 29:29).

Made known in the Son. What we cannot find out, God has made known in his Son: “No one has ever seen God; the only God, who is at the Father’s side, he has made him known” (John 1:18). You do not need to understand God’s whole work to trust him and obey what he has revealed.

8.text: <sup>1</sup>Who is like the wise? And who knows the interpretation of a thing? A man's wisdom makes his face shine, and the hardness of his face is changed.<sup>2</sup>I say: Keep the king's command, because of God's oath to him.<sup>3</sup>Be not hasty to go from his presence. Do not take your stand in an evil cause, for he does whatever he pleases.<sup>4</sup>For the word of the king is supreme, and who may say to him, "What are you doing?"<sup>5</sup>Whoever keeps a command will know no evil thing, and the wise heart will know the proper time and the just way.<sup>6</sup>For there is a time and a way for everything, although man's trouble lies heavy on him.<sup>7</sup>For he does not know what is to be, for who can tell him how it will be?<sup>8</sup>No man has power to retain the spirit, or power over the day of death. There is no discharge from war, nor will wickedness deliver those who are given to it.<sup>9</sup>All this I observed while applying my heart to all that is done under the sun, when man had power over man to his hurt.<sup>10</sup>Then I saw the wicked buried. They used to go in and out of the holy place and were praised in the city where they had done such things. This also is vanity.<sup>11</sup>Because the sentence against an evil deed is not executed speedily, the heart of the children of man is fully set to do evil.<sup>12</sup>Though a sinner does evil a hundred times and prolongs his life, yet I know that it will be well with those who fear God, because they fear before him.<sup>13</sup>But it will not be well with the wicked, neither will he prolong his days like a shadow, because he does not fear before God.<sup>14</sup>There is a vanity that takes place on earth, that there are righteous people to whom it happens according to the deeds of the wicked, and there are wicked people to whom it happens according to the deeds of the righteous. I said that this also is vanity.<sup>15</sup>And I commend joy, for man has nothing better under the sun but to eat and drink and be joyful, for this will go with him in his toil through the days of his life that God has given him under the sun.<sup>16</sup>When I applied my heart to know wisdom, and to see the business that is done on earth, how neither day nor night do one's eyes see sleep,<sup>17</sup>then I saw all the work of God, that man cannot find out the work that is done under the sun. However much man may toil in seeking, he will not find it out. Even though a wise man claims to know, he cannot find it out.
8.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 7 ended with the Preacher’s one sure finding: God made man upright, but we have sought out many schemes. Chapter 8 carries on the wisdom for living in a world we cannot control, first at the court of a powerful king, then in the long wait for justice.

The message. Wisdom submits to rightful authority for God’s sake, yet knows that no ruler has power over the day of death. God’s judgment is slow, and the wicked often prosper and are praised, but his slowness is patience, not indifference: it will be well with those who fear God. So the believer receives God’s daily gifts with joy and trusts the God whose whole work he cannot find out.

Why it was said. The first hearers lived under kings whose word could not be questioned, and watched evil go unpunished, even honoured (see the introduction). The Preacher shows them how to live faithfully under power and through delay without becoming either rebels or cynics.

How the chapter makes its case. Wisdom brightens a face (v. 1) and keeps the king’s command because of an oath before God (vv. 2–4). The wise heart knows there is a proper time and way, though no one knows the future (vv. 5–7), and no one, not even a king, has power over the day of death (vv. 8–9). Then the Preacher sees the wicked buried with honour (v. 10) and slow justice emboldening evil (v. 11). Yet he knows that it will be well with those who fear God (vv. 12–13), even while the righteous and the wicked often get each other’s deserts (v. 14). So he commends joy (v. 15), and confesses that no one, however wise, can find out the whole work of God (vv. 16–17).

Where it leads. To Christ by the need the chapter exposes and by the character of God revealed in him. No man has power over the day of death (v. 8), but Jesus said of his life, “I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again” (John 10:18), and entered death to destroy its power (Hebrews 2:14). The delay that makes sinners bold is the patience of God, who waits so that many may repent (2 Peter 3:9) before the day he has fixed to judge the world by the man he has appointed (Acts 17:31).

For us. Be a good citizen for God’s sake, and know where obedience to God must come first. Do not mistake God’s patience for permission. And when you cannot make sense of the world, eat your bread with joy, and trust the God who has revealed enough.
8.theology:
God ordains civil authority, and believers submit to it for his sake (vv. 2-4; Rom 13:1; 1 Pet 2:13-17), unless commanded to disobey God (Acts 5:29). No one has power over death (v. 8) except Christ, who laid down his life and took it up again (John 10:18; Heb 2:14).

God's delay in judgment is patience meant to lead to repentance, not indifference (v. 11; 2 Pet 3:9; Rom 2:4-5). It will be well with those who fear God (vv. 12-13), though for now things are often the wrong way round (v. 14; Luke 16:25).

The full work of God cannot be found out by human wisdom (vv. 16-17; Job 26:14); what he has revealed is enough to live by (Deut 29:29).
8.examples:
Then: a courtier who stormed out of an ancient king's presence could lose his head, so the Preacher teaches patience and good timing before those in power.

Now: the same wisdom applies before a manager or an official, though few of us risk more than our jobs. And every generation has heard a eulogy that bore no resemblance to the life, or seen a fraud go unnoticed for years. The Preacher's word for such times is that God's slowness is patience, not indifference.

keyVerse.quote: Though a sinner does evil a hundred times and prolongs his life, yet I know that it will be well with those who fear God, because they fear before him.
keyVerse.note: Here the Preacher speaks as a believer against the evidence of his eyes. He admits that sinners often prosper for a long time, yet he knows how the story ends: it will be well with those who fear God. The verse holds the chapter together, explaining how the wise can submit, wait and even rejoice while justice is delayed.

8.reflection:
Verses 2–4 call for obedience to rulers for God’s sake, and Acts 5:29 marks the limit. Where do you find it hard to be a good citizen or employee? Where might faithfulness to God require you to say no?

“No man has … power over the day of death” (v. 8). How does Jesus’ authority over his own life and death (John 10:18) change the way you face yours?

Verse 11 says delayed judgment emboldens evil, and 2 Peter 3:9 calls the delay God’s patience. Is there a sin you continue in because nothing has happened yet? What would turning from it look like this week?

After facing injustice he cannot fix, the Preacher commends joy (v. 15). How can joy in God’s ordinary gifts be an act of trust rather than denial? Where could you practise it this week?

9.title: One Event for All, and Bread Eaten with Joy

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Same Event Happens to All
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The righteous are safe in God’s hand, yet death comes to everyone alike, and while there is life there is still hope. The Preacher holds on to God’s keeping, but admits that no one can read God’s love or hate from events (v. 1). The same event, death, comes to the righteous and the wicked, the worshipper and the scoffer, and behind it lies the evil and madness of the human heart (vv. 2–3). Yet a living dog is better than a dead lion: the living can still act, while the dead have no more share in anything done under the sun (vv. 4–6).
verseByVerse.theology: Circumstances cannot tell you whether God loves you; death comes to all; and life, while it lasts, is hope.

verseByVerse.quote: But all this I laid to heart, examining it all, how the righteous and the wise and their deeds are in the hand of God. Whether it is love or hate, man does not know; both are before him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The righteous and their deeds are safe in God’s hand, but no one can read from his circumstances whether God’s face toward him is love or hate.

In the hand of God. After confessing that no one can find out the work of God (8:17), the Preacher holds on to one thing: the righteous are in the hand of God. That is the believer’s security when nothing else is clear. Jesus said of his sheep, “no one is able to snatch them out of the Father’s hand” (John 10:29).

Whether it is love or hate, man does not know. But he adds a hard truth: you cannot read God’s heart toward you from your circumstances. A promotion is not proof of his favour; a diagnosis is not proof of his anger. Everything ahead is in his view, not ours.

Look to the cross. So the believer does not look to his circumstances to learn whether God loves him. He looks to the cross, where God proved it: “God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew is brief: literally, both love and hate man does not know; all is before them. Most take it, as here, of God’s favour or disfavour, which events do not reveal. Some take it of human love and hate, which no one can foresee in himself or others (compare v. 6). Either way, the future lies before God and not before us.

verseByVerse.quote: It is the same for all, since the same event happens to the righteous and the wicked, to the good and the evil, to the clean and the unclean, to him who sacrifices and him who does not sacrifice. As the good one is, so is the sinner, and he who swears is as he who shuns an oath. This is an evil in all that is done under the sun, that the same event happens to all. Also, the hearts of the children of man are full of evil, and madness is in their hearts while they live, and after that they go to the dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Death comes to everyone alike, the godly and the ungodly, and behind it lies the evil in every human heart.

The same event. The event is death, and six pairs show that it comes to everyone: the hearse comes for the worshipper and the scoffer alike.

Full of evil. Death is an evil, not natural or friendly. And he names a second evil, inside the heart, which is why death comes to all: “The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick” (Jeremiah 17:9). Madness while we live, and then the grave: that is the human race left to itself, without God’s rescue.

What it does not mean. Not that there is no difference between the righteous and the wicked, but that death does not show it. God “makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good” (Matthew 5:45), and he lets the shadow of death fall on both. The difference will be shown on the other side.

Textual note. “And the evil” (v. 2) comes from ancient translations; the Hebrew lacks it (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: But he who is joined with all the living has hope, for a living dog is better than a dead lion. For the living know that they will die, but the dead know nothing, and they have no more reward, for the memory of them is forgotten. Their love and their hate and their envy have already perished, and forever they have no more share in all that is done under the sun.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While there is life there is hope; the dead have no more share in anything done under the sun.

A living dog. Dogs were despised scavengers; David called himself “a dead dog” to show how low he was (1 Samuel 24:14). Lions were the kings of beasts. Yet a living dog is better off, because while there is life there is hope: the living at least know that they will die, and can act on it.

Not too late. This is a word to anyone who feels like the dog. While you are alive, it is not too late to repent and begin again with God. The thief on the cross had hours left, and they were enough.

Is the soul asleep? Are the dead unconscious, the soul asleep until the resurrection? Some sincere Christians read it so, because Scripture calls death a sleep (1 Thessalonians 4:13); but that word describes how death looks from this side, and the certainty of waking. The key is the last phrase: “they have no more share in all that is done under the sun.” The Preacher speaks of the dead in relation to this world: they know nothing of it, earn nothing in it, love and hate nothing in it. What lies beyond, the New Testament makes clear. Jesus told of a poor man who “was carried by the angels to Abraham’s side”, and a rich man fully conscious “in Hades” (Luke 16:22–23). Paul longed “to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better” (Philippians 1:23). “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord”, “that they may rest from their labors, for their deeds follow them!” (Revelation 14:13). Their share under the sun is over; their life with God is not. So this commentary holds, with the Westminster Confession (32.1), a seventeenth-century summary of Reformed belief, that the souls of the righteous are received at death into the presence of God, while their bodies rest until the resurrection.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–10 — Go, Eat Your Bread with Joy
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because life is short and God is its giver, the Preacher commands wholehearted joy. Eat your bread and drink your wine gladly, for God has already approved what you do (v. 7). Dress for a feast, with white garments and oil on your head (v. 8). Enjoy life with the husband or wife you love, your portion in a fleeting life (v. 9). And whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your might, because the grave ends all work (v. 10). Death is not a reason to stop living but a reason to live fully now.
verseByVerse.theology: Life is short and death is certain, so receive each day's gifts gladly and work at each day's task wholeheartedly.

verseByVerse.quote: Go, eat your bread with joy, and drink your wine with a merry heart, for God has already approved what you do. Let your garments be always white. Let not oil be lacking on your head.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since life is short and God is its giver, eat and drink gladly and live festively, as people whom God has already accepted.

Go, eat your bread with joy. This is the fullest of the book’s calls to joy, and it comes straight after death: the shortness of life is a reason to take each meal as a gift.

God has already approved what you do. The person who fears God need not eat his supper wondering whether God frowns on his enjoying it. God gave it, and is pleased when it is received gladly. For the Christian the root goes deeper: he does not work to win God’s approval; he lives from it. “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). You can enjoy your bread tonight because God has already given his verdict on you: no condemnation.

Let your garments be always white. White garments and oil on the head were how people dressed for a feast: “You anoint my head with oil; my cup overflows” (Psalm 23:5). Live festively: not in excess, but in gladness. Many Christians have also heard an echo of the risen Christ’s promise that his faithful people “will walk with me in white” (Revelation 3:4), a feast begun in faith here that will go on for ever.

How do I eat my bread with joy? Receiving joy at the table can become a habit. Stop and thank him. A short grace is the moment you notice who gave the meal. Be there. Put the phone away, taste what is in front of you, and enjoy the people around it. Share it. The first Christians “received their food with glad and generous hearts” (Acts 2:46), and an extra place laid for someone who lives alone is the surest way to double the joy. Leave the guilt off the table. If you have confessed your sin, do not eat as if you were still on probation. Mark the feasts. Birthdays, anniversaries, the Lord’s Day: dress up a little, as the white garments suggest. The Son of Man “has come eating and drinking” (Luke 7:34), and at his own table he gives the bread and the cup as a pledge of the feast to come; every ordinary meal can be eaten in its light.

Wine. Wine is God’s good gift, to be enjoyed with thanks (Psalm 104:15), but never to drunkenness (Ephesians 5:18). Those who abstain for conscience or because they cannot drink safely are right to do so.

verseByVerse.quote: Enjoy life with the wife whom you love, all the days of your vain life that he has given you under the sun, because that is your portion in life and in your toil at which you toil under the sun.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Marriage is one of God’s best gifts in a fleeting life, so enjoy the husband or wife he has given you as your portion.

Enjoy life with the wife whom you love. Life is short; do not waste it in coldness toward your spouse. Proverbs says the same: “rejoice in the wife of your youth” (Proverbs 5:18).

Your portion. Your spouse is the share God has given you: not some imagined other person, but this one, and many marriages are poisoned by comparison. For Christians the pattern is higher still, a love first shown to us: “Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25).

In everyday life. When did you last simply enjoy your husband or wife, not as someone who helps you run the household, but as God’s gift?

And if you are single or widowed? The verse does not say that a life without a spouse is no life. Each person’s portion differs, and the same call holds for all: receive with joy the gifts God has given you, the friends, the work, the bread, and the Lord himself. Nor is the verse a call to endure abuse; anyone in danger at home should seek safety at once.

verseByVerse.quote: Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your might, for there is no work or thought or knowledge or wisdom in Sheol, to which you are going.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Throw yourself into the work in front of you while you can, because death ends every opportunity to work.

Whatever your hand finds to do. Joy in the gifts, energy in the work: the task in front of you, not waiting for a more important one. The reason is the grave: in Sheol, the place of the dead, “there is no work.” Jesus said, “We must work the works of him who sent me while it is day; night is coming, when no one can work” (John 9:4).

A second reason. “Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men” (Colossians 3:23). The dishes, the spreadsheet, the hospital shift: do it with your might, as service to Christ, who has already accepted you and gives his Spirit to strengthen the work.

Does this teach that the dead know nothing? As at verses 5–6, Sheol here is the grave as seen from this world: the work of this life ends there. It does not deny conscious life after death, which Scripture teaches plainly for those in Christ (Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ability does not guarantee the outcome, and no one knows when his time will come. The swift do not always win the race, nor the strong the battle, nor the wise their bread, because time and chance happen to them all (v. 11). From under the sun it looks like chance; the rest of Scripture shows God’s hand behind it. And like a fish swimming into a net, people are caught by evil times that fall suddenly (v. 12). The wise will be humble when they succeed, unembittered when they fail, and ready at every hour.
verseByVerse.theology: Ability does not guarantee outcomes; only God holds the times.

verseByVerse.quote: Again I saw that under the sun the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, nor bread to the wise, nor riches to the intelligent, nor favor to those with knowledge, but time and chance happen to them all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ability does not guarantee success; outcomes lie in a hand above ours.

The race is not to the swift. Five things we expect to follow from ability usually do, but not always: the favourite stumbles; the brilliant graduate cannot find work.

Time and chance. From under the sun, it looks like chance. Scripture shows what lies behind it: “The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD” (Proverbs 16:33), and “The horse is made ready for the day of battle, but the victory belongs to the LORD” (Proverbs 21:31). Not one sparrow “will fall to the ground apart from your Father” (Matthew 10:29). That frees us from two errors: pride when we win, as if our ability guaranteed it, and bitterness when we lose, as if no one were in control.

The lottery we call merit. Our culture says the race goes to the swift, and the swift deserve it. The Preacher has looked more closely. Who chose your parents, your country, your health, the teacher who noticed you at eleven, the interview that happened to fall on a good day? Warren Buffett, one of the richest men alive, has called it the ovarian lottery: much of what he has, he says, came from where and when he happened to be born. Once you see it, two attitudes look strange. The successful man who believes he made himself has forgotten most of what was given to him, and the man who failed and believes he deserved it has forgotten that chance fell on him too. Paul asked the proud Corinthians the question that ends both: what do you have that you did not receive (1 Corinthians 4:7)? The gospel goes further still. The greatest thing anyone can have, a place at God’s table, is given only to those who know they have earned nothing, and in that race the slow, the weak and the overlooked are welcome.

verseByVerse.quote: For man does not know his time. Like fish that are taken in an evil net, and like birds that are caught in a snare, so the children of man are snared at an evil time, when it suddenly falls upon them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one knows when his time will come; evil days fall suddenly, like a net on an unsuspecting fish.

Like fish that are taken in an evil net. The fish swims into the net without seeing it. So with the accident, the heart attack, the day of death.

The end of the age. Jesus used the same picture for the end of the age. In Noah’s day “they were eating and drinking and marrying and being given in marriage, until the day when Noah entered the ark, and the flood came and destroyed them all” (Luke 17:27). “Therefore you also must be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect” (Matthew 24:44). The only preparation for an unknown hour is to be ready at every hour.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–18 — The Poor Wise Man Who Saved the City
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wisdom can do what strength cannot, yet the world rarely honours it. The Preacher tells of a little city besieged by a great king and saved by a poor, wise man, whom no one remembered afterwards (vv. 13–15). So wisdom is better than might, though a poor man’s wisdom is despised (v. 16); quiet words of the wise are better than a ruler’s shouting (v. 17); and wisdom is better than weapons, though one sinner can destroy much good (v. 18). The last line prepares for the dead flies of 10:1.
verseByVerse.theology: Wisdom saves more than strength, and the world rarely thanks the one who saved it.

verseByVerse.quote: I have also seen this example of wisdom under the sun, and it seemed great to me. There was a little city with few men in it, and a great king came against it and besieged it, building great siegeworks against it. But there was found in it a poor, wise man, and he by his wisdom delivered the city. Yet no one remembered that poor man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A poor, wise man saved a whole city and was then forgotten: wisdom can do what strength cannot, yet the world rarely honours it.

A little city with few men in it. Parable or memory, the odds are hopeless, and the rescuer is not a general but a poor man with wisdom. Scripture has a real example: when Joab besieged the town of Abel, “a wise woman called from the city”, and “the woman went to all the people in her wisdom”, and the city was spared (2 Samuel 20:16, 22).

No one remembered that poor man. Then the sting: the saviour was forgotten. It is hard to read this story without thinking of another poor man. “Though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9). He came to a world under siege by death and delivered it, and he was “despised and rejected by men” (Isaiah 53:3). The Preacher did not have him in view, but the pattern he saw is the pattern of the gospel: “God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong” (1 Corinthians 1:27). The difference is that this poor man will not be forgotten. God has given him the name above every name.

verseByVerse.quote: But I say that wisdom is better than might, though the poor man's wisdom is despised and his words are not heard. The words of the wise heard in quiet are better than the shouting of a ruler among fools. Wisdom is better than weapons of war, but one sinner destroys much good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom is stronger than might and weapons, yet it is easily ignored and easily undone by one sinner.

Wisdom is better than might. Yet a wise idea from someone without status is ignored, and a foolish one from someone important applauded: that says something about us, not about wisdom.

Heard in quiet. The words of the wise are “heard in quiet”: loudness is not authority, so listen for the quiet voices.

One sinner. Wisdom is stronger than weapons, and one sinner can undo it. Achan’s single act of theft brought defeat on all Israel (Joshua 7:1). “Do you not know that a little leaven leavens the whole lump?” (1 Corinthians 5:6). It takes a lifetime to build what one act of folly can destroy, and the next chapter opens with the same warning.

9.text: <sup>1</sup>But all this I laid to heart, examining it all, how the righteous and the wise and their deeds are in the hand of God. Whether it is love or hate, man does not know; both are before him.<sup>2</sup>It is the same for all, since the same event happens to the righteous and the wicked, to the good and the evil, to the clean and the unclean, to him who sacrifices and him who does not sacrifice. As the good one is, so is the sinner, and he who swears is as he who shuns an oath.<sup>3</sup>This is an evil in all that is done under the sun, that the same event happens to all. Also, the hearts of the children of man are full of evil, and madness is in their hearts while they live, and after that they go to the dead.<sup>4</sup>But he who is joined with all the living has hope, for a living dog is better than a dead lion.<sup>5</sup>For the living know that they will die, but the dead know nothing, and they have no more reward, for the memory of them is forgotten.<sup>6</sup>Their love and their hate and their envy have already perished, and forever they have no more share in all that is done under the sun.<sup>7</sup>Go, eat your bread with joy, and drink your wine with a merry heart, for God has already approved what you do.<sup>8</sup>Let your garments be always white. Let not oil be lacking on your head.<sup>9</sup>Enjoy life with the wife whom you love, all the days of your vain life that he has given you under the sun, because that is your portion in life and in your toil at which you toil under the sun.<sup>10</sup>Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your might, for there is no work or thought or knowledge or wisdom in Sheol, to which you are going.<sup>11</sup>Again I saw that under the sun the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, nor bread to the wise, nor riches to the intelligent, nor favor to those with knowledge, but time and chance happen to them all.<sup>12</sup>For man does not know his time. Like fish that are taken in an evil net, and like birds that are caught in a snare, so the children of man are snared at an evil time, when it suddenly falls upon them.<sup>13</sup>I have also seen this example of wisdom under the sun, and it seemed great to me.<sup>14</sup>There was a little city with few men in it, and a great king came against it and besieged it, building great siegeworks against it.<sup>15</sup>But there was found in it a poor, wise man, and he by his wisdom delivered the city. Yet no one remembered that poor man.<sup>16</sup>But I say that wisdom is better than might, though the poor man's wisdom is despised and his words are not heard.<sup>17</sup>The words of the wise heard in quiet are better than the shouting of a ruler among fools.<sup>18</sup>Wisdom is better than weapons of war, but one sinner destroys much good.
9.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 8 ended with the confession that no one can find out the whole work of God (8:17). Now the Preacher turns to the one certainty left when all else is hidden: death.

The message. Death comes to the righteous and the wicked alike, and nothing in our circumstances tells us whether God smiles or frowns on us. Yet the Preacher’s answer is not despair but the fullest call to joy in the whole book: while you live, eat your bread gladly, love your husband or wife, and throw yourself into your work, because God gives these things and the day is short. And since outcomes lie beyond our control, wisdom is to be valued even when the world forgets it.

Why it was said. He speaks to people who expect life to reward the righteous visibly, and are shaken when it does not (see the introduction). He will not let them deny death, and he will not let death rob them of the gifts God gives now.

How the chapter makes its case. The righteous are in God’s hand, but love or hate cannot be read from events (v. 1). The same event, death, comes to all, and the human heart is full of evil (vv. 2–3). While there is life there is hope, for the dead have no more share in this world (vv. 4–6). So: eat, drink, dress for the feast, enjoy marriage and work with all your might (vv. 7–10). Yet ability does not guarantee success, and evil times fall like a net (vv. 11–12). A poor, wise man saves a city and is forgotten; wisdom is better than weapons, though one sinner can undo it (vv. 13–18).

Where it leads. To Christ by the need the chapter exposes and by the pattern it shows. The same event comes to all, and Christ entered it and came out the other side, so that for those in him death is no longer the end but the way to be “with Christ, for that is far better” (Philippians 1:23). The approval the Preacher’s joy rests on is made certain in him: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). And the forgotten poor man who delivered his city is a pattern that only Jesus fulfils, who became poor to rescue a world under siege and will never be forgotten.

For us. Do not read God’s love from your circumstances; read it from the cross. Then take today’s meal, marriage and work as gifts from a God who has already accepted you in Christ, and give yourself to them gladly, ready for an hour you do not know.
9.theology:
God's people are in his hand (v. 1; John 10:29), but his love cannot be read from circumstances. Death comes to all because human hearts are evil (vv. 2-3; Jer 17:9). The dead have no share in this world (vv. 5-6), but those who die in the Lord are with him (Luke 16:22; Phil 1:23; Rev 14:13).

Joy in God's gifts and wholehearted work are commanded, grounded in God's approval (vv. 7-10); for believers that approval rests on Christ (Rom 8:1). What seems chance is governed by God (v. 11; Prov 16:33; Matt 10:29). Wisdom saves, yet the world forgets its deliverers (vv. 13-15), a pattern the gospel echoes in Christ, who became poor to make many rich (2 Cor 8:9).
9.examples:
Then: a city under siege in Israel had no way out but surrender or rescue, and the Preacher's hearers would have known how quickly a city forgets the one who saved it.

Now: the brilliant graduate cannot find work, while a less able friend walks into a job. In the meeting, the quiet voice with the right answer goes unheard. And a Christian can sit down to supper tonight without wondering whether God is frowning at the enjoyment, because the verdict on him is already in.

keyVerse.quote: Go, eat your bread with joy, and drink your wine with a merry heart, for God has already approved what you do.
keyVerse.note: Straight after looking death full in the face, the Preacher gives his warmest command to joy. The ground of it is not the absence of trouble but God’s approval, and the gospel shows where that approval is finally secured: in Christ, in whom there is no condemnation. So the believer can receive the ordinary gifts of each day without guilt, as from a Father’s hand.

9.reflection:
Verse 1 says that love or hate cannot be read from circumstances. When have you been tempted to judge God’s heart toward you from what was happening to you? Where should a Christian look instead?

The Preacher answers the certainty of death with a command to joy (vv. 7–10). How can thinking honestly about death make us more grateful and more wholehearted rather than more gloomy?

“God has already approved what you do” (v. 7). What difference would it make to your meals, your marriage or your work this week to live from God’s approval in Christ rather than for it?

The poor wise man saved the city and was forgotten (vv. 13–15). Who are the quiet, overlooked people whose wisdom has helped you, and how does this story point us to Jesus?

10.title: Dead Flies and Sharp Iron

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — A Little Folly, and Folly in High Places
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A little folly spoils much, and folly in high places turns the world upside down. A few dead flies make a jar of perfume stink, and a little folly outweighs a great deal of wisdom and honour (v. 1). The wise heart leans the right way and the fool’s the wrong way, and the fool shows what he is the moment he walks down the road (vv. 2–3). When a ruler is angry, keep your place and stay calm (v. 4). Yet rulers themselves err: fools are set in high places, and slaves ride while princes walk (vv. 5–7).
verseByVerse.theology: A little folly spoils much, and a world where folly rules is a world turned upside down.

verseByVerse.quote: Dead flies make the perfumer's ointment give off a stench; so a little folly outweighs wisdom and honor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A small folly can spoil a great deal of wisdom and a good name, as a few dead flies spoil a jar of perfume.

Dead flies. Chapter 9 ended, “one sinner destroys much good.” Chapter 10 pictures it: a few flies crawl into a jar of costly perfume and die, and soon the whole jar stinks.

A little folly outweighs wisdom and honor. A pastor’s thirty years of faithful ministry can be overshadowed by one affair, and a businessman’s name for integrity by one fraudulent signature. A father may be patient for years, and his child never forget one explosion of rage.

Small compromises. The flies were small. Which small compromise are you tolerating because it seems too minor to matter?

If the jar is already spoiled. Reputation may take years to rebuild, and some of it may never come back. But the soul is not ruined beyond repair. Peter denied Christ three times and was restored by him (John 21:15–17). What folly spoils, Christ can forgive and make new.

verseByVerse.quote: A wise man's heart inclines him to the right, but a fool's heart to the left. Even when the fool walks on the road, he lacks sense, and he says to everyone that he is a fool.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wise heart leans toward what is right and the fool’s away from it, and the fool shows what he is in the most ordinary moments.

To the right. The right hand in Scripture is the hand of strength and favour (nothing to do with modern politics). The heart’s lean decides the direction of the whole life.

He says to everyone that he is a fool. The fool need not announce his folly; he walks down the road, and everyone can see it. “A fool’s mouth is his ruin” (Proverbs 18:7). Character leaks out in ordinary moments.

verseByVerse.quote: If the anger of the ruler rises against you, do not leave your place, for calmness will lay great offenses to rest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When someone over you is angry, do not storm off or hit back: a calm answer heals and settles great offences.

If the anger of the ruler rises against you. Counsel for anyone with a boss: when the person over you is angry, the instinct is to walk out or hit back. Stay steady. “Calmness” is in Hebrew “healing” (ESV note): a calm response heals.

A soft answer. “A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger” (Proverbs 15:1). “With patience a ruler may be persuaded, and a soft tongue will break a bone” (Proverbs 25:15). This is not cowardice, nor a call to stay under abuse. It takes more strength to stay calm under anger than to return it, the strength of one who knows that God, not the boss, holds his life.

verseByVerse.quote: There is an evil that I have seen under the sun, as it were an error proceeding from the ruler: folly is set in many high places, and the rich sit in a low place. I have seen slaves on horses, and princes walking on the ground like slaves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rulers err too, and the world is turned upside down when fools are promoted and the capable pushed aside.

Folly is set in many high places. Now the “error” is at the top.

Slaves on horses. Slaves ride and princes walk: the world is upside down. Isaiah pronounced it as a judgment: “I will make boys their princes, and infants shall rule over them” (Isaiah 3:4).

The Prince of all walked on the ground. See what Jesus did with the upside-down world. The Prince of all walked on the ground, and rode into Jerusalem not on a warhorse but on a donkey. “For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). The Preacher grieved to see princes walk like slaves. Christ, the true Prince, chose to walk as a servant, and so began to put the world right.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–15 — Risks, Sharp Tools and the Fool's Tongue
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Every task carries risk, wisdom is the sharpening that helps it succeed, and the fool’s tongue undoes him. The man who digs a pit or breaks through a wall, quarries stones or splits logs meets the hazards of his work (vv. 8–9). A blunt blade takes more strength, but wisdom helps one succeed, and skill is useless if it comes too late (vv. 10–11). The wise man’s words win favour, while the fool’s talk begins in folly and ends in madness, full of confident words about a future no one knows (vv. 12–14). His toil exhausts him, and he cannot even find the way to town (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: Wisdom sharpens the edge of ordinary work and guards the tongue.

verseByVerse.quote: He who digs a pit will fall into it, and a serpent will bite him who breaks through a wall. He who quarries stones is hurt by them, and he who splits logs is endangered by them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every kind of work carries its own danger, so do it with care.

He who digs a pit will fall into it. The pit, the snake in the old wall: every activity has its risk. Scripture often uses the pit for the wicked caught in their own trap: “Whoever digs a pit will fall into it” (Proverbs 26:27), and Haman was hanged “on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai” (Esther 7:10). But here the point seems wider: every job has its danger.

He who splits logs is endangered by them. The quarryman gets crushed fingers; the woodcutter a slipped axe. Wisdom does not remove all risk; it reduces it.

verseByVerse.quote: If the iron is blunt, and one does not sharpen the edge, he must use more strength, but wisdom helps one to succeed. If the serpent bites before it is charmed, there is no advantage to the charmer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom is like a sharpened blade: it gets more done with less strength, but only if it is used in time.

If the iron is blunt. Anyone who has cut wood with a dull axe knows this verse: you swing harder, sweat more, and get less done. Wisdom is the sharpening.

Working with a blunt edge. Many people are working harder and harder with a blunt edge, and the wise thing is sometimes to stop swinging. Rest, pray, learn, plan, ask advice. Time spent sharpening is not time lost.

If the serpent bites before it is charmed. The snake charmer’s skill is useless if the snake bites before he uses it. Skill must be used in time: the right word tomorrow does not help today.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 10 is among the hardest in the book, though the sense, effort against skill, is clear; the ESV notes that the last line may be rendered “wisdom is an advantage for success”. In verse 11 the charmer is literally the master of the tongue, which may be a deliberate bridge to the sayings about the tongue that follow (vv. 12–14).

verseByVerse.quote: The words of a wise man's mouth win him favor, but the lips of a fool consume him. The beginning of the words of his mouth is foolishness, and the end of his talk is evil madness. A fool multiplies words, though no man knows what is to be, and who can tell him what will be after him?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wise man’s words win him favour, but the fool talks himself into ruin, pouring out confident words about a future no one knows.

The words of a wise man’s mouth. The wise man’s words “win him favor”, or “are gracious” (ESV note). The fool’s “consume him”: he talks himself into trouble. “Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt” (Colossians 4:6).

From foolishness to madness. It gets worse the longer it goes on. “When words are many, transgression is not lacking” (Proverbs 10:19). Anyone who has watched an argument escalate has seen it.

A fool multiplies words. The fool talks endlessly about the future as if he knew it: the predictions, the plans, the confident forecasts. But no one knows what is to be. James calls the tongue “a fire” (James 3:6), and Jesus warned that “on the day of judgment people will give account for every careless word they speak” (Matthew 12:36). How many of your words this week were about things you could not possibly know?

verseByVerse.quote: The toil of a fool wearies him, for he does not know the way to the city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fool wears himself out with work that goes nowhere, because he never learned the road.

The toil of a fool wearies him. A slightly comic picture: worn out, and he cannot even find the road into town.

The way to the city. It is possible to be busy all day and get nowhere because you never asked where you were going. The Preacher means plain good sense, but Christians may add a further thought: the road to the city that matters most is not hidden. The one who said “I am the way” (John 14:6) leads his people to “the city that is to come” (Hebrews 13:14).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–20 — Kings, Sloth, Money and the Whispered Curse
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The welfare of a land and a home depends on self-control, diligence and guarded speech. A land is cursed when its king is immature and its princes feast in the morning, and blessed when its leaders eat at the proper time, for strength and not for drunkenness (vv. 16–17). Sloth lets the roof sink and the house leak (v. 18). Bread, wine and money have their uses, but money cannot answer everything (v. 19). And do not curse the king or the rich even in private, for words find their way out (v. 20).
verseByVerse.theology: Self-control in those who lead, diligence in those who work, and restraint in what we say in private.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to you, O land, when your king is a child, and your princes feast in the morning! Happy are you, O land, when your king is the son of the nobility, and your princes feast at the proper time, for strength, and not for drunkenness!
verseByVerse.commentary:
A land suffers when its leaders indulge themselves and is blessed when they eat and drink with self-control.

Woe to you, O land. The king is immature and his officials are drinking at breakfast. “Woe to those who rise early in the morning, that they may run after strong drink” (Isaiah 5:11). When leaders indulge themselves, the people pay.

Happy are you. Feasting is not wrong; eating is for strength. But “It is not for kings to drink wine”, “lest they drink and forget what has been decreed” (Proverbs 31:4–5). Self-control in leaders blesses a whole people, and the same applies to anyone who leads a family or a church. Such self-control is the Spirit’s fruit, not mere willpower: “do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit” (Ephesians 5:18).

Uncertain wording. The word for “child” (v. 16) can also mean a servant, and the contrast with “the son of the nobility”, literally a son of free men (v. 17), has led some to think of an upstart of low birth, like the slaves on horses of verse 7. Others take it of a king who is young or immature. Either way the problem is the same: a ruler unfit to rule.

verseByVerse.quote: Through sloth the roof sinks in, and through indolence the house leaks. Bread is made for laughter, and wine gladdens life, and money answers everything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Neglect brings slow ruin, and money, useful as it is, cannot answer everything.

Through sloth the roof sinks in. A tile slips and is not replaced; years later the ceiling collapses. Sloth works slowly, and its results arrive suddenly. The sluggard’s vineyard in Proverbs was “all overgrown with thorns”, and “its stone wall was broken down” (Proverbs 24:31). Marriages and souls fall the same way, through the neglected prayer life and the conflict never addressed.

Money answers everything. In context this sounds like the careless princes speaking, and it is partly true: money solves many practical problems. But the book has shown what money cannot answer: “He who loves money will not be satisfied with money” (5:10), and it cannot buy the power to enjoy (6:2). Money answers everything except the questions that matter most.

verseByVerse.quote: Even in your thoughts, do not curse the king, nor in your bedroom curse the rich, for a bird of the air will carry your voice, or some winged creature tell the matter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not curse those over you even in private, for words get out, and God hears every one.

Do not curse the king. Words spoken in private get out. But the verse goes deeper than caution: the curse begins in the heart before it reaches the lips. Scripture commands honour for those in authority: “You shall not revile God, nor curse a ruler of your people” (Exodus 22:28). This does not forbid honest criticism or opposition to injustice. It forbids the private contempt that poisons the one who nurses it.

One listener. There is one listener no one can hide from. Jesus said, “whatever you have said in the dark shall be heard in the light” (Luke 12:3). Speak in private as you would if the one you speak of were in the room, because the one who judges all things always is.
