10.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 9 ended with a warning: wisdom is better than weapons, “but one sinner destroys much good” (9:18). Chapter 10 takes up that warning in a string of short, sharp sayings, much like a page of Proverbs.

The message. A little folly does great damage, and wisdom, though it guarantees nothing in an uncertain world, is still the better way to live. It shows in everyday things: how you answer an angry boss, how you handle an axe, how much you talk, how leaders eat and drink, whether you mend the roof, what you say in private. God cares about ordinary life, and the fool and the wise man part company in its small choices.

Why it was said. The first hearers lived under kings and officials who were not always wise, did dangerous manual work, and knew the power of gossip and loose talk (see the introduction). The Preacher gives them practical wisdom for living well in a world turned upside down.

How the chapter makes its case. A few dead flies spoil a jar of perfume, and a little folly outweighs wisdom; the fool’s heart leans the wrong way and shows itself on the road (vv. 1–3). When a ruler is angry, stay calm, though rulers themselves often put fools in high places (vv. 4–7). Every task has its risk, and wisdom is like a sharpened blade, but skill must be used in time (vv. 8–11). The wise man’s words win favour, while the fool talks himself into ruin and wears himself out without finding the way (vv. 12–15). A land is blessed or cursed by its leaders’ self-control; sloth brings the roof down; money has its uses and its limits; and even private curses are overheard (vv. 16–20).

Where it leads. To Christ by the need the chapter exposes and by the pattern of the wise king that only he fulfils. The chapter longs for a ruler who is no fool, whose princes feast “for strength, and not for drunkenness” (v. 17), and whose words are gracious (v. 12). Jesus is that King: people “marveled at the gracious words that were coming from his mouth” (Luke 4:22), and the true Prince walked on the ground as a servant (vv. 5–7) to set an upside-down world right. Where a little folly spoils a lifetime, he forgives and makes new.

For us. Watch the small things: the compromise you tolerate, the word spoken in anger or in private, the tile you have not replaced. Sharpen the blade before you swing harder. And when folly has already spoiled the jar, go to Christ, who restored Peter and still restores those who fall.
10.theology:
Small sins do great damage (v. 1; 1 Cor 5:6), and character shows in ordinary conduct (v. 3). Calm, gracious speech heals and persuades (vv. 4, 12; Prov 15:1; Col 4:6); careless words will be judged (Matt 12:36).

Wisdom does not remove risk but makes work effective (vv. 8-11). Leaders are to exercise self-control for the good of the people (vv. 16-17; Prov 31:4-5), and those under authority are to honour them, even in thought (v. 20; Exod 22:28). Christ, the Prince who walked as a servant, puts right the world’s upside-down rule (vv. 5-7; Mark 10:45).
10.examples:
Then: the Preacher's hearers knew the perfumer's jar, the woodcutter's axe and the flat roof that let in the rain, and he built his sayings from them.

Now: the same wisdom fits the office. It means staying calm when the boss is shouting, and stopping to sharpen the blade instead of swinging harder. It also means remembering that a complaint made in the car has a way of reaching the person it was about.

keyVerse.quote: Dead flies make the perfumer’s ointment give off a stench; so a little folly outweighs wisdom and honor.
keyVerse.note: The verse picks up the last line of chapter 9 and sets the theme for the sayings that follow: a small folly does damage out of all proportion to its size. It calls for watchfulness over small things, and it leaves us needing a Saviour who can make new what folly has spoiled.

10.reflection:
“A little folly outweighs wisdom and honor” (v. 1). Which small compromise might be the dead fly in your own life, and what would it take to deal with it now?

Verse 4 counsels calm when someone over us is angry. What makes that so hard, and how does knowing that God, not the boss, holds our life give us strength to answer softly?

If the iron is blunt you must use more strength (v. 10). Where are you working harder and harder with a blunt edge, and what would sharpening look like: rest, prayer, learning, advice?

Verses 12–14 and 20 are about words, spoken in public and in private. How do the gracious words of Jesus (Luke 4:22) both judge and reshape the way we speak?

11.title: Cast Your Bread upon the Waters

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Cast Your Bread, Sow Your Seed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because no one knows the future or the work of God, the Preacher calls for bold generosity and steady sowing rather than hoarding and waiting. Cast your bread on the waters, for it will return; give to seven, even to eight, since disaster may come (vv. 1–2). Some things are beyond our control, like rain and a falling tree, and the one who waits for perfect conditions never sows or reaps (vv. 3–4). As no one knows how life forms in the womb, no one knows the work of God (v. 5), so sow morning and evening and leave the outcome to him (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: Uncertainty about the future is a reason for generosity and diligence, not for hoarding and hesitation.

verseByVerse.quote: Cast your bread upon the waters, for you will find it after many days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Give freely in an uncertain world, for what is sent out in faith comes back, even if only after many days.

Cast your bread upon the waters. You might expect: since you cannot know the future, hold on tight. The Preacher says the opposite. Throwing bread onto water looks like pure waste, yet it returns. The person who holds everything close never sees a harvest. “Whoever is generous to the poor lends to the LORD, and he will repay him” (Proverbs 19:17). “One gives freely, yet grows all the richer” (Proverbs 11:24).

Nothing given in faith is lost. Jesus put it at its fullest: “give, and it will be given to you. Good measure, pressed down, shaken together, running over” (Luke 6:38). Some of the return may come only in eternity, but nothing given in faith is lost.

Uncertain wording. It is not certain what picture the Preacher has in mind. Many take it of generosity: what is given freely comes back. Others see sea trade, sending goods out on ships and waiting for the return. On either reading the point is the same: the one who risks nothing gains nothing.
verseByVerse.note: Probably a call to bold generosity or enterprise, trusting God with the outcome.

verseByVerse.quote: Give a portion to seven, or even to eight, for you know not what disaster may happen on earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because disaster may come, give widely while you can, rather than hoarding.

Give a portion to seven. Be generous widely. The world reasons, “Disaster may come, so hoard.” The Preacher reasons, “Disaster may come, so give while you can.” The verse can also be read as sensible advice to spread your risk; both senses fit a world where no one knows what is coming. Jesus said, “make friends for yourselves by means of unrighteous wealth, so that when it fails they may receive you into the eternal dwellings” (Luke 16:9). Money will fail. Use it now in ways that last.

How to do it. Generosity in an uncertain world is planned, not left to whatever is over. Give first. When the pay comes in, set the giving aside before the bills and the treats, as Paul told the Corinthians: “On the first day of every week, each of you is to put something aside and store it up, as he may prosper” (1 Corinthians 16:2). Spread it. Seven, even eight: your church, a mission, a neighbour in difficulty, a work whose end you will never see. Do not wait for certainty. If you hold back until the economy settles or the mortgage is paid, you will never give. Give gladly, and let it go. “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7), and bread on the water does not come back by being watched. The power for this is not a budgeting technique but the grace of the one who gave first and most: “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich” (2 Corinthians 8:9). Someone who has received that much can afford to let a portion go.

verseByVerse.quote: If the clouds are full of rain, they empty themselves on the earth, and if a tree falls to the south or to the north, in the place where the tree falls, there it will lie. He who observes the wind will not sow, and he who regards the clouds will not reap.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some things are beyond our control, so do not wait for perfect conditions before you act.

Where the tree falls. Full clouds rain, and a tree falls where it falls: we do not control them.

He who observes the wind will not sow. The farmer waiting for the ideal day never sows. There is always a reason to wait.

For the perfectionist. This is a word for the perfectionist and the procrastinator. The right time to have the conversation, share the gospel with your neighbour, or begin giving will never look perfect. “Let us not grow weary of doing good, for in due season we will reap, if we do not give up” (Galatians 6:9). What are you putting off until conditions are perfect?

verseByVerse.quote: As you do not know the way the spirit comes to the bones in the womb of a woman with child, so you do not know the work of God who makes everything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As no one can explain how life forms in the womb, no one can fathom the work of God who makes everything.

The way the spirit comes. The verse sets two mysteries side by side. No one can explain how life forms in the womb, how breath and bone become a person. And no one can explain “the work of God who makes everything.”

In the womb. Modern medicine can describe the stages of a baby’s growth in detail, and still marvel at it. The psalmist worshipped: “you knitted me together in my mother’s womb. I praise you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made” (Psalm 139:13–14). Jesus used the wind to describe the new birth: “The wind blows where it wishes”, “but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes” (John 3:8).

You do not know the work of God. You cannot calculate the outcome of your sowing. That is no reason to stop. It is a reason to trust the one who does understand.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that most Hebrew manuscripts read, “As you do not know the way of the wind, or how the bones grow in the womb”. The difference comes from one Hebrew word, ruach, which can mean wind, breath or spirit. Either way the point stands: life’s beginning and God’s work are beyond us.

verseByVerse.quote: In the morning sow your seed, and at evening withhold not your hand, for you do not know which will prosper, this or that, or whether both alike will be good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since you cannot know which effort God will bless, sow widely and leave the growth to him.

In the morning sow your seed. Sow widely, morning and evening. This is the principle of every faithful ministry, parent and worker: you teach the class, raise your children, pray for your friends, and do not know which of it God will make fruitful. Jesus said the kingdom is like a man who scatters seed: “He sleeps and rises night and day, and the seed sprouts and grows; he knows not how” (Mark 4:27). Paul said, “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:6). Sow; God gives the growth. That frees you from the need to see results, and from the despair of not seeing them yet.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Life and light are sweet, and the young are to enjoy them, remembering the coming darkness and the judgment of God. Light is pleasant to the eyes, and a person should rejoice in all his years while remembering that the days of darkness will be many (vv. 7–8). The young man is to rejoice in his youth and follow his heart, but to know that God will bring him into judgment for all of it (v. 9). So he should put away vexation and harm, because youth is fleeting (v. 10), and the next chapter will tell him to remember his Creator.
verseByVerse.theology: Joy and accountability belong together; youth is to be enjoyed before God, because it will not last.

verseByVerse.quote: Light is sweet, and it is pleasant for the eyes to see the sun. So if a person lives many years, let him rejoice in them all; but let him remember that the days of darkness will be many. All that comes is vanity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Light and life are sweet gifts to be enjoyed every year, with a clear eye on the dark days to come.

Light is sweet. So far the sun has been the ceiling over a weary world. Here it is simply lovely, morning light through a window, a pleasure from God the Preacher wants us to feel. “This is the day that the LORD has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it” (Psalm 118:24).

Rejoice, and remember. The remembering does not spoil the joy; it makes it urgent. People who never think about death waste their days, and so do people who think about nothing else. The Preacher asks for gladness and a clear eye.

verseByVerse.quote: Rejoice, O young man, in your youth, and let your heart cheer you in the days of your youth. Walk in the ways of your heart and the sight of your eyes. But know that for all these things God will bring you into judgment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The young are to enjoy their youth to the full, knowing that God will judge how they spend it.

Rejoice, O young man. His first word to the young is not “be careful” but “Rejoice”. God is not the enemy of youthful energy, adventure and delight.

Is that not dangerous? Moses warned Israel “not to follow after your own heart and your own eyes” (Numbers 15:39). The difference is in the next sentence, about judgment, which controls everything before it.

Into judgment. This is not a threat that cancels the joy. It is what makes the joy safe: the young person who knows he will stand before God enjoys life in ways he will not be ashamed of. “So then each of us will give an account of himself to God” (Romans 14:12). “So flee youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace” (2 Timothy 2:22). For the young believer, the judge is the one who died for him: “whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life. He does not come into judgment” (John 5:24). He can enjoy his youth without dread, and where he has wasted it, there is forgiveness to come back to.

Joy and judgment together. Joy with no thought of judgment turns into doing whatever we like; judgment without joy becomes grim religion. The Preacher holds them together.

verseByVerse.quote: Remove vexation from your heart, and put away pain from your body, for youth and the dawn of life are vanity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Put away whatever spoils your youth, because youth passes quickly.

Remove vexation from your heart. Get rid of what spoils youth: anxieties that eat at the heart, and the sins that damage the body (“pain” may be rendered “evil”, ESV note).

Youth and the dawn of life are vanity. The word is hebel again, breath: youth is not worthless, but it is fleeting, and passes faster than anyone at twenty can believe. “The glory of young men is their strength” (Proverbs 20:29), and strength does not last.

Leading into chapter 12. This leads straight into the great poem of chapter 12, and its first word: “Remember”. The best use of a fleeting youth is to give it to the God who will not pass away. “It is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth” (Lamentations 3:27).

11.text: <sup>1</sup>Cast your bread upon the waters, for you will find it after many days.<sup>2</sup>Give a portion to seven, or even to eight, for you know not what disaster may happen on earth.<sup>3</sup>If the clouds are full of rain, they empty themselves on the earth, and if a tree falls to the south or to the north, in the place where the tree falls, there it will lie.<sup>4</sup>He who observes the wind will not sow, and he who regards the clouds will not reap.<sup>5</sup>As you do not know the way the spirit comes to the bones in the womb of a woman with child, so you do not know the work of God who makes everything.<sup>6</sup>In the morning sow your seed, and at evening withhold not your hand, for you do not know which will prosper, this or that, or whether both alike will be good.<sup>7</sup>Light is sweet, and it is pleasant for the eyes to see the sun.<sup>8</sup>So if a person lives many years, let him rejoice in them all; but let him remember that the days of darkness will be many. All that comes is vanity.<sup>9</sup>Rejoice, O young man, in your youth, and let your heart cheer you in the days of your youth. Walk in the ways of your heart and the sight of your eyes. But know that for all these things God will bring you into judgment.<sup>10</sup>Remove vexation from your heart, and put away pain from your body, for youth and the dawn of life are vanity.
11.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 10 gave short sayings for daily life in an upside-down world. Now the book turns from observing to acting, and moves toward its close: from here to 12:7 the Preacher speaks directly to his hearers, and especially to the young.

The message. You cannot know the future or understand the work of God, but that is no reason to hoard, wait or hold back. Give generously, sow steadily and leave the outcome to God. And while you are young, enjoy the light and the life he gives, wholeheartedly and without fear, as someone who knows that God will bring every life into judgment.

Why it was said. The Preacher has shown that the future is hidden and that disaster can fall at any time (see the introduction). His hearers might draw the wrong lesson: clutch what you have, wait until it is safe, or grab every pleasure before it is gone. He answers both fear and recklessness.

How the chapter makes its case. Cast your bread on the waters and give a portion to seven or eight, because you do not know what disaster may come (vv. 1–2). Clouds rain and trees fall where they will, and the farmer who waits for perfect weather never sows (vv. 3–4). As no one understands how life forms in the womb, no one understands the work of God, so sow morning and evening and let God decide what prospers (vv. 5–6). Light is sweet: rejoice in every year, remembering the dark days to come (vv. 7–8). Rejoice in your youth, knowing that God will judge (v. 9), and put away what spoils it, for youth is fleeting (v. 10).

Where it leads. To Christ by the character of God revealed in him and by the need the chapter exposes. The call to give freely reflects a God who gave first and most: “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9). The call to sow without seeing the harvest is the shape of Christ’s own kingdom, where God gives the growth (Mark 4:26–29). And the judgment that hangs over the young man’s joy is borne for believers by the Judge himself, so that whoever believes “does not come into judgment” (John 5:24).

For us. Do not wait for certainty before you give, serve, speak or begin. Sow widely and trust God with the harvest. And enjoy the light he gives today, young or old, as someone who will give account to a Judge who has already shown his mercy in Christ.
11.theology:
Uncertainty about the future calls for generosity and diligence rather than hoarding and delay (vv. 1-6; Luke 6:38; Gal 6:9). God's work, like the forming of a child in the womb, is beyond human understanding (v. 5; Ps 139:13-14); we sow and God gives the growth (1 Cor 3:6-7).

Joy in life is commanded, and so is remembrance of death and judgment (vv. 7-9). Every person will give account to God for how he used his youth and his gifts (v. 9; Rom 14:12; 2 Cor 5:10). Youth is fleeting and best given to God (v. 10; Lam 3:27).
11.examples:
Then: a farmer in Israel who waited for perfect weather would never sow, and a merchant who sent nothing out on the ships would never see a return.

Now: the Sunday school teacher rarely sees what becomes of the class, and the parent cannot tell which of a thousand ordinary days will bear fruit. The Preacher's counsel is the same for both: keep sowing, and leave the growth to God.

keyVerse.quote: Rejoice, O young man, in your youth, and let your heart cheer you in the days of your youth. Walk in the ways of your heart and the sight of your eyes. But know that for all these things God will bring you into judgment.
keyVerse.note: The verse holds together the two notes of the whole book, joy and the fear of God. The first word to the young is not a warning but a command to rejoice, and the reminder of judgment does not cancel the joy but keeps it clean. It also prepares for the book’s conclusion, where God will bring every deed into judgment (12:14).

11.reflection:
“Cast your bread upon the waters” (v. 1). Where is God calling you to give or serve without knowing what will come of it? What makes that hard?

The farmer who watches the wind never sows (v. 4). What good thing are you putting off until conditions are perfect, and what would it look like to begin this week?

Verses 5–6 say we cannot understand the work of God, so we sow morning and evening. How does that free parents, teachers and anyone who shares the gospel from the need to see results?

The young are told both to rejoice and to remember the judgment (v. 9). How can a church help young people hold these together, and how does Christ’s bearing of judgment for us make joy safe?

12.title: Remember Your Creator: The End of the Matter

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Remember Your Creator Before the Evil Days
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Remember your Creator while you are young, before old age and death come. The Preacher’s last poem paints the decline of age as a darkening sky where the clouds return after the rain (vv. 1–2), and as a great house falling into decay: trembling keepers, bent strong men, few grinders and dim windows, shut doors and failing song (vv. 3–4). The old fear heights, the almond tree blossoms and desire fails, because man is going to his eternal home (v. 5). Death comes as a cord snapping, a lamp breaking and a pitcher shattered, and the dust returns to the earth and the spirit to God (vv. 6–7). The opening verdict returns: all is vanity (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: The whole of life, from youth to the grave, is to be lived in remembrance of the God who made it and to whom the spirit returns.

verseByVerse.quote: Remember also your Creator in the days of your youth, before the evil days come and the years draw near of which you will say, "I have no pleasure in them";
verseByVerse.commentary:
Live now as one who belongs to the God who made you, while you are young, before the days of decline arrive.

Remember also. Chapter 12 continues the sentence of 11:9 with “also”: joy is safest and deepest when received from the one who made you.

What it means to remember. To remember in Scripture is to keep in mind and act on, as God “remembered” Noah and sent the wind (Genesis 8:1). To remember your Creator is to live aware that he made you, owns you, and has a claim on your days.

Your Creator. For eleven chapters the Preacher has said “God”. Here he says “Creator”, a word that reaches back to creation. The one who formed man from the dust (Genesis 2:7) is the one to remember before you return to it (v. 7). The Creator is not under the sun.

In the days of your youth. Now, not when you have settled down: the habits of a lifetime are set early. Those who give their youth to God have a lifetime of walking with him to draw on when strength fails. “O God, from my youth you have taught me”, “So even to old age and gray hairs, O God, do not forsake me” (Psalm 71:17–18). Timothy knew the Scriptures “from childhood” (2 Timothy 3:15).

How do I remember my Creator? Remembering God is a set of small, daily acts. Start the day with him. Before the phone, a few minutes in his Word and a prayer that hands him the day. Thank him for what you have been given. “I praise you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made” (Psalm 139:14); the energy, looks and abilities of youth are his, on loan. Let his ownership shape the big choices. Which course, which job, which relationship, what you do with your body on a Saturday night: “You are not your own, for you were bought with a price” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). Gather with his people. Weekly worship is how Christians keep remembering, and at his Table Jesus himself says, “Do this in remembrance of me” (1 Corinthians 11:24). Underneath all of it is a deeper remembering. The Word through whom all things were made took flesh and gave himself for people who had forgotten him (John 1:3, 14). We remember our Creator because he first remembered us.

If you are not young. The day to remember your Creator is still today. It will be too late only after death (v. 7).
verseByVerse.note: Verses 1–7 are one long sentence, a single picture of old age and death; its images are explained at verses 2-7.

verseByVerse.quote: before the sun and the light and the moon and the stars are darkened and the clouds return after the rain,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Old age comes like a darkening sky, when the brightness fades and troubles return one after another.

The clouds return after the rain. In youth the sun comes out after a storm; in age the clouds come back, one trouble after another. Scripture uses a darkening sky for the end of a world, and death ends each person’s world; but the point here is tender and personal: the brightness fades.

A light that does not darken. For the believer, there is a light that does not: “even to your old age I am he, and to gray hairs I will carry you” (Isaiah 46:4).

verseByVerse.quote: in the day when the keepers of the house tremble, and the strong men are bent, and the grinders cease because they are few, and those who look through the windows are dimmed, and the doors on the street are shut—when the sound of the grinding is low, and one rises up at the sound of a bird, and all the daughters of song are brought low—
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ageing body is pictured as a great house in decay: its keepers tremble, its workers fail, its windows grow dim and its doors close.

The keepers of the house tremble. Most readers have taken each image as part of the ageing body: the keepers are the trembling arms, the strong men the bent legs and back, the grinders the teeth, those at the windows the eyes.

The doors on the street are shut. The old go out less, and perhaps hear less; they chew little, so the grinding is low; sleep is light, broken at dawn by the birds; the singing voice weakens.

Why he writes this. Anyone who has cared for an ageing parent recognises every line. The Preacher does not mock the old; he writes so that the young will see where the road goes, and so that the old will know God has seen what they are going through and put it in his book.

Uncertain wording. The exact reference of the pictures is not certain. The reading followed here, the parts of the ageing body, is the oldest and most common. Others take them more literally, as a great household falling silent in mourning, or a storm darkening a town. Either way, the house is closing down.

verseByVerse.quote: they are afraid also of what is high, and terrors are in the way; the almond tree blossoms, the grasshopper drags itself along, and desire fails, because man is going to his eternal home, and the mourners go about the streets—
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the body fails, man is going to his eternal home, and the mourners are already in the streets.

The almond tree blossoms. The old fear heights, and the street that once was easy is full of “terrors”. The white almond blossom is the white hair of age. The grasshopper, made for leaping, drags itself along. Appetite, ambition and longing fade.

His eternal home. And the reason: “man is going to his eternal home.” The body’s house is failing because its occupant is moving house, while the mourners already wait in the streets (see Mourning Customs).

Renewed day by day. Paul saw the same decay and said something the Preacher could not: “Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4:16). “For we know that if the tent that is our earthly home is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (2 Corinthians 5:1). For the believer the eternal home is not the grave, but the Father’s house.

Uncertain wording. The grasshopper line may be rendered “is a burden” (ESV note), and the word for “desire” is the name of the caper berry, which was eaten to stir the appetite; either way the picture is of failing strength and appetite.

verseByVerse.quote: before the silver cord is snapped, or the golden bowl is broken, or the pitcher is shattered at the fountain, or the wheel broken at the cistern, and the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Death breaks precious and ordinary things alike, and then the dust returns to the earth and the spirit to God who gave it.

The silver cord. Four pictures of the moment of death: the silver cord snaps and the golden bowl of the lamp falls and breaks, the pitcher shatters, the wheel at the well breaks. Death breaks precious things and ordinary things alike, and suddenly.

The dust returns. Here the creation story runs backward. In Genesis, “the LORD God formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life” (Genesis 2:7). At death the two part again. The dust returns to the earth: “for you are dust, and to dust you shall return” (Genesis 3:19).

The spirit returns to God. This answers the question of 3:21, whether the spirit of man goes upward: the spirit returns to God. Death is not extinction. Every person meets his Maker.

A homecoming. For those who belong to Christ, that return is a homecoming. Jesus died doing what this verse describes: “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” (Luke 23:46). And Stephen, as the stones fell, prayed, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit” (Acts 7:59). The spirit that returns to God can return in trust, into the hands of a Father, because Christ went that way first.

verseByVerse.quote: Vanity of vanities, says the Preacher; all is vanity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The verdict on life under the sun has not changed: everything here is breath, so build your life on the one who is not under the sun.

Vanity of vanities. The book comes full circle, and the verdict has not changed.

The reader has changed. But the reader has. We have heard that God gives joy, makes everything beautiful in its time and has put eternity in the heart, that it will be well with those who fear him, and that the spirit returns to him. “All is vanity” now sounds less like the end of hope and more like a clearing of the ground. Everything under the sun is breath, so do not build your life on it.

Says the Preacher. The closing voice that frames the book speaks again, as in 1:2 and 7:27, and takes over for the book’s last words.
verseByVerse.note: A shortened form of 1:2, so that the same verdict frames the whole book.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–14 — The End of the Matter
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The closing voice commends the Preacher’s words and draws the conclusion of the whole book. The Preacher was wise and taught the people, weighing and arranging many proverbs, seeking words that were both delightful and true (vv. 9–10). Such words goad like a stick and hold like nails, and they are given by one Shepherd, so look for nothing beyond them; endless books and study only weary the flesh (vv. 11–12). Now everything has been heard: fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole duty of man, because God will bring every deed into judgment, with every secret thing, good or evil (vv. 13–14).
verseByVerse.theology: Everything under the sun is breath; the words of the one Shepherd are not, and they call us to fear God.

verseByVerse.quote: Besides being wise, the Preacher also taught the people knowledge, weighing and studying and arranging many proverbs with great care. The Preacher sought to find words of delight, and uprightly he wrote words of truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Preacher’s words were weighed with care and written to be both delightful and true.

Weighing and studying and arranging. The closing voice shows us the Preacher, the “Collector” of 1:1, at work: weighing, studying, arranging. Of Solomon it is written, “He also spoke 3,000 proverbs” (1 Kings 4:32). So Ecclesiastes is not a raw diary of despair but carefully crafted teaching. Every hard saying was weighed.

Words of truth. He wanted words that delight, but never at the cost of truth. This commentary holds, with the historic confessions, that Scripture as first given is without error: these are “words of truth” through and through. Truth without delight is hard to hear; delight without truth is flattery. The words of Scripture are both: “More to be desired are they than gold”, “sweeter also than honey” (Psalm 19:10), and “your word is truth” (John 17:17).

verseByVerse.quote: The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails firmly fixed are the collected sayings; they are given by one Shepherd.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wise words sting us into action and stay fixed in the memory, and behind these words stands one Shepherd, God himself.

Like goads, and like nails. A goad stings and keeps the ox in the furrow, and Ecclesiastes has been goading us for twelve chapters. Nails, once driven in, hold: years later a person remembers “Two are better than one”.

What the word of God does. The word of God does both. “For the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword” (Hebrews 4:12): it goads. “All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction” (2 Timothy 3:16): it holds us fast.

Given by one Shepherd. Behind the Preacher’s pen stands one Shepherd. Many wise men wrote; one Shepherd gave the words. This is one of the clearest statements in the wisdom books that these sayings come from God. “The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want” (Psalm 23:1). God promised, “I will set up over them one shepherd, my servant David” (Ezekiel 34:23).

The Shepherd come in person. The book that began with “the son of David, king in Jerusalem” (1:1) ends by pointing to one Shepherd, God himself, and the New Testament shows the shepherd God of Israel come in person. “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11). The wisest son of David collected sayings; the greater Son of David is the Shepherd who gives them, “the great shepherd of the sheep” (Hebrews 13:20).

Uncertain wording. “Collected sayings” translates a rare phrase, literally masters of collections (or of assemblies): the gathered sayings, or the wise men who gathered them. A few take the “one Shepherd” to be a human teacher; this commentary, with most interpreters, takes him to be God, the shepherd of Israel, set above all the wise.
verseByVerse.note: Goads were pointed sticks for driving oxen.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, beware of anything beyond these. Of making many books there is no end, and much study is a weariness of the flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The words given by the one Shepherd are enough; beyond them lies only endless and wearying searching.

My son. A father’s voice, as in Proverbs. Do not look for wisdom beyond the Shepherd’s words or against them.

Of making many books. Every generation writes more books on the meaning of life. This is not an attack on learning but a warning against the endless search that never arrives, the search of chapter 1 (1:18).

Not more books but the right one. What the soul needs is not more books but the right one, and the believer is freed from always searching. God has spoken, and “in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son” (Hebrews 1:2).

verseByVerse.quote: The end of the matter; all has been heard. Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole duty of man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When everything has been heard, the conclusion is simple: fear God and keep his commandments, for that is what human life is for.

The end of the matter. The hard questions and the calls to joy have all been laid out. Now, the verdict.

Fear God. Not “understand everything”, which the Preacher showed we cannot, but fear the God who does. The fear of God has been the quiet thread through the book (3:14; 5:7; 7:18; 8:12–13), and now it is the last word. It is where Proverbs began: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge” (Proverbs 1:7). Wisdom begins and ends in the same place.

And keep his commandments. Fear that does not obey is not fear of God. Moses said the same: “what does the LORD your God require of you, but to fear the LORD your God”, “and to keep the commandments and statutes of the LORD” (Deuteronomy 10:12–13). Moses spoke to a people the LORD had already set his love on and redeemed, and the order still holds, love first and then obedience: Jesus said, “If you love me, you will keep my commandments” (John 14:15), and John adds, “his commandments are not burdensome” (1 John 5:3). We never keep them perfectly (7:20). Christ did, in our place, and “by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19). And the Spirit he gives now writes the law on the heart and causes his people to walk in it (Ezekiel 36:27).

The whole duty of man. Rich or poor, young or old, this is what life is for; everything else is breath. After a lifetime of searching, the Preacher lands on something a child can understand. That is not a letdown. It is grace.

Is this salvation by works? Which commandments? God’s moral law, which still stands, and which we now read in the light of Christ. Obedience is the fruit of fearing God, not the price of acceptance; verse 14 shows why we need more than our own obedience, for every deed will be judged, and only in Christ can a sinner stand.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew is compressed, literally this is the whole of man. The ESV supplies “duty”, and notes that it may be rendered “the duty of all mankind”. Either way, fearing and obeying God is the whole of what a human being is for, and it is for everyone.

verseByVerse.quote: For God will bring every deed into judgment, with every secret thing, whether good or evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will bring every deed into judgment, even every secret thing, so nothing done under the sun is finally lost or hidden.

God will bring every deed into judgment. The final reason to fear God: everything the Preacher saw go wrong under the sun, the oppression with no comforter, the wicked praised, the poor wise man forgotten, will be brought before God (or “into the judgment on every secret thing”, ESV note).

The answer to the great complaint. Life is not lived only under the sun, and nothing is too small or too hidden. “Nothing is covered up that will not be revealed” (Luke 12:2). The Lord “will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness and will disclose the purposes of the heart. Then each one will receive his commendation from God” (1 Corinthians 4:5). So toil is not finally in vain; every good deed done in secret will be seen.

Who can stand? But the verse also leaves every reader exposed. If that is the last word, who can stand? The Preacher has already told us: “there is not a righteous man on earth who does good and never sins” (7:20).

Not the last book. So the book, for all its wisdom, cannot be the last book; it leaves us needing the gospel. God “has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed”, and has given assurance of it by raising him from the dead (Acts 17:31). He “judges the secrets of men by Christ Jesus” (Romans 2:16), and the judge is the one who bore the judgment for sinners. “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21). So Jesus can say, “whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life. He does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life” (John 5:24).

How the book ends. Ecclesiastes ends with judgment, and it is right to end there. Fear God, because he will judge. And then run to the Shepherd who laid down his life for the sheep, because in him “There is therefore now no condemnation” (Romans 8:1).

12.text: <sup>1</sup>Remember also your Creator in the days of your youth, before the evil days come and the years draw near of which you will say, "I have no pleasure in them";<sup>2</sup>before the sun and the light and the moon and the stars are darkened and the clouds return after the rain,<sup>3</sup>in the day when the keepers of the house tremble, and the strong men are bent, and the grinders cease because they are few, and those who look through the windows are dimmed,<sup>4</sup>and the doors on the street are shut—when the sound of the grinding is low, and one rises up at the sound of a bird, and all the daughters of song are brought low—<sup>5</sup>they are afraid also of what is high, and terrors are in the way; the almond tree blossoms, the grasshopper drags itself along, and desire fails, because man is going to his eternal home, and the mourners go about the streets—<sup>6</sup>before the silver cord is snapped, or the golden bowl is broken, or the pitcher is shattered at the fountain, or the wheel broken at the cistern,<sup>7</sup>and the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it.<sup>8</sup>Vanity of vanities, says the Preacher; all is vanity.<sup>9</sup>Besides being wise, the Preacher also taught the people knowledge, weighing and studying and arranging many proverbs with great care.<sup>10</sup>The Preacher sought to find words of delight, and uprightly he wrote words of truth.<sup>11</sup>The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails firmly fixed are the collected sayings; they are given by one Shepherd.<sup>12</sup>My son, beware of anything beyond these. Of making many books there is no end, and much study is a weariness of the flesh.<sup>13</sup>The end of the matter; all has been heard. Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole duty of man.<sup>14</sup>For God will bring every deed into judgment, with every secret thing, whether good or evil.
12.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 11 told the young to rejoice, knowing that God will judge. Chapter 12 finishes the sentence and the book: the Preacher’s last poem, his opening verdict once more, and the closing voice that sums up everything.

The message. Remember your Creator now, while you are young, before old age dims every pleasure and death returns the dust to the earth and the spirit to God. Everything under the sun is breath, but the words of this book are not: they come from one Shepherd. So the whole of life comes down to this: fear God and keep his commandments, because he will bring every deed into judgment.

Why it was said. The book was written for people searching for what makes life worth living, and tempted to put off God until later (see the introduction). The Preacher shows them where every road under the sun ends, and the closing voice tells them what to do about it.

How the chapter makes its case. Remember your Creator before the evil days (v. 1). Old age is painted as a darkening sky (v. 2), a great house falling into decay, its keepers trembling and its windows dim (vv. 3–4), and a slow walk toward the “eternal home” while the mourners wait (v. 5). Death comes as a lamp falling and a pitcher breaking, and the dust returns to the earth and the spirit to God (vv. 6–7). The verdict of 1:2 returns: all is vanity (v. 8). Then the closing voice commends the Preacher’s careful, truthful words, given by one Shepherd, and warns against endless searching beyond them (vv. 9–12). The end of the matter: fear God, keep his commandments, for God will judge every deed, even every secret thing (vv. 13–14).

Where it leads. To Christ by the character of God revealed in him and by the need the chapter exposes. The Creator to be remembered is the one through whom “all things were made” (John 1:3), who took flesh and remembered us. The one Shepherd who gives these words is the God who came in person: “I am the good shepherd” (John 10:11). And the judgment of every secret thing leaves every reader needing what only the gospel gives, for God “judges the secrets of men by Christ Jesus” (Romans 2:16), the Judge who bore judgment for sinners.

For us. Do not wait to remember your Creator; whatever your age, the day is today. Let the body’s wasting send you to the one who renews the inner self. Fear God and keep his commandments as a child of grace, not a wage-earner, and face the judgment sheltered in Christ, in whom there is no condemnation.
12.theology:
God is the Creator to be remembered from youth onward (v. 1). At death the body returns to dust and the spirit to God (v. 7; Gen 2:7; 3:19), answering the open question of 3:21; for believers that return is into a Father's hands (Luke 23:46; Acts 7:59; 2 Cor 5:1).

The words of the wise are given by one Shepherd (v. 11): Scripture is God's word, sufficient and final (v. 12; 2 Tim 3:16; Heb 1:2), and the shepherd God of Israel is revealed in Christ (John 10:11; Heb 13:20).

The whole duty of every person is to fear God and keep his commandments (v. 13; Prov 1:7; Deut 10:12-13). God will judge every deed and secret thing (v. 14; Rom 2:16; 1 Cor 4:5), and since none is righteous (7:20), the only refuge is Christ, in whom there is no condemnation (John 5:24; Rom 8:1; 2 Cor 5:21).
12.examples:
Then: the Preacher's hearers knew the great house with its grinding women and watchmen, the oil lamp hung on a cord, and the ox driven with a goad, and he used them all to speak of age, death and the word of God.

Now: anyone caring for an ageing parent will recognise verses 3-5 line by line. The young can give God their best years rather than their leftovers, and every reader can stop looking for one more book on the meaning of life and listen to the one Shepherd.

keyVerse.quote: The end of the matter; all has been heard. Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole duty of man.
keyVerse.note: This is the conclusion of the whole book, the answer to everything it has searched. After every hope under the sun has proved to be breath, what remains is to fear the God who is not under the sun and to obey him. It is where Proverbs begins and where Ecclesiastes ends, and in Christ, who kept the commandments for us, it becomes the glad obedience of forgiven children.

12.reflection:
“Remember also your Creator in the days of your youth” (v. 1). What would it look like for you to remember your Creator this week, in your habits, your choices and your worship? If you are not young, what does the verse say to you?

Verses 2–7 paint old age and death without flinching. How does this honest picture help both the young and the old? How does Paul’s hope in 2 Corinthians 4:16–5:1 change the way we face it?

The words of the wise are “like goads” and “like nails firmly fixed” (v. 11). Which words of Scripture have goaded you, and which have held you fast?

The book ends with God judging every deed, “with every secret thing” (v. 14). Why is that both a comfort and a terror, and how does the gospel answer it?
